- D (False) – SAFE (~7000 ICU patients) showed **no** difference in overall 28-day mortality between 4 % albumin and saline.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812; Finfer S, et al. SAFE. *N Engl J Med* 2004;350:2247–2256.

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock develops new atrial fibrillation on high-dose catecholamines. Which earlier choice would most likely have increased this risk?
options: Use of balanced crystalloids
Adding vasopressin
A MAP target of 80–85 mmHg
A MAP target of 65 mmHg
Starting vasopressors peripherally
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In SEPSISPAM a MAP target of 80–85 mmHg increased atrial fibrillation compared with 65–70 mmHg (~6.7 % vs 2.8 %), because more catecholamine was needed, without any survival benefit.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Balanced crystalloids are not arrhythmogenic.
- B – Vasopressin is catecholamine-sparing and, if anything, associated with less AF.
- D – A MAP target of 65 mmHg minimises catecholamine exposure.
- E – The route of vasopressor administration does not influence AF risk.

**Ref:** Asfar P, et al. SEPSISPAM. *N Engl J Med* 2014;370:1583–1593; McIntyre WF, et al. *JAMA* 2018;319:1889–1900.

questions.stem: Regarding SOFA-2:
options: Immune dysfunction is a new seventh organ system.
The coagulation system was renamed "hemostasis".
It was published in JAMA in 2025.
The CNS system was renamed "brain".
questions.expl:
- A (False) – Immune and GI dysfunction were **not** included; SOFA-2 keeps six organ systems.
- B (True) – Coagulation was renamed "hemostasis".
- C (True) – Published in *JAMA* in 2025 (Ranzani et al.).
- D (True) – The CNS system was renamed "brain".

**Ref:** Ranzani OT, et al. SOFA-2. *JAMA* 2025;334:2090–2103.

questions.stem: In the CLASSIC trial, the restrictive group received a median ICU IV fluid volume of approximately:
options: 6 L
500 mL
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In CLASSIC the restrictive group received a median of 1798 mL of IV fluid in the ICU vs 3811 mL with standard care, with similar 90-day mortality (~42 % in both arms).

**Why not the others:**

- A – 3.8 L was the standard-care (liberal) arm.
- B – 10 L is far above either arm.
- D – 6 L is far above either arm.
- E – 500 mL is too low; the restrictive protocol still allowed fluid for severe hypoperfusion, overt losses and dehydration.

**Ref:** Meyhoff TS, et al. CLASSIC. *N Engl J Med* 2022;386:2459–2470.

questions.stem: A patient has septic shock. Which statements about lactate are correct?
options: Adrenaline infusion may increase lactate independently of hypoperfusion.
Lactate > 2 mmol/L is part of the Sepsis-3 septic shock definition.
Serial lactate measurements are suggested to guide resuscitation.
Fluids should be continued until lactate normalises.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – Adrenaline raises lactate through β2-mediated aerobic glycolysis, independently of hypoperfusion.
- B (True) – Lactate > 2 mmol/L plus a vasopressor for MAP ≥ 65 mmHg despite fluids defines septic shock.
- C (True) – Serial lactate measurements are suggested to guide resuscitation when lactate is elevated (conditional, low).
- D (False) – Fluids should not be continued merely because lactate is not yet normal; capillary refill time is a useful adjunct (ANDROMEDA-SHOCK).

**Ref:** Singer M, et al. *JAMA* 2016; Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: The main reason dopamine is not recommended as first-line vasopressor is:
options: It is only available as an oral drug
It is ineffective at raising MAP
Higher arrhythmia rate and worse outcomes in cardiogenic shock (SOAP II)
It causes renal failure in all patients
It causes severe hyponatraemia
questions.expl:
**Why C:** SOAP II showed about twice as many arrhythmic events with dopamine (24 % vs 12 %) and higher mortality in the cardiogenic shock subgroup, with no advantage elsewhere. SSC therefore recommends noradrenaline over dopamine (strong, high certainty); dopamine is reserved for selected bradycardic patients at low risk of tachyarrhythmia.

**Why not the others:**

- A – Dopamine is an IV drug.
- B – It does raise MAP (α effect at higher doses); efficacy is not the problem.
- D – It does not cause renal failure; it simply offers no renal protection.
- E – Hyponatraemia relates to vasopressin, not dopamine.

**Ref:** De Backer D, et al. SOAP II. *N Engl J Med* 2010;362:779–789.

questions.stem: Regarding vasopressor administration and monitoring:
options: Invasive arterial monitoring is appropriate when vasopressor doses are high or escalating.
Optimal duration of peripheral vasopressors is well established.
Peripheral initiation of vasopressors is suggested rather than delaying for central access.
Extravasation should be monitored with peripheral administration.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – An arterial line is appropriate with high, escalating or multiple vasopressors, frequent blood gases or unreliable NIBP; otherwise SSC 2026 accepts invasive or non-invasive monitoring (conditional, very low).
- B (False) – Data on the safe duration, dose and route of peripheral vasopressors are insufficient.
- C (True) – Peripheral initiation rather than delaying for central access is suggested (conditional, very low).
- D (True) – With peripheral use, a large proximal cannula and regular checks for extravasation are needed; switch to a central line for prolonged or high-dose use.

**Ref:** Prescott HC, et al. Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026. *Intensive Care Med* 2026 / *Crit Care Med* 2026;54:725–812.

questions.stem: Which statement about balanced crystalloids vs saline is most accurate?
options: All large RCTs (SMART, BaSICS, PLUS) showed significant mortality reduction with balanced solutions
PLUS showed harm with Plasma-Lyte
SMART showed a reduction in the composite MAKE30; BaSICS and PLUS showed no significant mortality difference
Saline is preferred in all septic patients
Balanced solutions are contraindicated in hyperkalaemia
questions.expl:
**Why C:** SMART (15,802 adults) showed a lower composite MAKE30 with balanced crystalloids (14.3 % vs 15.4 %), whereas BaSICS and PLUS showed no significant 90-day mortality difference. This is why SSC suggests balanced over saline only conditionally (moderate certainty).

**Why not the others:**

- A – Only SMART was positive, and only for a composite outcome.
- B – PLUS showed no harm (21.8 % vs 22.0 %).
- D – Saline is preferred only in TBI.
- E – A myth: balanced solutions contain K⁺ (~4–5 mmol/L), but saline causes acidosis that shifts K⁺ out of cells, so balanced fluids do not worsen hyperkalaemia more than saline.

**Ref:** Semler MW, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2018; Zampieri FG, et al. *JAMA* 2021; Finfer S, et al. *N Engl J Med* 2022.

title: W02 · D1 – Antibiotic PK/PD in the critically ill and prolonged β-lactam infusion

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with polytrauma develops ventilator-associated pneumonia on day 6. Serum creatinine is 55 µmol/L. Measured 8-h urinary creatinine clearance is 190 mL/min/1.73 m². Which statement is most accurate?
options: He has augmented renal clearance and is at risk of subtherapeutic β-lactam concentrations
Aminoglycoside trough monitoring is unnecessary in this patient
Standard meropenem dosing will reliably achieve target concentrations because renal function is normal
The loading dose of meropenem should be reduced
The Cockcroft-Gault equation is the best method to detect this condition
questions.expl:
**Why A:** A measured CrCl > 130 mL/min/1.73 m² from a timed (8–24 h) urine collection defines augmented renal clearance (ARC); 190 mL/min/1.73 m² in a young polytrauma patient is the classic picture (ICU incidence 14–80 %). ARC accelerates elimination of renally cleared hydrophilic β-lactams, so trough concentrations fall below the MIC – manage with higher/more frequent doses or continuous infusion plus TDM.

**Why not the others:**
- B – ARC also increases aminoglycoside clearance, and routine aminoglycoside TDM is recommended regardless (efficacy and toxicity).
- C – a "normal" creatinine hides ARC; standard meropenem dosing frequently underexposes these patients.
- D – the loading dose is determined by Vd, not by renal function, and is never reduced.
- E – Cockcroft-Gault and other estimating equations do not reliably detect ARC; a measured urine collection is required.

**Ref:** Abdul-Aziz MH et al., Antimicrobial TDM Position Paper, Intensive Care Med 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding pharmacokinetic changes in septic shock:
options: The volume of distribution of hydrophilic antibiotics is typically increased.
The loading dose of a β-lactam should be reduced in acute kidney injury.
Aminoglycosides and β-lactams are lipophilic antibiotics.
Hypoalbuminaemia may increase the clearance of highly protein-bound drugs such as ceftriaxone.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – capillary leak, fluid resuscitation, oedema, drains and ECMO expand the extracellular space in which hydrophilic drugs distribute → low concentrations after the first dose.
- B (False) – the loading dose depends on Vd and is independent of renal function; only maintenance dosing is adjusted, and not reflexively in the first 24–48 h, as septic AKI is often transient.
- C (False) – β-lactams and aminoglycosides are hydrophilic (extracellular distribution, renal elimination); fluoroquinolones and macrolides are lipophilic.
- D (True) – hypoalbuminaemia raises the free fraction of highly bound drugs (ceftriaxone, ertapenem, flucloxacillin, teicoplanin) → larger Vd and faster clearance → low trough levels.

**EDIC trap:** early in sepsis the main β-lactam risk is underdosing, not toxicity.

**Ref:** Abdul-Aziz MH et al., Intensive Care Med 2020.

questions.stem: The pharmacodynamic index that best predicts the efficacy of meropenem is:
options: Post-antibiotic effect duration
Trough concentration relative to the toxic threshold
Cmax/MIC
AUC₀₋₂₄/MIC
Percentage of the dosing interval during which the free concentration exceeds the MIC (% fT>MIC)
questions.expl:
**Why E:** β-lactams (including meropenem) show time-dependent killing; efficacy correlates with the percentage of the dosing interval during which the free concentration exceeds the MIC (% fT>MIC). Classic animal targets were 40–70 % fT>MIC; for the critically ill the 2020 Position Paper proposes 100 % fT>MIC – the rationale for prolonged/continuous infusion after a loading bolus.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the post-antibiotic effect modifies dosing but is not the PK/PD index; β-lactams have little PAE against Gram-negatives.
- B – trough relative to a toxic threshold is a safety parameter (aminoglycosides), not an efficacy index.
- C – Cmax/MIC (≥ 8–10) predicts aminoglycoside efficacy.
- D – AUC₀₋₂₄/MIC is the index for vancomycin (≥ 400) and fluoroquinolones.

**Ref:** Abdul-Aziz MH et al., Intensive Care Med 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding the BLING III trial:
options: It enrolled fewer than 1000 critically ill adults with sepsis.
Piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem was given by continuous or intermittent infusion.
90-day all-cause mortality was significantly lower with continuous infusion.
Clinical cure was similar in both groups.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – BLING III randomised 7031 patients (primary analysis) in 104 ICUs, the largest β-lactam infusion trial.
- B (True) – piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem by continuous vs intermittent infusion, open-label.
- C (False) – 90-day mortality 24.9 vs 26.8 %, OR 0.91 (95 % CI 0.81–1.01), p = 0.08 – not significant, although the CI includes a clinically important benefit.
- D (False) – clinical cure was higher with continuous infusion (55.7 vs 50.0 %); new MDR colonisation/infection and *C. difficile* did not differ.

**EDIC trap:** BLING III was formally negative; the positive (Bayesian) result was the companion meta-analysis in the same JAMA issue.

**Ref:** Dulhunty JM et al., BLING III, JAMA 2024.

questions.stem: According to the 2020 ESICM/ESCMID-endorsed Position Paper on antimicrobial TDM, routine TDM in critically ill patients is recommended for:
options: Echinocandins and fluconazole
Only vancomycin and aminoglycosides
Daptomycin and polymyxin B
Aminoglycosides, β-lactams, vancomycin, teicoplanin, linezolid and voriconazole
Fluoroquinolones and colistin
questions.expl:
**Why D:** The joint ESICM/ESCMID/IATDMCT/ISAC Position Paper recommends routine TDM in the critically ill for aminoglycosides, β-lactams, linezolid, teicoplanin, vancomycin and voriconazole – drugs with highly variable ICU pharmacokinetics, defined exposure targets and/or a narrow therapeutic window.

**Why not the others:**
- A – for echinocandins and fluconazole (most antifungals) the panel neither recommends nor advises against TDM; voriconazole is the only antifungal on the list.
- B – too narrow: it omits β-lactams, linezolid, teicoplanin and voriconazole.
- C – daptomycin and polymyxin B: no recommendation for or against.
- E – fluoroquinolones and colistin: no recommendation for or against.

**EDIC trap:** "neither recommends nor advises against" is not the same as "recommends against".

**Ref:** Abdul-Aziz MH et al., Intensive Care Med 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding the 2024 JAMA meta-analysis of prolonged vs intermittent β-lactam infusion in sepsis:
options: It used a Bayesian primary analysis.
Prolonged infusion was associated with lower 90-day mortality.
The certainty of evidence for mortality was rated as high.
It included 18 randomised trials with over 9000 patients.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the primary analysis was Bayesian, reporting a risk ratio with a 95 % credible interval and a posterior probability of benefit (99.1 %).
- B (True) – 90-day mortality RR 0.86 (95 % CrI 0.72–0.98) favouring prolonged infusion.
- C (True) – certainty of the mortality benefit was rated high (GRADE); clinical cure also improved (RR 1.16) and ICU mortality fell.
- D (True) – 18 RCTs with 9108 patients, including BLING III; "prolonged" covered both continuous and extended infusion.

**EDIC trap:** K′ items with all four statements true do occur – do not force a "False".

**Ref:** Abdul-Aziz MH et al., JAMA 2024.

questions.stem: Which vancomycin target is recommended for efficacy in critically ill patients?
options: Trough 5–10 mg/L
Peak 40 mg/L
AUC₀₋₂₄/MIC ≥ 400
Time above MIC 100 %
Cmax/MIC ≥ 10
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Vancomycin efficacy is best predicted by AUC₀₋₂₄/MIC ≥ 400 (assuming MIC 1 mg/L). The trough is a poor surrogate for AUC, and targeting troughs of 15–20 mg/L increases nephrotoxicity without better efficacy; AUC-guided dosing (Bayesian or two-level sampling) is now standard.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a trough of 5–10 mg/L is too low for serious infection, and troughs are not the efficacy target anyway.
- B – vancomycin is not peak-driven; a peak of 40 mg/L is not a target.
- D – 100 % fT>MIC is the β-lactam target in the critically ill.
- E – Cmax/MIC ≥ 8–10 is the aminoglycoside efficacy target.

**EDIC trap:** "trough 15–20 mg/L" is the outdated answer.

**Ref:** Abdul-Aziz MH et al., Intensive Care Med 2020; Rybak MJ et al., ASHP/IDSA/PIDS/SIDP vancomycin consensus, Am J Health Syst Pharm 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding aminoglycoside dosing in the ICU:
options: Dosing in three divided daily doses is preferred to once-daily administration.
Efficacy is concentration-dependent.
A high trough concentration is the target for efficacy.
A Cmax/MIC ratio of about 8–10 is a commonly used efficacy target.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – once-daily high-dose (extended-interval) dosing is preferred: it maximises Cmax/MIC and allows a low trough, reducing nephro- and ototoxicity.
- B (True) – aminoglycoside killing is concentration-dependent.
- C (False) – a high trough predicts toxicity, not efficacy; targets are amikacin < 2.5 mg/L and gentamicin/tobramycin < 0.5 mg/L.
- D (True) – Cmax/MIC ≥ 8–10 is the usual efficacy target (alternatively AUC 80–120 mg·h/L).

**EDIC trap:** peak = efficacy, trough = toxicity for aminoglycosides.

**Ref:** Abdul-Aziz MH et al., Intensive Care Med 2020.

questions.stem: In BLING II (AJRCCM 2015), continuous vs intermittent β-lactam infusion in 432 patients with severe sepsis resulted in:
options: Higher rates of Clostridioides difficile infection with continuous infusion
A significant reduction in 90-day mortality
No significant difference in ICU-free days
Early termination for harm
Significantly more ICU-free days with continuous infusion
questions.expl:
**Why C:** BLING II (432 patients with severe sepsis, multicentre) found no difference in ICU-free days to day 28 (18 vs 20 days, p = 0.38), clinical cure or survival between continuous and intermittent β-lactam infusion. It was underpowered for mortality and led to the much larger BLING III.

**Why not the others:**
- A – no excess of *C. difficile* infection was reported (BLING III also found none).
- B – there was no significant reduction in 90-day mortality.
- D – the trial was completed, not stopped for harm.
- E – ICU-free days were numerically lower with continuous infusion (18 vs 20) and the difference was not significant.

**Ref:** Dulhunty JM et al., BLING II, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2015.

questions.stem: When starting a prolonged meropenem infusion in septic shock:
options: SSC 2026 recommends prolonged infusion for maintenance with a strong recommendation.
Drug stability at room temperature should be considered.
An initial loading bolus should precede the infusion.
Prolonged infusion makes TDM unnecessary in patients on ECMO.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SSC 2026 recommends prolonged β-lactam infusion for maintenance after an initial bolus – strong, moderate certainty (upgraded from weak in SSC 2021 after BLING III and the meta-analysis).
- B (True) – meropenem has limited stability at room temperature → more frequent syringe changes or an extended (e.g. 3-h) rather than 24-h infusion.
- C (True) – without a loading bolus, the target concentration takes hours to reach.
- D (False) – ECMO (circuit sequestration, ↑ Vd), RRT, ARC, obesity and high-MIC pathogens are exactly where β-lactam TDM is most useful, including with prolonged infusion.

**Ref:** Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2026 (Prescott HC et al., Crit Care Med 2026); Abdul-Aziz MH et al., Intensive Care Med 2020.

open.q: A 24-year-old with polytrauma and VAP is started on meropenem. Outline how you would plan his antibiotic dosing, explaining the pharmacokinetic changes that put him at risk of underdosing.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ↑ Vd of hydrophilic drugs (capillary leak, fluids, oedema, drains) → full loading dose, independent of renal function.
- Suspect ARC (young polytrauma): CrCl > 130 mL/min/1.73 m² on an 8–24 h urine collection; Cockcroft-Gault and normal creatinine do not exclude it.
- Meropenem is time-dependent (% fT>MIC); in the critically ill aim for 100 % fT>MIC.
- After the bolus, prolonged/continuous infusion (SSC 2026: strong, moderate certainty); consider room-temperature stability and line compatibility.
- With ARC use higher/more frequent doses or continuous infusion.
- β-lactam TDM (trough 24–48 h after start, or any time at steady state with continuous infusion), especially useful in ARC, obesity, RRT/ECMO, high-MIC pathogens.
- Consider hypoalbuminaemia if a highly protein-bound drug is used.

open.q: Explain why BLING III was "negative" while the meta-analysis published alongside it was "positive", and how you would interpret the evidence for prolonged β-lactam infusion.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- BLING III: 7031 patients, 104 ICUs, pip-tazo or meropenem, open-label; 90-d mortality 24.9 vs 26.8 %, OR 0.91 (95 % CI 0.81–1.01), p = 0.08 – NS.
- Its CI includes a clinically important benefit; clinical cure was higher (55.7 vs 50.0 %); no difference in MDR colonisation/infection or C. difficile.
- The meta-analysis (18 RCTs, 9108 patients, Bayesian) included BLING III and gained precision.
- Result: 90-d mortality RR 0.86 (95 % CrI 0.72–0.98), 99.1 % posterior probability of benefit, high certainty; ↑ clinical cure (RR 1.16), ↓ ICU mortality.
- BLING II (432 patients) showed no difference in ICU-free days (18 vs 20, p = 0.38) – underpowered.
- Interpretation: strongest evidence to date that prolonged β-lactam infusion (after a loading bolus) reduces mortality in sepsis.

title: W02 · D2 – De-escalation, duration of therapy and procalcitonin

questions.stem: A 60-year-old with E. coli bacteraemia from pyelonephritis is afebrile and haemodynamically stable on day 5 of appropriate therapy, with no abscess on imaging. According to the BALANCE trial, the most appropriate total antibiotic duration is:
options: 7 days
14 days
Until procalcitonin is undetectable
21 days
3 days
questions.expl:
**Why A:** BALANCE randomised 3608 hospitalised patients with bacteraemia (~55 % in ICU) to 7 vs 14 days: 90-day mortality 14.5 vs 16.1 % (difference −1.6 points, non-inferiority margin 4 points), relapse 2.6 vs 2.2 %, and more antibiotic-free days. A stable patient with uncomplicated *E. coli* bacteraemia and no abscess is a typical eligible patient.

**Why not the others:**
- B – 14 days was not better and only adds antibiotic exposure.
- C – "undetectable PCT" is not a validated rule; PCT stopping rules use < 0.5 µg/L or a ≥ 80 % fall, as an aid to clinical judgement.
- D – 21 days has no role in uncomplicated Gram-negative bacteraemia.
- E – 3 days was not tested and is too short for bacteraemia.

**EDIC trap:** BALANCE does not apply to *S. aureus* bacteraemia or candidaemia.

**Ref:** BALANCE Investigators, N Engl J Med 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding the PRORATA trial:
options: 28-day mortality was significantly lower in the PCT group.
The PCT group had more antibiotic-free days by day 28.
Antibiotics were discontinued only when PCT fell below 0.1 µg/L.
Relapse of infection was significantly more frequent in the PCT group.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – 28-day mortality 21.2 vs 20.4 % – non-inferior (margin 10 %), not lower.
- B (True) – antibiotic-free days to day 28 were 14.3 vs 11.6 (difference 2.7 days, p < 0.0001).
- C (False) – stopping was encouraged at PCT < 0.5 µg/L or a fall ≥ 80 % from peak (strongly at < 0.25 µg/L), not < 0.1 µg/L.
- D (False) – relapse 6.5 vs 5.1 %, not significant.

**EDIC trap:** 60-day mortality was numerically higher with PCT (30.0 vs 26.1 %, NS).

**Ref:** Bouadma L et al., PRORATA, Lancet 2010.

questions.stem: In ADAPT-Sepsis (JAMA 2025), which strategy reduced total antibiotic duration while being non-inferior for 28-day mortality?
options: Daily CRP-guided protocol
Fixed 5-day course
Both CRP and procalcitonin protocols
Neither protocol
Daily procalcitonin-guided protocol
questions.expl:
**Why E:** ADAPT-Sepsis (2760 adults, 41 UK ICUs, three arms) found that a daily procalcitonin-guided protocol shortened antibiotic duration (9.8 vs 10.7 days; difference 0.88 days, p = 0.01) with non-inferior 28-day mortality (20.9 vs 19.4 %). The CRP protocol did not shorten therapy.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the CRP protocol shortened duration by only 0.09 days and non-inferiority for mortality was not demonstrated.
- B – a fixed 5-day course was not one of the trial arms.
- C – only the PCT protocol achieved both outcomes.
- D – the PCT protocol was effective.

**EDIC trap:** CRP is not a substitute for PCT in guiding antibiotic duration.

**Ref:** Dark P et al., ADAPT-Sepsis, JAMA 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding the PneumA trial of 8 vs 15 days of antibiotics for VAP:
options: The 8-day group had more antibiotic-free days.
It was conducted in the United States.
28-day mortality was similar in both groups.
Recurrence was lower with 8 days among patients with non-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the 8-day group had more antibiotic-free days without excess mortality.
- B (False) – PneumA was conducted in 51 French ICUs (401 patients).
- C (True) – 28-day mortality 18.8 vs 17.2 % – non-inferior.
- D (False) – with non-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli (e.g. *Pseudomonas*) recurrence was higher with 8 days (40.6 vs 25.4 %).

**EDIC trap:** the penalty of short courses for non-fermenters is more recurrence, not higher mortality (see also iDIAPASON).

**Ref:** Chastre J et al., PneumA, JAMA 2003.

questions.stem: Which patient would NOT have been eligible for the BALANCE trial?
options: Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteraemia from pneumonia
E. coli bacteraemia from cholangitis after drainage
Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia
Enterococcus faecalis bacteraemia without endocarditis
Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteraemia from a urinary source in the ICU
questions.expl:
**Why C:** BALANCE excluded *S. aureus* and *S. lugdunensis* bacteraemia (high risk of endocarditis/metastatic foci; ≥ 14 days needed), candidaemia, severe immunosuppression, prosthetic valves/vascular grafts, infections requiring prolonged therapy (endocarditis, osteomyelitis, undrainable abscess) and contaminants.

**Why not the others:**
- A – *P. aeruginosa* bacteraemia from pneumonia was eligible; Gram-negatives including non-fermenters were included.
- B – cholangitis after drainage has source control and was eligible.
- D – *E. faecalis* bacteraemia without endocarditis was eligible.
- E – *K. pneumoniae* urinary bacteraemia in the ICU was eligible (~55 % of patients were in ICU).

**EDIC trap:** candidaemia has its own rule – 14 days from the first negative blood culture.

**Ref:** BALANCE Investigators, N Engl J Med 2025.

questions.stem: According to SSC 2021:
options: Double Gram-negative coverage should be continued after susceptibilities are known to prevent resistance.
Longer over shorter duration of therapy is suggested when source control is adequate.
Daily assessment for de-escalation is suggested.
Procalcitonin plus clinical evaluation is suggested to decide when to discontinue antimicrobials.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – SSC 2021 suggests against continuing double Gram-negative coverage once the pathogen and susceptibilities are known (weak, very low quality).
- B (False) – with adequate source control SSC 2021 suggests shorter over longer duration (weak, very low quality).
- C (True) – daily assessment for de-escalation is suggested (weak, very low quality); SSC 2026 upgraded de-escalation itself to a strong recommendation (very low certainty).
- D (True) – PCT plus clinical evaluation is suggested to decide when to discontinue antimicrobials (weak, low quality) – not to decide when to start.

**Ref:** Evans L et al., Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021, Intensive Care Med 2021; SSC 2026 (Prescott HC et al., Crit Care Med 2026).

questions.stem: In the SAPS trial (Lancet Infect Dis 2016), procalcitonin-guided discontinuation in Dutch ICUs resulted in:
options: No change in antibiotic duration
Shorter antibiotic duration and lower 28-day mortality
Shorter duration but higher 1-year mortality
Increased relapse of infection requiring early termination
Longer antibiotic duration and higher mortality
questions.expl:
**Why B:** SAPS randomised 1575 patients in Dutch ICUs with non-binding advice to stop antibiotics at a ≥ 80 % fall from peak or PCT ≤ 0.5 µg/L. Median duration fell from 7 to 5 days (DDD 7.5 vs 9.3) and 28-day mortality was lower (19.6 vs 25.0 %, p = 0.0122); 1-year mortality 34.8 vs 40.9 %.

**Why not the others:**
- A – antibiotic duration was clearly shorter.
- C – 1-year mortality was lower, not higher, with PCT guidance.
- D – the trial was not stopped early for relapse.
- E – the opposite of the result.

**EDIC trap:** the SAPS mortality benefit is unexplained and was not reproduced by PRORATA or ADAPT-Sepsis – the consistent finding is safe shortening of therapy.

**Ref:** de Jong E et al., SAPS, Lancet Infect Dis 2016.

questions.stem: Antimicrobial de-escalation:
options: Is synonymous with shortening treatment duration.
Refers only to switching from intravenous to oral administration.
Includes adding an agent to the empirical regimen when the patient deteriorates.
Has high-quality evidence demonstrating a reduction in antimicrobial resistance (ESICM/ESCMID 2020).
questions.expl:
- A (False) – de-escalation changes the spectrum or number of drugs; duration of therapy is a separate decision.
- B (False) – IV-to-oral switch is a different stewardship intervention; de-escalation means narrowing the spectrum according to cultures and/or stopping a component of a combination.
- C (False) – adding an agent when the patient deteriorates is escalation.
- D (False) – the ESICM/ESCMID position statement (13 statements, Delphi) stresses that high-quality research on the effect of de-escalation on resistance is lacking and that its definition varies.

**EDIC trap:** a K′ item with no true statement is possible.

**Ref:** Tabah A et al., ESICM/ESCMID position statement, Intensive Care Med 2020.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient treated for pneumonia has a PCT peak of 12 µg/L on day 1; on day 5 PCT is 2.0 µg/L and he is clinically improving. Based on the PRORATA/SAPS stopping rules:
options: Stopping can be considered because PCT has fallen by more than 80 % from peak
Antibiotics should be escalated
CRP must be measured before any decision
Antibiotics cannot be stopped because PCT is > 0.5 µg/L
PCT is not interpretable in ventilated patients
questions.expl:
**Why A:** 2.0/12 µg/L = 17 % of peak, i.e. an 83 % fall – this meets the "≥ 80 % fall from peak" criterion. The PRORATA/SAPS rules are either/or (PCT < 0.5 µg/L **or** ≥ 80 % fall), so with clinical improvement stopping can be considered even though PCT is still > 0.5 µg/L.

**Why not the others:**
- B – he is improving; there is no indication to escalate.
- C – CRP is not needed and is not a substitute for PCT (ADAPT-Sepsis).
- D – this ignores the relative-fall criterion.
- E – both PRORATA and SAPS included ventilated ICU patients.

**EDIC trap:** do the arithmetic – a fall to 2.0 from 12 is > 80 %.

**Ref:** Bouadma L et al., Lancet 2010; de Jong E et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016.

questions.stem: Regarding biomarkers in antibiotic stewardship:
options: In PRORATA, 60-day mortality was numerically higher in the PCT group.
PCT is primarily used in the ICU to decide when to stop antibiotics.
In ADAPT-Sepsis, a CRP-guided protocol did not shorten antibiotic duration.
PCT guidance requires no adherence to the algorithm to be effective.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – PRORATA 60-day mortality was 30.0 vs 26.1 %, numerically higher with PCT but not significant.
- B (True) – in the ICU, PCT is used mainly to decide when to stop antibiotics, not when to start them.
- C (True) – the CRP protocol shortened therapy by only 0.09 days and non-inferiority for mortality was not shown.
- D (False) – the effect depends on adherence; in the trials the algorithm was often overruled, diluting its effect.

**Ref:** Bouadma L et al., Lancet 2010; Dark P et al., ADAPT-Sepsis, JAMA 2025.

open.q: On day 3 of broad-spectrum therapy for E. coli bacteraemia from pyelonephritis in the ICU, outline your "antibiotic time-out", including de-escalation and the planned duration of therapy, with supporting evidence.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Reassess the diagnosis (cultures, imaging, alternative causes) and confirm source control (drainage, catheter removal; exclude abscess).
- De-escalate according to susceptibility: narrow the spectrum and stop unnecessary agents (e.g. anti-MRSA drug, second gram-negative drug); SSC 2021 suggests daily reassessment (weak).
- De-escalation is distinct from shortening duration – a separate decision.
- Plan a stop date: 7 days for uncomplicated G− bacteraemia (BALANCE: 90-d mortality 14.5 vs 16.1 %, non-inferior; more antibiotic-free days).
- BALANCE does not apply to S. aureus, S. lugdunensis or candidaemia, prosthetic material or infections needing long therapy.
- Serial PCT as an aid to stopping (PCT < 0.5 µg/L or ≥ 80 % fall from peak) combined with clinical evaluation.
- Rationale: each extra day of broad spectrum increases selection pressure, MDR colonisation, C. difficile and toxicity.

open.q: Compare PRORATA, SAPS and ADAPT-Sepsis and explain what they tell us about using biomarkers to guide antibiotic duration in the ICU.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- PRORATA (630, France): stop at PCT < 0.5 µg/L or ≥ 80 % fall; +2.7 antibiotic-free days (14.3 vs 11.6); 28-d mortality 21.2 vs 20.4 % (non-inferior); 60-d mortality numerically higher 30.0 vs 26.1 %.
- SAPS (1575, Netherlands): median duration 5 vs 7 days; 28-d mortality lower 19.6 vs 25.0 % – surprising, mechanism unexplained.
- ADAPT-Sepsis (2760, 41 UK ICUs): PCT shortened duration by 0.88 days (9.8 vs 10.7) with non-inferior mortality; CRP did not shorten therapy and non-inferiority was not shown.
- PCT safely shortens exposure by ~1–2 days; CRP is not a substitute for PCT.
- Effect depends on adherence to the algorithm, often overruled in trials.
- PCT is for stopping, not starting antibiotics (SSC 2021: PCT + clinical evaluation, weak, low quality).

title: W02 · D3 – MDR gram-negative bacteria: ESBL, AmpC, CRE, DTR Pseudomonas, CRAB

questions.stem: A 68-year-old in septic shock has bacteraemia with ceftriaxone-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae (ESBL), susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam and meropenem. The most appropriate definitive therapy is:
options: Ceftazidime-avibactam
Tigecycline
Meropenem
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 6 h
Cefepime
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In MERINO (ceftriaxone-resistant *E. coli*/*K. pneumoniae* bacteraemia) 30-day mortality was 12.3 % with piperacillin-tazobactam vs 3.7 % with meropenem; non-inferiority was not shown and the trial stopped early. ESCMID 2022 recommends a carbapenem (imipenem or meropenem) for BSI/severe infection – strong, moderate certainty; ertapenem only without septic shock.

**Why not the others:**
- A – active, but new BL/BLIs should be reserved for XDR/carbapenem-resistant strains (good practice).
- B – ESCMID strongly recommends against tigecycline (low serum concentrations).
- D – this is exactly the MERINO arm that failed, despite in vitro susceptibility.
- E – cefepime is conditionally recommended against for ESBL infections.

**Ref:** Harris PNA et al., MERINO, JAMA 2018; Paul M et al., ESCMID guidelines, Clin Microbiol Infect 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding the MERINO trial:
options: The trial was stopped early.
Non-inferiority of piperacillin-tazobactam was demonstrated.
Patients had bloodstream infection with carbapenem-resistant E. coli or K. pneumoniae.
30-day mortality was 12.3 % with piperacillin-tazobactam vs 3.7 % with meropenem.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the trial was stopped early after an interim analysis (391 randomised).
- B (False) – the mortality difference (8.6 %) meant non-inferiority of piperacillin-tazobactam was not demonstrated.
- C (False) – patients had ceftriaxone-resistant (mainly ESBL) *E. coli* or *K. pneumoniae* susceptible to both piperacillin-tazobactam and meropenem – by definition carbapenem-susceptible.
- D (True) – 30-day mortality 12.3 % (23/187) vs 3.7 % (7/191).

**EDIC trap:** "susceptible in vitro" to piperacillin-tazobactam does not make it adequate for ESBL bacteraemia.

**Ref:** Harris PNA et al., MERINO, JAMA 2018.

questions.stem: A patient with VAP has Enterobacter cloacae complex susceptible to ceftriaxone, cefepime (MIC 1 mg/L) and meropenem; no ESBL detected. The preferred definitive agent is:
options: Ceftazidime-avibactam
Amoxicillin-clavulanate
Colistin
Ceftriaxone
Cefepime
questions.expl:
**Why E:** *Enterobacter cloacae* complex carries an inducible chromosomal AmpC; third-generation cephalosporins can select derepressed mutants during therapy, causing failure despite initial susceptibility. Cefepime is a weak AmpC inducer and stable to AmpC hydrolysis, so with a low MIC (1 mg/L) and no ESBL it is the preferred agent (IDSA 2024).

**Why not the others:**
- A – ceftazidime-avibactam would work but should be reserved for carbapenem-resistant organisms.
- B – *Enterobacter* is intrinsically resistant to amoxicillin-clavulanate (AmpC hydrolyses aminopenicillins; clavulanate does not inhibit AmpC).
- C – colistin is a toxic last-resort drug and inappropriate when β-lactams are active.
- D – IDSA 2024 advises against ceftriaxone for invasive infections with AmpC-prone organisms.

**Ref:** Tamma PD et al., IDSA 2024 Guidance, Clin Infect Dis 2024.

questions.stem: Regarding β-lactamase inhibitors:
options: Avibactam inhibits KPC but not OXA-48 carbapenemases.
Vaborbactam is active against OXA-48.
Avibactam inhibits metallo-β-lactamases such as NDM.
Aztreonam is not hydrolysed by metallo-β-lactamases.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – avibactam inhibits class A (ESBL, KPC), class C (AmpC) and some class D enzymes including OXA-48 – hence ceftazidime-avibactam is the drug of choice for OXA-48.
- B (False) – vaborbactam (like relebactam) inhibits mainly KPC and AmpC, not OXA-48 or MBL.
- C (False) – none of the new inhibitors (avibactam, vaborbactam, relebactam) inhibits zinc-dependent metallo-β-lactamases.
- D (True) – aztreonam is not hydrolysed by MBL, but is destroyed by co-produced ESBL/AmpC – the rationale for combining it with avibactam.

**Ref:** Paul M et al., ESCMID guidelines, Clin Microbiol Infect 2022; Tamma PD et al., IDSA 2024, Clin Infect Dis 2024.

questions.stem: Bloodstream infection with NDM-producing K. pneumoniae in a patient with septic shock. Which regimen is most appropriate?
options: Imipenem-relebactam
Aztreonam-avibactam (or ceftazidime-avibactam plus aztreonam)
Meropenem-vaborbactam
Ceftazidime-avibactam alone
Ceftolozane-tazobactam
questions.expl:
**Why B:** NDM is a class B metallo-β-lactamase that hydrolyses all β-lactams except aztreonam; MBL producers usually co-carry ESBL/AmpC, so aztreonam must be protected by avibactam. IDSA 2024 prefers aztreonam-avibactam (or ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam) or cefiderocol; ESCMID 2022: aztreonam + ceftazidime-avibactam (conditional, moderate) or cefiderocol (conditional, low).

**Why not the others:**
- A – relebactam does not inhibit MBL.
- C – vaborbactam does not inhibit MBL.
- D – avibactam does not inhibit MBL, so ceftazidime is hydrolysed; the combination works only when aztreonam is added.
- E – tazobactam does not inhibit carbapenemases, and ceftolozane is hydrolysed by them.

**Ref:** Tamma PD et al., IDSA 2024, Clin Infect Dis 2024; Paul M et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB):
options: ESCMID 2022 recommends against polymyxin plus meropenem combination therapy.
In ATTACK, sulbactam-durlobactam was compared with colistin, both combined with imipenem-cilastatin.
In CREDIBLE-CR, mortality was higher with cefiderocol in the Acinetobacter subgroup.
In AIDA, adding meropenem to colistin did not reduce clinical failure.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESCMID 2022 strongly recommends against polymyxin + meropenem and polymyxin + rifampicin for CRAB.
- B (True) – ATTACK compared sulbactam-durlobactam with colistin, both plus imipenem-cilastatin; 28-day mortality 19 vs 32 %, with less nephrotoxicity.
- C (True) – in CREDIBLE-CR, mortality was higher with cefiderocol, especially with *Acinetobacter* (end of study 50 vs 18 %) – the basis for ESCMID's conditional recommendation against cefiderocol for CRAB.
- D (True) – AIDA (406 patients, 77 % *Acinetobacter*): clinical failure at day 14 79 vs 73 %, RR 0.93 (0.83–1.03).

**EDIC trap:** IDSA 2024 prefers sulbactam-durlobactam + a carbapenem for invasive CRAB.

**Ref:** Paul M et al., AIDA, Lancet Infect Dis 2018; Kaye KS et al., ATTACK, Lancet Infect Dis 2023.

questions.stem: Difficult-to-treat resistance (DTR) in Pseudomonas aeruginosa means:
options: Resistance to at least one agent in three antimicrobial classes
Resistance to colistin only
Resistance to aminoglycosides
Non-susceptibility to all first-line agents including β-lactams, carbapenems and fluoroquinolones
Production of an ESBL
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Difficult-to-treat resistance (DTR) means non-susceptibility to all first-line agents: piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, cefepime, aztreonam, meropenem, imipenem, ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin (IDSA; ESCMID uses an analogous concept). Treatment relies on ceftolozane-tazobactam (preferred for pneumonia), ceftazidime-avibactam or imipenem-relebactam, with cefiderocol as an alternative.

**Why not the others:**
- A – non-susceptibility to ≥ 1 agent in ≥ 3 categories is the MDR definition (Magiorakos 2012).
- B – colistin resistance alone is not DTR; colistin is not a first-line agent.
- C – aminoglycosides are not part of the DTR definition.
- E – ESBL production is a mechanism (typical of Enterobacterales), not a resistance category.

**Ref:** Tamma PD et al., IDSA 2024, Clin Infect Dis 2024; Paul M et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2022.

questions.stem: According to ESCMID 2022 guidelines for carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales:
options: Meropenem-vaborbactam or ceftazidime-avibactam is suggested for severe infection if active.
Tigecycline is suggested as first-line monotherapy for bloodstream infection and HAP/VAP.
Cefiderocol is suggested for metallo-β-lactamase producers.
Combination therapy is recommended even when the isolate is susceptible to ceftazidime-avibactam.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – for severe CRE infection meropenem-vaborbactam or ceftazidime-avibactam is suggested if active in vitro (conditional).
- B (False) – ESCMID suggests against tigecycline for bloodstream infection and HAP/VAP because of low serum concentrations.
- C (True) – cefiderocol is suggested for MBL producers or strains resistant to all other agents (conditional, low); aztreonam + ceftazidime-avibactam is the other option (conditional, moderate).
- D (False) – combination therapy is recommended against when the strain is susceptible to ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam or cefiderocol (strong, low); ≥ 2 active drugs only when only old agents are active.

**Ref:** Paul M et al., ESCMID guidelines, Clin Microbiol Infect 2022.

questions.stem: Which drug is a siderophore cephalosporin that uses bacterial iron transport to enter the cell?
options: Ceftaroline
Cefiderocol
Cefepime
Ceftobiprole
Ceftolozane
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Cefiderocol carries a catechol side chain that chelates ferric iron, so it is actively transported across the Gram-negative outer membrane via bacterial iron-uptake (siderophore) channels – the "Trojan horse" mechanism. It is stable against all carbapenemase classes, including MBL, but CREDIBLE-CR showed excess mortality in *Acinetobacter* infections.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ceftaroline is an anti-MRSA cephalosporin (binds PBP2a), not a siderophore.
- C – cefepime is a fourth-generation cephalosporin entering via porins.
- D – ceftobiprole is an anti-MRSA cephalosporin with antipseudomonal activity, not a siderophore.
- E – ceftolozane is an antipseudomonal cephalosporin (with tazobactam) that enters via porins and is inactive against carbapenemases.

**Ref:** Bassetti M et al., CREDIBLE-CR, Lancet Infect Dis 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding ESCMID 2022 recommendations for third-generation cephalosporin-resistant Enterobacterales:
options: Ertapenem may be used for bloodstream infection without septic shock.
For low-risk non-severe infections, piperacillin-tazobactam may be considered.
Cefepime is suggested as targeted therapy for ESBL bloodstream infection.
New β-lactam/β-lactamase inhibitors should be reserved for extensively resistant bacteria.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ertapenem may be used for BSI without septic shock (conditional, moderate); with shock, meropenem or imipenem.
- B (True) – for low-risk, non-severe infections piperacillin-tazobactam, amoxicillin-clavulanate or a quinolone may be considered (carbapenem-sparing stewardship).
- C (False) – ESCMID conditionally recommends against cefepime (and cephamycins) for ESBL infections.
- D (True) – new BL/BLIs (e.g. ceftazidime-avibactam) should be reserved for extensively resistant bacteria (good practice statement).

**EDIC trap:** cefepime is acceptable for AmpC producers, not for ESBL producers.

**Ref:** Paul M et al., ESCMID guidelines, Clin Microbiol Infect 2022.

open.q: Explain why piperacillin-tazobactam should not be used for ESBL bacteraemia even when the isolate is reported susceptible, and outline your targeted therapy for 3GC-resistant Enterobacterales according to ESCMID 2022.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- MERINO (JAMA 2018): 391 patients with ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli/K. pneumoniae BSI, pip-tazo 4.5 g q6h vs meropenem 1 g q8h.
- 30-d mortality 12.3 vs 3.7 % (difference 8.6 %) – non-inferiority not demonstrated; stopped early.
- Hence carbapenem (imipenem or meropenem) for BSI/severe infection – strong, moderate certainty.
- Ertapenem possible for BSI without septic shock (conditional).
- Low-risk, non-severe infections: pip-tazo, amoxicillin-clavulanate or quinolone (stewardship).
- Against tigecycline (strong), cephamycins and cefepime for ESBL (conditional); reserve new BL/BLIs for XDR strains.
- Contrast: cefepime is appropriate for AmpC producers (Enterobacter, K. aerogenes, C. freundii) if MIC ≤ 8 and no ESBL.

open.q: Outline how the carbapenemase type determines your choice of agent for CRE, and explain the pharmacological rationale for combining aztreonam with avibactam.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- KPC (class A serine): meropenem-vaborbactam, ceftazidime-avibactam, imipenem-relebactam (IDSA 2024 preferred options).
- OXA-48-like (class D): ceftazidime-avibactam (avibactam inhibits some class D; vaborbactam and relebactam do not).
- MBL (NDM, VIM, IMP; class B, zinc): avibactam does not inhibit MBL → aztreonam-avibactam (or ceftazidime-avibactam + aztreonam) or cefiderocol.
- Aztreonam is stable against MBL but hydrolysed by co-produced ESBL/AmpC; avibactam protects it from these.
- Cefiderocol: siderophore cephalosporin entering via iron transport, stable against all carbapenemase classes.
- Monotherapy if susceptible to ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam or cefiderocol (strong, low); ≥ 2 active drugs only if only old drugs are active; no tigecycline for BSI or HAP/VAP.

title: W02 · D4 – Invasive fungal infections in the ICU: candidaemia and aspergillosis

questions.stem: A 55-year-old on day 10 after colectomy has Candida albicans in 2 of 2 blood culture sets. He is on noradrenaline 0.2 µg/kg/min. The most appropriate initial antifungal is:
options: No therapy until repeat cultures are positive
Voriconazole
Fluconazole 400 mg daily
An echinocandin (e.g. caspofungin with loading dose)
Flucytosine monotherapy
questions.expl:
**Why D:** In a critically ill patient (on vasopressors) with candidaemia, an echinocandin is the recommended initial therapy (IDSA 2016 – strong, high quality; ECMM/ISHAM/ASM 2025 – first choice). Caspofungin is given as 70 mg loading, then 50 mg/d; echinocandins are fungicidal and active against most fluconazole-resistant species. Add early CVC removal, repeat blood cultures and an eye examination.

**Why not the others:**
- A – *Candida* in blood is never a contaminant; delaying therapy increases mortality.
- B – voriconazole offers no advantage as initial therapy and has many interactions; it is a step-down option for selected species.
- C – fluconazole is an alternative only for non-critically ill patients at low risk of resistance (and requires an 800 mg loading dose).
- E – flucytosine monotherapy rapidly selects resistance; it is used only in combination.

**Ref:** Pappas PG et al., IDSA 2016, Clin Infect Dis 2016; Cornely OA et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding management of candidaemia (IDSA 2016):
options: A dilated ophthalmological examination is recommended within the first week.
Step-down to fluconazole is possible once the patient is stable, cultures have cleared and the isolate is susceptible.
Central venous catheter removal is never necessary if an echinocandin is used.
Treatment should continue for 6 weeks after documented clearance of the bloodstream and resolution of symptoms.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – a dilated ophthalmological examination is recommended within the first week of diagnosis.
- B (True) – step-down to fluconazole is possible (usually within 5–7 days) when the patient is clinically stable, the isolate is susceptible and repeat blood cultures are negative.
- C (False) – the CVC should be removed as early as possible when it is the presumed source (individualised); echinocandin use does not make removal unnecessary.
- D (False) – treatment continues for 2 weeks after documented clearance of the bloodstream and resolution of symptoms, in the absence of metastatic complications.

**EDIC trap:** the 14 days are counted from the first negative blood culture, not from the start of therapy.

**Ref:** Pappas PG et al., IDSA 2016, Clin Infect Dis 2016.

questions.stem: In EMPIRICUS, empirical micafungin in non-neutropenic ICU patients with ICU-acquired sepsis, Candida colonisation and multiple organ failure:
options: Increased mortality
Was effective only when β-D-glucan was > 80 pg/mL
Was compared with fluconazole
Did not significantly improve invasive fungal infection–free survival but reduced new invasive fungal infections
Significantly improved invasive fungal infection–free survival at day 28
questions.expl:
**Why D:** EMPIRICUS (260 patients, 19 French ICUs, double-blind) compared 14 days of micafungin with placebo. Invasive fungal infection–free survival at day 28 was 68.0 vs 60.2 % (HR 1.35, 95 % CI 0.87–2.08) – not significant – although new invasive fungal infections were fewer (3 vs 12 %, p = 0.008).

**Why not the others:**
- A – mortality was not increased with micafungin.
- B – even the subgroup with β-D-glucan > 80 pg/mL did not benefit.
- C – the comparator was placebo, not fluconazole.
- E – the primary outcome was not significantly improved.

**EDIC trap:** fewer new infections ≠ better survival; routine empirical antifungals in non-neutropenic patients do not reduce mortality.

**Ref:** Timsit JF et al., EMPIRICUS, JAMA 2016.

questions.stem: Regarding Candida in the ICU:
options: Echinocandins achieve excellent concentrations in the vitreous humour.
Isolation of Candida from tracheal aspirates usually indicates Candida pneumonia requiring antifungal therapy.
Albumin or immunoglobulin infusion can cause false-positive β-D-glucan results.
(1→3)-β-D-glucan has a high positive predictive value.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – echinocandins penetrate poorly into the eye, CNS and urine; endophthalmitis is treated with an azole or amphotericin B.
- B (False) – *Candida* in tracheal aspirate almost always reflects colonisation; IDSA states that treatment is rarely indicated (strong, moderate) – *Candida* pneumonia is extremely rare.
- C (True) – albumin, immunoglobulins, certain haemodialysis membranes and surgical gauze can cause false-positive β-D-glucan results.
- D (False) – β-D-glucan has a high negative but low positive predictive value in the ICU; it is most useful to rule out invasive candidiasis and stop empirical therapy.

**Ref:** Pappas PG et al., IDSA 2016, Clin Infect Dis 2016.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old previously healthy man is ventilated in the ICU for severe influenza A pneumonia. On day 4 new nodular infiltrates appear; BAL galactomannan is strongly positive. The most appropriate treatment is:
options: No treatment, because he lacks an EORTC/MSG host factor
Voriconazole or isavuconazole
Caspofungin
Nebulised amphotericin B alone
Fluconazole
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Severe influenza is an independent risk factor for invasive aspergillosis (adj. OR 5.19); IAPA occurred in 19 % of ICU influenza patients, including 14 % of immunocompetent ones. The expert definition replaces host factors with an entry criterion (ICU respiratory failure + positive influenza test), so new infiltrates plus a positive BAL galactomannan = probable IAPA. First-line therapy is voriconazole or isavuconazole.

**Why not the others:**
- A – an EORTC/MSG host factor is not required for IAPA.
- C – echinocandins are not first-line for aspergillosis.
- D – nebulised amphotericin B alone does not treat invasive disease.
- E – fluconazole has no activity against *Aspergillus*.

**Ref:** Schauwvlieghe AFAD et al., Lancet Respir Med 2018; Verweij PE et al., Intensive Care Med 2020.

questions.stem: Regarding influenza-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (IAPA):
options: It occurred only in immunocompromised patients.
The expert case definition uses an entry criterion instead of host factors.
In a Dutch-Belgian cohort, it occurred in about 19 % of ICU patients with influenza.
It was associated with higher 90-day mortality.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – IAPA also occurred in 14 % of immunocompetent influenza patients.
- B (True) – the case definition uses an entry criterion (ICU respiratory failure with a positive influenza test temporally related to admission) instead of host factors.
- C (True) – 83/432 patients (19 %) in the Dutch-Belgian retrospective cohort.
- D (True) – 90-day mortality was 51 vs 28 %; other risk factors were corticosteroids, APACHE II and male sex.

**Ref:** Schauwvlieghe AFAD et al., Lancet Respir Med 2018; Verweij PE et al., Intensive Care Med 2020.

questions.stem: According to the ECMM/ISHAM 2020 criteria, which finding supports probable COVID-19-associated pulmonary aspergillosis in a patient with an otherwise unexplained infiltrate?
options: BAL galactomannan index ≥ 1.0
Serum galactomannan index of 0.2
Candida albicans in tracheal aspirate
Elevated serum procalcitonin
Positive serum cryptococcal antigen
questions.expl:
**Why A:** In ECMM/ISHAM 2020, probable pulmonary CAPA requires an otherwise unexplained infiltrate plus at least one mycological criterion: BAL galactomannan index ≥ 1.0, serum galactomannan > 0.5, positive BAL culture or microscopy, or positive PCR. Proven CAPA requires histology or *Aspergillus* from a sterile site.

**Why not the others:**
- B – a serum GM index of 0.2 is below the > 0.5 threshold (and serum GM is insensitive in non-neutropenic patients).
- C – *Candida* in tracheal aspirate is colonisation and irrelevant to aspergillosis.
- D – procalcitonin is not part of the CAPA criteria.
- E – cryptococcal antigen detects *Cryptococcus*, not *Aspergillus*.

**Ref:** Koehler P et al., ECMM/ISHAM consensus, Lancet Infect Dis 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding rezafungin (ReSTORE trial):
options: It was non-inferior to caspofungin for candidaemia and invasive candidiasis.
The maintenance dose is 200 mg weekly after a 400 mg first dose.
It is an echinocandin dosed once weekly.
It is licensed for candidaemia and invasive candidiasis, not for invasive aspergillosis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ReSTORE (199 randomised) showed non-inferiority to caspofungin: 30-day mortality 24 vs 21 %, global cure at day 14 59 vs 61 %.
- B (True) – 400 mg in week 1, then 200 mg once weekly.
- C (True) – rezafungin is a long-half-life echinocandin, which allows once-weekly dosing.
- D (True) – it is licensed for candidaemia and invasive candidiasis in adults, not for invasive aspergillosis; the ECMM/ISHAM/ASM 2025 guideline lists it among first-choice echinocandins.

**Ref:** Thompson GR 3rd et al., ReSTORE, Lancet 2023; Cornely OA et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2025.

questions.stem: According to SSC 2021, empirical antifungal therapy in adults with sepsis:
options: Is recommended for all patients with septic shock
Is recommended only after positive blood cultures
Is strongly recommended for all patients on parenteral nutrition
Should always include amphotericin B
Is suggested for patients at high risk of fungal infection and suggested against for those at low risk
questions.expl:
**Why E:** SSC 2021 suggests empirical antifungal therapy for adults at high risk of fungal infection and suggests against it at low risk (weak, low quality). SSC 2026 moved further towards stewardship: it suggests against routine empirical antifungals, reserving them for specific risk factors or strong clinical suspicion (conditional, low certainty) – consistent with EMPIRICUS showing no survival benefit.

**Why not the others:**
- A – there is no blanket recommendation for all patients with septic shock.
- B – therapy after positive blood cultures is targeted, not empirical.
- C – parenteral nutrition is only one risk factor, and no recommendation is strong.
- D – when empirical therapy is given, an echinocandin is preferred, not amphotericin B.

**Ref:** Evans L et al., SSC 2021, Intensive Care Med 2021; SSC 2026 (Prescott HC et al., Crit Care Med 2026).

questions.stem: Regarding invasive aspergillosis in the ICU:
options: Serum galactomannan is less sensitive in non-neutropenic patients than BAL galactomannan.
Echinocandin monotherapy is preferred if azole resistance is suspected.
Therapeutic drug monitoring of voriconazole is recommended.
Fluconazole is active against Aspergillus fumigatus.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in non-neutropenic patients neutrophils clear circulating galactomannan, so serum GM has low sensitivity; BAL GM is the better test.
- B (False) – if azole resistance is suspected (e.g. endemic resistant *A. fumigatus* in the Netherlands), liposomal amphotericin B is preferred; echinocandins are not first-line monotherapy.
- C (True) – voriconazole TDM is recommended (non-linear PK, genetic polymorphism, interactions); it is on the ICM 2020 routine TDM list.
- D (False) – fluconazole has no activity against *Aspergillus*; first line is voriconazole or isavuconazole.

**Ref:** Koehler P et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2021; Abdul-Aziz MH et al., Intensive Care Med 2020.

open.q: Outline your management of a septic patient on vasopressors with Candida albicans in blood cultures on day 10 after colectomy, from initial therapy to the end of treatment.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Start an echinocandin (critically ill): caspofungin 70 mg loading then 50 mg/d, micafungin 100 mg/d or anidulafungin 200 mg loading then 100 mg/d (IDSA strong, high quality); fluconazole only for non-critically ill patients at low risk of resistance.
- Remove the CVC as early as possible if it is the presumed source; look for and control abdominal source.
- Repeat blood cultures daily or every other day until negative.
- Dilated ophthalmological examination within the first week (echinocandins penetrate poorly into the eye).
- Step-down to fluconazole within 5–7 days if clinically stable, isolate susceptible and repeat cultures negative.
- Duration 2 weeks after documented clearance of candidaemia and resolution of symptoms, in the absence of metastatic complications.
- Rezafungin (once weekly) is a non-inferior alternative (ReSTORE).

open.q: Explain why classic EORTC/MSG criteria miss invasive aspergillosis in many ICU patients and how IAPA and CAPA definitions and diagnostics address this.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- EORTC/MSG require a host factor (neutropenia, transplantation, haematological malignancy) – most ICU patients lack one.
- IAPA occurred in 19 % of ICU influenza patients, including 14 % of immunocompetent ones; 90-d mortality 51 vs 28 %; influenza an independent risk factor (adj. OR 5.19).
- IAPA definition (Verweij 2020) uses an entry criterion (ICU respiratory failure + positive influenza test) instead of host factors; probable IAPA = BAL GM or culture + infiltrates, or tracheobronchitis with positive culture.
- CAPA (ECMM/ISHAM 2020): possible/probable/proven; probable = unexplained infiltrate + BAL GM ≥ 1.0, serum GM > 0.5, BAL culture, microscopy or PCR.
- Serum GM has low sensitivity in non-neutropenic patients → BAL GM is preferred.
- Treatment: voriconazole or isavuconazole first line (with voriconazole TDM); L-AmB if azole resistance suspected; 6–12 weeks; echinocandins and fluconazole not appropriate.

title: W02 · D5 – HAP/VAP: definitions, diagnosis, treatment and prevention

questions.stem: A patient intubated for 6 days after a cardiac arrest develops fever, purulent secretions and a new right lower lobe infiltrate. He received piperacillin-tazobactam 10 days ago, now requires noradrenaline 0.4 µg/kg/min. Local Gram-negative resistance is > 25 %. The most appropriate empirical regimen per ERS/ESICM 2017 is:
options: Ceftriaxone monotherapy
Two antipseudomonal Gram-negative agents, plus MRSA coverage if MRSA risk is present
Withhold antibiotics until BAL results are available
Ertapenem monotherapy
Moxifloxacin monotherapy
questions.expl:
**Why B:** He is high risk by ERS/ESICM 2017 criteria: septic shock, recent antibiotics, hospitalisation > 5 days and a unit with > 25 % resistance. For high-risk HAP/VAP the guideline recommends empirical combination of two Gram-negative agents covering *P. aeruginosa* and ESBL, plus anti-MRSA cover if MRSA risk is present (strong, moderate), with de-escalation to monotherapy once cultures return.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ceftriaxone is a low-risk option and does not cover *Pseudomonas*.
- C – sample before antibiotics, but never delay treatment in septic shock.
- D – ertapenem has no antipseudomonal activity and is a low-risk option.
- E – moxifloxacin is not reliably antipseudomonal and is a low-risk option.

**Ref:** Torres A et al., ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT guidelines, Eur Respir J 2017.

questions.stem: According to the IDSA/ATS 2016 HAP/VAP guidelines:
options: The concept of healthcare-associated pneumonia was retained.
A 14-day course is recommended for VAP.
Noninvasive sampling with semiquantitative cultures is suggested.
Procalcitonin should be used to decide whether to start antibiotics.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – HCAP was abandoned: these patients did not carry as many MDR pathogens as assumed, and the concept drove excessive broad-spectrum therapy.
- B (False) – a 7-day course is recommended for both HAP and VAP.
- C (True) – non-invasive sampling (endotracheal aspirate) with semiquantitative culture is suggested; invasive techniques are not required.
- D (False) – PCT, CRP and CPIS should not be used to decide whether to start antibiotics; clinical criteria decide (PCT may help with discontinuation).

**EDIC trap:** ERS/ESICM 2017 instead suggests distal quantitative samples in stable patients.

**Ref:** Kalil AC et al., IDSA/ATS guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2016.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed by IDSA/ATS 2016 as a risk factor for multidrug-resistant VAP?
options: Acute renal replacement therapy prior to VAP
Septic shock at the time of VAP
ARDS preceding VAP
IV antibiotic use within the previous 90 days
Age > 65 years
questions.expl:
**Why E:** IDSA/ATS 2016 lists five risk factors for MDR VAP: IV antibiotics within the previous 90 days, septic shock at the time of VAP, ARDS preceding VAP, ≥ 5 days of hospitalisation before VAP, and acute RRT before VAP. Age is not on the list.

**Why not the others:**
- A – acute RRT before VAP is a listed risk factor.
- B – septic shock at the time of VAP is a listed risk factor.
- C – ARDS preceding VAP is a listed risk factor.
- D – IV antibiotics within 90 days is a listed risk factor (and the most consistent one).

**EDIC trap:** negatively phrased item – read "NOT" carefully.

**Ref:** Kalil AC et al., IDSA/ATS guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2016.

questions.stem: Regarding the iDIAPASON trial:
options: Non-inferiority of 8 days compared with 15 days was demonstrated.
The composite of death or recurrence was numerically higher in the 8-day group.
It included only Pseudomonas aeruginosa VAP.
It was stopped early because of slow recruitment.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – non-inferiority of 8 days was not demonstrated.
- B (True) – death or recurrence by day 90 was 35.2 vs 25.5 % in the 8-day vs 15-day group.
- C (True) – only *P. aeruginosa* VAP was included (186 patients, ITT).
- D (True) – it was stopped early for slow recruitment (~1/3 of the planned sample), so it is underpowered and inconclusive.

**EDIC trap:** "non-inferiority not demonstrated" does not mean "8 days proven inferior".

**Ref:** Bouglé A et al., iDIAPASON, Intensive Care Med 2022.

questions.stem: In the AMIKINHAL trial, inhaled amikacin given once daily for 3 days to patients ventilated for 72–96 h:
options: Reduced the incidence of VAP by day 28
Reduced 28-day mortality
Increased VAP incidence because of resistance selection
Was given at 20 mg/kg actual body weight twice daily
Was compared with intravenous amikacin
questions.expl:
**Why A:** AMIKINHAL (847 patients ventilated for 72–96 h, double-blind) gave inhaled amikacin 20 mg/kg ideal body weight once daily for 3 days vs placebo. VAP by day 28 fell from 22 to 15 %, and infection-related ventilator-associated complications from 26 to 18 %.

**Why not the others:**
- B – the trial was not powered for mortality and showed no mortality benefit.
- C – VAP decreased; resistance selection remains a long-term concern, not an observed increase in VAP.
- D – the dose was based on ideal body weight and given once daily.
- E – the comparator was placebo, not IV amikacin.

**Ref:** Ehrmann S et al., AMIKINHAL, N Engl J Med 2023.

questions.stem: According to ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT 2017:
options: A 14-day course is suggested for VAP in immunocompetent patients with good response.
Distal quantitative samples before antibiotics are suggested in stable patients with suspected VAP.
Routine serial procalcitonin is recommended to shorten a planned 7–8-day course.
Short courses are also appropriate for necrotising pneumonia and lung abscess.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – a 7–8-day course is suggested for VAP in immunocompetent patients with a good response (weak, moderate).
- B (True) – in stable patients, distal quantitative samples (BAL, PSB, mini-BAL) before antibiotics are suggested to reduce antibiotic exposure (weak, low).
- C (False) – routine serial PCT is recommended against when the planned course is 7–8 days (strong, moderate); consider it with inadequate initial therapy, severe immunosuppression or highly resistant pathogens.
- D (False) – short courses do not apply to necrotising pneumonia, lung abscess, empyema, cavitation, secondary bacteraemia, immunosuppression or cystic fibrosis.

**Ref:** Torres A et al., ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT guidelines, Eur Respir J 2017.

questions.stem: Ventilator-associated pneumonia is defined as pneumonia that develops:
options: Within 48 h of hospital admission in a non-ventilated patient
After extubation only
Within 24 h of intubation
Only after 7 days of mechanical ventilation
More than 48 h after endotracheal intubation
questions.expl:
**Why E:** VAP is pneumonia developing more than 48 h after endotracheal intubation. HAP is pneumonia arising ≥ 48 h after admission, not incubating at admission, in a non-ventilated patient. Early (< 5 days) vs late onset is historically relevant, but MDR risk now depends more on individual risk factors and local epidemiology.

**Why not the others:**
- A – pneumonia within 48 h of admission was probably incubating at admission (community-acquired); HAP requires ≥ 48 h.
- B – VAP arises during invasive ventilation; it is not restricted to the post-extubation period.
- C – pneumonia within 24 h of intubation was most likely present or aspirated at intubation.
- D – 7 days of ventilation is not required; early-onset VAP (< 5 days) exists.

**Ref:** Kalil AC et al., Clin Infect Dis 2016; Torres A et al., Eur Respir J 2017.

questions.stem: Regarding empirical MRSA and antipseudomonal coverage in VAP (IDSA/ATS 2016):
options: MRSA coverage is suggested only when MRSA accounts for more than 50 % of S. aureus isolates locally.
Vancomycin or linezolid are options for MRSA coverage.
Double antipseudomonal coverage is recommended for all patients with VAP.
Local antibiograms should guide the empirical regimen.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – empirical MRSA coverage is suggested when there are MRSA risk factors or MRSA accounts for > 10–20 % of local *S. aureus* isolates, not > 50 %.
- B (True) – vancomycin or linezolid are the recommended options.
- C (False) – double antipseudomonal coverage only with MDR risk factors or if > 10 % of Gram-negative isolates are resistant to the agent being considered for monotherapy.
- D (True) – empirical regimens should be guided by the local (ideally ICU-specific) antibiogram.

**Ref:** Kalil AC et al., IDSA/ATS guidelines, Clin Infect Dis 2016.

questions.stem: A patient with low-risk early-onset HAP, no septic shock and no MDR risk factors in a low-resistance unit. Which empirical antibiotic fits ERS/ESICM 2017 guidance?
options: Ceftazidime-avibactam
Tigecycline
Meropenem plus amikacin plus vancomycin
Ceftriaxone
Colistin
questions.expl:
**Why D:** With no septic shock, no MDR risk factors and low local resistance, ERS/ESICM 2017 suggests a narrow-spectrum agent: ertapenem, ceftriaxone, cefotaxime, moxifloxacin or levofloxacin (weak, very low). Ceftriaxone covers the likely pathogens (*S. pneumoniae*, *H. influenzae*, MSSA, susceptible Enterobacterales).

**Why not the others:**
- A – ceftazidime-avibactam should be reserved for carbapenem-resistant organisms.
- B – tigecycline achieves low serum concentrations and performed poorly in HAP/VAP; it is not recommended.
- C – a triple broad-spectrum regimen is for high-risk patients only.
- E – colistin is a toxic last-resort agent.

**Ref:** Torres A et al., ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT guidelines, Eur Respir J 2017.

questions.stem: Regarding VAP prevention:
options: ERS/ESICM 2017 strongly recommends chlorhexidine oral care.
ERS/ESICM 2017 suggests selective oropharyngeal decontamination (SOD), not SDD, in settings with low antibiotic resistance.
Head-of-bed elevation is part of standard prevention bundles.
Minimising sedation and duration of ventilation reduces VAP risk.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – ERS/ESICM 2017 makes no recommendation on chlorhexidine oral care because of an unclear balance of benefit and a possible increase in mortality.
- B (True) – SOD (not SDD) is suggested only in settings with low resistance and low antibiotic consumption (weak, low).
- C (True) – head-of-bed elevation to 30–45° is a standard bundle element.
- D (True) – daily sedation interruption and SBTs shorten ventilation and reduce VAP risk; other elements include subglottic drainage, cuff pressure control and avoiding unnecessary reintubation.

**Ref:** Torres A et al., ERS/ESICM/ESCMID/ALAT guidelines, Eur Respir J 2017.

open.q: A patient ventilated for 6 days develops suspected VAP with septic shock in a unit with > 25 % Gram-negative resistance. Outline your diagnostic and empirical treatment approach, and how you would adjust therapy over the following days.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- VAP = pneumonia > 48 h after intubation; suspicion = new/progressive infiltrate + ≥ 2 of fever, purulent secretions, leucocytosis/leucopenia, worsening oxygenation.
- Take a lower respiratory tract sample before antibiotics (ERS/ESICM: distal quantitative if stable; IDSA/ATS: non-invasive semiquantitative) without delaying therapy in an unstable patient.
- Do not use PCT, CRP or CPIS to decide on starting therapy.
- High risk (septic shock, > 5 days, > 25 % resistance, prior antibiotics) → two antipseudomonal G− agents + anti-MRSA if MRSA risk (strong, moderate); guided by local antibiogram.
- After cultures → de-escalate to monotherapy (combination only for XDR/PDR non-fermenters and CRE).
- Duration 7 (–8) days if immunocompetent with good response; not for abscess, empyema, necrotising pneumonia, cavitation, secondary bacteraemia or immunosuppression.
- For non-fermenters (Pseudomonas) beware higher recurrence with 8 days (PneumA) and non-inferiority not shown (iDIAPASON).

open.q: Explain the evidence for inhaled amikacin and other measures to prevent VAP, including the guideline position on decontamination and chlorhexidine.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- AMIKINHAL (NEJM 2023): double-blind RCT, 847 patients ventilated 72–96 h.
- Amikacin 20 mg/kg ideal body weight inhaled once daily for 3 days vs placebo.
- VAP by d28 15 vs 22 %; IVACs 18 vs 26 %; not powered for mortality; resistance concerns remain.
- ERS/ESICM 2017: SOD (not SDD) suggested only in low-resistance, low-antibiotic-use settings (weak, low).
- Chlorhexidine oral care: no recommendation (unclear benefit, possible ↑ mortality).
- Bundle: head-of-bed 30–45°, daily sedation interruption and SBT, subglottic drainage, cuff pressure, avoid unnecessary reintubations/transports, NIV where indicated.

title: W02 · Saturday – weekly review: Infections I

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman with 40 % burns develops Pseudomonas bacteraemia. Measured creatinine clearance is 170 mL/min/1.73 m², albumin 18 g/L. Which dosing strategy for an antipseudomonal β-lactam is most appropriate?
options: Single dose followed by oral step-down
Loading dose followed by prolonged or continuous infusion, guided by therapeutic drug monitoring
Once-daily high dose to maximise Cmax/MIC
Reduced dose because of hypoalbuminaemia
Standard intermittent bolus every 12 h
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Burns increase Vd, a measured CrCl of 170 mL/min/1.73 m² indicates augmented renal clearance, and albumin 18 g/L increases the free fraction and clearance – all predict subtherapeutic β-lactam levels. Give a full loading dose, then prolonged/continuous infusion to maximise fT>MIC (SSC 2026: strong), and individualise with TDM (routinely recommended for β-lactams).

**Why not the others:**
- A – there is no adequate oral antipseudomonal β-lactam; bacteraemia needs IV therapy.
- C – Cmax/MIC is the aminoglycoside index; β-lactams are time-dependent.
- D – hypoalbuminaemia lowers concentrations; reducing the dose compounds underdosing.
- E – infrequent intermittent boluses are the worst option for a time-dependent drug with ARC.

**Ref:** Abdul-Aziz MH et al., Intensive Care Med 2020; SSC 2026 (Prescott HC et al., Crit Care Med 2026).

questions.stem: Match the trial with its main finding:
options: BALANCE – 14 days of antibiotics superior to 7 days for bloodstream infection.
BLING III – significantly lower 90-day mortality with continuous β-lactam infusion.
EMPIRICUS – empirical micafungin did not significantly improve invasive fungal infection–free survival.
MERINO – piperacillin-tazobactam non-inferior to meropenem for ESBL bacteraemia.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – BALANCE showed 7 days non-inferior to 14 days (90-day mortality 14.5 vs 16.1 %).
- B (False) – BLING III 90-day mortality 24.9 vs 26.8 %, p = 0.08 – not significant (clinical cure was higher).
- C (True) – EMPIRICUS: IFI-free survival 68.0 vs 60.2 %, NS, although new IFIs were fewer (3 vs 12 %).
- D (False) – MERINO: mortality 12.3 vs 3.7 % with piperacillin-tazobactam vs meropenem; non-inferiority not shown, stopped early.

**Ref:** BALANCE, N Engl J Med 2025; BLING III, JAMA 2024; EMPIRICUS, JAMA 2016; MERINO, JAMA 2018.

questions.stem: A ventilated patient has VAP due to Pseudomonas aeruginosa non-susceptible to piperacillin-tazobactam, ceftazidime, cefepime, aztreonam, carbapenems and fluoroquinolones, but susceptible to ceftolozane-tazobactam. The preferred therapy is:
options: Ceftolozane-tazobactam
Meropenem-vaborbactam
Tigecycline
Ertapenem
Meropenem high-dose extended infusion
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Non-susceptibility to all first-line β-lactams, carbapenems and fluoroquinolones defines DTR *P. aeruginosa*. ESCMID 2022 suggests ceftolozane-tazobactam if active (conditional, very low) and IDSA 2024 prefers it for pneumonia; ceftazidime-avibactam, imipenem-relebactam and cefiderocol are alternatives.

**Why not the others:**
- B – vaborbactam inhibits KPC and adds nothing against *Pseudomonas* carbapenem resistance (porin loss, efflux).
- C – tigecycline is intrinsically inactive against *P. aeruginosa*.
- D – ertapenem has no antipseudomonal activity.
- E – high-dose extended-infusion meropenem cannot overcome documented carbapenem non-susceptibility.

**Ref:** Paul M et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2022; Tamma PD et al., IDSA 2024, Clin Infect Dis 2024.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old has candidaemia with C. albicans (fluconazole-susceptible) and is on caspofungin. On day 5 he is off vasopressors and repeat blood cultures from day 2 are negative.
options: An ophthalmological examination should have been performed within the first week.
Total treatment should be 14 days from the start of caspofungin.
Treatment can stop on day 7 if procalcitonin is low.
Step-down to fluconazole is reasonable.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – a dilated ophthalmological examination is recommended within the first week of candidaemia.
- B (False) – the 14 days are counted from the first negative blood culture (here day 2) and resolution of symptoms, not from the start of caspofungin.
- C (False) – procalcitonin does not guide antifungal duration, and 7 days is too short for candidaemia.
- D (True) – he is stable, the isolate is fluconazole-susceptible and cultures have cleared → step-down to fluconazole (usually within 5–7 days).

**Ref:** Pappas PG et al., IDSA 2016, Clin Infect Dis 2016; Cornely OA et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2025.

questions.stem: Which statement about procalcitonin in the ICU is best supported by RCT evidence?
options: PCT should be used to decide whether to start antibiotics in suspected sepsis
PCT-guided therapy increased 28-day mortality in SAPS
PCT-guided discontinuation reduces antibiotic exposure without increasing mortality
Serial PCT is strongly recommended by ERS/ESICM to shorten 7-day VAP courses
CRP-guided discontinuation is as effective as PCT-guided discontinuation
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Three RCTs show that PCT-guided discontinuation reduces antibiotic exposure without increasing mortality: PRORATA (+2.7 antibiotic-free days, non-inferior mortality), SAPS (5 vs 7 days, lower 28-day mortality) and ADAPT-Sepsis (−0.88 days, non-inferior mortality).

**Why not the others:**
- A – PCT should not be used to decide on starting antibiotics; the clinical picture decides.
- B – SAPS showed lower, not higher, 28-day mortality (19.6 vs 25.0 %).
- D – ERS/ESICM 2017 recommends against routine serial PCT when a 7–8-day VAP course is planned (strong, moderate).
- E – in ADAPT-Sepsis the CRP protocol did not shorten therapy and non-inferiority was not shown.

**Ref:** Bouadma L et al., Lancet 2010; de Jong E et al., Lancet Infect Dis 2016; Dark P et al., JAMA 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales:
options: Meropenem-vaborbactam is active against NDM producers.
Cefiderocol is an option for metallo-β-lactamase producers.
Ceftazidime-avibactam is inactive against OXA-48 producers.
Combination therapy is recommended when the isolate is susceptible to ceftazidime-avibactam.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – vaborbactam inhibits KPC (and AmpC), not metallo-β-lactamases; NDM → aztreonam-avibactam or cefiderocol.
- B (True) – cefiderocol is stable against all carbapenemase classes and is an option for MBL producers (ESCMID conditional, low).
- C (False) – avibactam inhibits OXA-48, so ceftazidime-avibactam is active and is the preferred agent (IDSA 2024).
- D (False) – ESCMID recommends against combination therapy when the isolate is susceptible to ceftazidime-avibactam (strong, low).

**Ref:** Paul M et al., Clin Microbiol Infect 2022; Tamma PD et al., IDSA 2024, Clin Infect Dis 2024.

questions.stem: A previously healthy 50-year-old ventilated for severe influenza develops new cavitating infiltrates; BAL galactomannan is positive. Serum galactomannan is negative. The most accurate statement is:
options: Invasive aspergillosis is unlikely because he has no EORTC/MSG host factor
Fluconazole is sufficient
Start an echinocandin as first-line therapy
