De-escalate to a single narrower-spectrum active agent, stop vancomycin and amikacin, and plan a total of about 7 days
questions.expl: De-escalate according to susceptibility, stop anti-MRSA therapy with a negative screen; SSC 2021 advises against continuing double Gram-negative coverage; BALANCE: 7 days non-inferior to 14 (except *S. aureus* and candidaemia). ([W02/D2](#W02-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding biomarker-guided antibiotic duration:
options: ERS/ESICM 2017 recommends routine serial procalcitonin to shorten a planned 7–8-day VAP course.
In SAPS, 28-day mortality was higher in the procalcitonin group (25.0 % vs 19.6 %).
In ADAPT-Sepsis, the CRP-guided protocol shortened therapy and was non-inferior for mortality.
In PRORATA, the procalcitonin group had about 2.7 more antibiotic-free days by day 28.
questions.expl: SAPS: 28-day mortality was **lower** with procalcitonin guidance (19.6 vs 25.0 %). ADAPT-Sepsis: only the PCT protocol shortened therapy; CRP did not shorten therapy and non-inferiority was not shown. ERS/ESICM does not recommend routine serial PCT when 7–8 days are planned (strong). ([W02/D2](#W02-D2), [W02/D5](#W02-D5))

questions.stem: A ventilated patient with pneumonia had a procalcitonin peak of 5.0 µg/L. On day 5 he is improving and PCT is 1.5 µg/L. Using the PRORATA/SAPS stopping rules:
options: Antibiotics can be stopped because PCT has fallen by more than 80 %
Antibiotics can be stopped because PCT is below 2 µg/L
The stopping criteria are not yet met (a 70 % fall); stopping could be considered once PCT is ≤ 1.0 µg/L (≥ 80 % fall) or < 0.5 µg/L
PCT cannot be used in ventilated patients
Antibiotics must be escalated
questions.expl: 1.5 / 5.0 = 30 % of peak → a 70 % fall; rule: < 0.5 µg/L or a fall ≥ 80 % (80 % of 5.0 = a value of 1.0). ([W02/D2](#W02-D2))

questions.stem: Matching resistance mechanisms with treatment (IDSA 2024 / ESCMID 2022):
options: OXA-48-producing Enterobacterales – meropenem-vaborbactam.
Ceftolozane-tazobactam is active against carbapenemase producers.
KPC-producing K. pneumoniae – meropenem-vaborbactam is among the preferred options.
NDM-producing Enterobacterales – meropenem-vaborbactam.
questions.expl: Vaborbactam is inactive against MBL and OXA-48; OXA-48 → ceftazidime-avibactam; NDM → aztreonam-avibactam or cefiderocol. Ceftolozane-tazobactam is potent against *Pseudomonas* but inactive against carbapenemases. ([W02/D3](#W02-D3))

questions.stem: A haemodynamically stable patient (no septic shock) has bacteraemia with ESBL-producing E. coli from a urinary source. According to ESCMID 2022, which targeted option is acceptable?
options: Tigecycline
Ceftazidime-avibactam as routine first choice
Cefepime
Ertapenem
Piperacillin-tazobactam, as MERINO showed non-inferiority
questions.expl: BSI without septic shock → ertapenem (conditional, moderate). Against tigecycline (strong) and cefepime for ESBL; MERINO did not show non-inferiority of pip-tazo; new BL/BLIs should be reserved for XDR. ([W02/D3](#W02-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB):
options: In ATTACK, 28-day mortality was 19 % with sulbactam-durlobactam vs 32 % with colistin.
Durlobactam protects sulbactam from Acinetobacter OXA β-lactamases.
Sulbactam has intrinsic activity against Acinetobacter through PBP binding.
IDSA 2024 prefers sulbactam-durlobactam combined with a carbapenem for invasive CRAB infection.
questions.expl: IDSA 2024: sulbactam-durlobactam + a carbapenem; caution with cefiderocol (CREDIBLE-CR – higher mortality with *Acinetobacter*). ([W02/D3](#W02-D3))

questions.stem: A patient on micafungin for Candida albicans candidaemia is found on fundoscopy to have endophthalmitis. Which is the most appropriate change?
options: Continue micafungin, as echinocandins are first-line for candidaemia
Change to an azole or amphotericin B, as echinocandins penetrate poorly into the eye
Add rezafungin
Stop antifungals once blood cultures are negative
Switch to caspofungin at a higher dose
questions.expl: Echinocandins penetrate poorly into the eye, CNS and urine → for endophthalmitis use an azole/amphotericin B. ([W02/D4](#W02-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding aspergillosis in the ICU:
options: In the Dutch-Belgian cohort, influenza was an independent risk factor for invasive aspergillosis, as were corticosteroids.
Classic EORTC/MSG criteria capture most ICU patients with aspergillosis, because host factors are common in the ICU.
Echinocandins are first-line therapy for invasive aspergillosis.
Serum galactomannan > 0.5 can support probable COVID-19-associated pulmonary aspergillosis.
questions.expl: A: adj. OR 5.19. B: classic criteria require a host factor and therefore **miss** most ICU patients. First line: voriconazole or isavuconazole; L-AmB for azole resistance. ([W02/D4](#W02-D4))

questions.stem: A non-neutropenic ICU patient with risk factors and fever without another cause was started on empirical caspofungin. After 5 days there is no clinical response, blood cultures are negative and β-D-glucan is negative. Per IDSA 2016, the best action is:
options: Continue for 14 days from the first negative blood culture
Consider stopping the antifungal
Add fluconazole for synergy
Switch to liposomal amphotericin B
Add voriconazole
questions.expl: No response after 4–5 days and no further evidence of invasive candidiasis (or a negative non-culture test with high NPV) → consider stopping. ([W02/D4](#W02-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding diagnosis of HAP/VAP:
options: ERS/ESICM 2017 suggests continuing antibiotics for a full 7 days even if HAP is unlikely and there is no deterioration within 72 h.
IDSA/ATS 2016 suggests invasive sampling with quantitative cultures.
Healthcare-associated pneumonia (HCAP) was abandoned because these patients had more MDR pathogens than expected.
IDSA/ATS 2016 suggests using PCT, CRP or CPIS to decide whether to start antibiotics.
questions.expl: ERS/ESICM: stop after 3 days if HAP is unlikely and there is no deterioration. IDSA/ATS 2016 suggests **non-invasive** sampling with semiquantitative cultures and **not** using PCT/CRP/CPIS to decide whether to start. HCAP was abandoned because the patients **did not** have as many MDR pathogens as assumed (excessive broad-spectrum therapy). ([W02/D5](#W02-D5))

questions.stem: A patient develops VAP. He has no MDR risk factors. In the unit, MRSA accounts for 25 % of S. aureus isolates and 5 % of Gram-negative isolates are resistant to the monotherapy being considered. Per IDSA/ATS 2016, the best empirical regimen is:
options: One antipseudomonal agent without MRSA coverage
Two antipseudomonal agents plus vancomycin
Ceftriaxone alone
Colistin plus meropenem
One antipseudomonal agent plus vancomycin or linezolid
questions.expl: MRSA coverage when MRSA > 10–20 %; double antipseudomonal coverage only with MDR risk factors or > 10 % resistance. ([W02/D5](#W02-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding duration of therapy for VAP:
options: ERS/ESICM 2017 does not apply the 7–8-day course to lung abscess or secondary bacteraemia.
In PneumA, 28-day mortality was similar with 8 and 15 days.
iDIAPASON demonstrated non-inferiority of 8 days for Pseudomonas aeruginosa VAP.
IDSA/ATS 2016 recommends 7 days for both HAP and VAP.
questions.expl: iDIAPASON: death/recurrence 35.2 vs 25.5 %, non-inferiority not shown, stopped early. ([W02/D5](#W02-D5), [W02/D2](#W02-D2))

questions.stem: A stable patient has catheter-related bloodstream infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa from a short-term jugular CVC. There is no endocarditis, thrombophlebitis or persistent bacteraemia. The best management is:
options: Remove the catheter and treat for about 7 days (uncomplicated Gram-negative BSI)
Guidewire exchange of the catheter and 14 days of therapy
Remove the catheter and treat for 6 weeks
Retain the catheter and treat for 14 days
Retain the catheter with antibiotic lock therapy
questions.expl: Remove a short-term CVC with Gram-negatives (including *Pseudomonas*); no salvage with *Pseudomonas*; guidewire exchange does not remove the biofilm; uncomplicated Gram-negative BSI 7 days (BALANCE). ([W03/D1](#W03-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding prevention of catheter-related infection:
options: In the Dressing trial, chlorhexidine-impregnated sponges reduced CRBSI (HR 0.24).
The Keystone (Pronovost) study was a cluster-randomised trial.
In 3SITES, the femoral site had the highest pneumothorax rate.
In CLEAN, chlorhexidine–alcohol did not reduce CRBSI compared with povidone iodine–alcohol.
questions.expl: Keystone was a before–after cohort, not an RCT. Pneumothorax was most frequent with the subclavian site (2.1 vs 1.4 vs 0.7 %); the subclavian site also had the fewest CRBSI + DVT. CLEAN: chlorhexidine–alcohol reduced CRBSI (HR 0.21), with more severe skin reactions. ([W03/D1](#W03-D1))

questions.stem: A patient has uncomplicated CRBSI with coagulase-negative staphylococci from a short-term CVC, which has been removed. The appropriate duration of therapy is:
options: 6–8 weeks
5–7 days
4–6 weeks
14 days from the first negative blood culture
10–14 days, as for catheter retention
questions.expl: CoNS: 5–7 days after removal; 10–14 days only if the catheter is retained with lock therapy. ([W03/D1](#W03-D1))

questions.stem: A 68-year-old on long-term oral corticosteroids presents with fever, neck stiffness and confusion; GCS 13, no focal deficit. Regarding management of suspected bacterial meningitis:
options: Severe immunocompromise is one of the indications for CT before lumbar puncture.
If Listeria monocytogenes is confirmed, dexamethasone should be continued for the full 4 days.
If lumbar puncture is delayed, antibiotics and dexamethasone should be given immediately after blood cultures.
Amoxicillin/ampicillin should be added to cover Listeria.
questions.expl: Age > 50 y and a cell-mediated immune defect (corticosteroids) → *Listeria*. Stop dexamethasone if the pathogen is other than *S. pneumoniae* or *H. influenzae*. ([W03/D2](#W03-D2), [W03/D4](#W03-D4))

questions.stem: A patient with suspected pneumococcal meningitis received the first dose of ceftriaxone 2 hours ago; dexamethasone was forgotten. According to ESCMID 2016:
options: Dexamethasone 10 mg every 6 h can still be started now
Dexamethasone should be withheld because it reduces vancomycin penetration into CSF
Give a single dose of dexamethasone after 24 h
Dexamethasone should no longer be given
Dexamethasone should be started only once CSF culture confirms pneumococcus
questions.expl: If antibiotics have already been started, dexamethasone can be started up to 4 h after the first dose. Reduced vancomycin penetration is not a reason to omit it. ([W03/D2](#W03-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding herpes simplex encephalitis:
options: Acyclovir can cause crystal nephropathy, so hydration and renal dose adjustment are needed.
In the French ICU cohort (Jaquet), 71 % had a poor functional outcome at 90 days.
MRI is the most sensitive imaging; bilateral temporal involvement is almost pathognomonic.
IDSA 2008 recommends routine adjunctive corticosteroids.
questions.expl: Corticosteroids in HSV encephalitis are not routinely recommended (only retrospective data). ([W03/D2](#W03-D2))

questions.stem: A previously healthy 28-year-old with chickenpox, who has been taking ibuprofen, develops severe thigh pain and shock. Surgical exploration shows necrotic fascia; Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in chains. The best definitive antibiotic therapy is:
options: Penicillin plus clindamycin
Doxycycline plus ceftriaxone
Clindamycin monotherapy
Piperacillin-tazobactam alone
Vancomycin alone
questions.expl: Type II NSTI (GAS; varicella, NSAID). GAS → penicillin + clindamycin (IDSA, strong); never clindamycin monotherapy (resistance). Doxycycline + ceftriaxone is for *Vibrio*. ([W03/D3](#W03-D3))

questions.stem: A patient with suspected NSTI has CRP 210 mg/L, WBC 18 × 10⁹/L, Hb 12.5 g/dL, Na⁺ 132 mmol/L, creatinine 120 µmol/L and glucose 8 mmol/L.
options: A score of ≥ 8 is classified as high risk.
A LRINEC score of at least 6 is required before surgical exploration.
The LRINEC score is 8.
In the Fernando meta-analysis, gas in the fascia on CT had a lower sensitivity than LRINEC ≥ 6.
questions.expl: CRP ≥ 150 = 4, WBC 15–25 = 1, Hb 11–13.5 = 1, Na < 135 = 2, creatinine ≤ 141 = 0, glucose ≤ 10 = 0 → **8**. LRINEC never delays exploration; CT gas sensitivity 88.5 % vs LRINEC 68.2 % (higher). ([W03/D3](#W03-D3))

questions.stem: Which feature favours streptococcal over staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome?
options: Negative blood cultures
Severe local pain with necrotising soft-tissue infection and positive blood cultures
Low mortality
Menstrual tampon use
Desquamation of palms and soles after 1–2 weeks
questions.expl: Streptococcal TSS: often NSTI, severe local pain, blood cultures often positive, high mortality (~38 %). The other options are typical of staphylococcal TSS. ([W03/D3](#W03-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding febrile neutropenia (IDSA 2010/2011, ECIL-4):
options: Persistent fever at 72–96 h in a haemodynamically stable patient is a reason to escalate antibacterial therapy.
Persistent fever beyond 4–7 days in profound neutropenia should prompt a search for invasive fungal infection.
Fever is defined as a single temperature ≥ 38.3 °C or ≥ 38.0 °C sustained for ≥ 1 h.
Cephalosporins are not appropriate for the escalation approach in centres with a high ESBL prevalence.
questions.expl: Persistent fever in a stable patient is not a reason to escalate; think of fungal infection (chest CT, galactomannan). ([W03/D4](#W03-D4))

questions.stem: A 40-year-old who underwent splenectomy after trauma presents with fulminant sepsis. Which group of pathogens is most typical for this immune defect?
options: Encapsulated bacteria such as S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae and N. meningitidis
Nocardia and Cryptococcus
Coagulase-negative staphylococci and Candida
Pneumocystis jirovecii and CMV
Aspergillus and Mucorales
questions.expl: Humoral immunity/asplenia → encapsulated bacteria. PJP/CMV/*Nocardia*/*Cryptococcus* = T cells; moulds = prolonged neutropenia; CoNS/*Candida* = barriers. ([W03/D4](#W03-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding selective decontamination:
options: SOD consists of an oropharyngeal paste plus surveillance cultures, without gastric suspension or IV antibiotics.
The SuDDICU ecological analysis confirmed non-inferiority for resistant organisms at unit level.
In SuDDICU, bacteraemia and cultures with resistant organisms were not reduced at the patient level.
In the Hammond meta-analysis, the mortality benefit was confined to regimens without an IV component.
questions.expl: C: reduced – 5.6 vs 8.1 %; 20.9 vs 32.5 %. D: the benefit was confined to regimens **with** an IV component (RR 0.84 vs 1.01). Ecological non-inferiority for resistant organisms was not confirmed. ([W03/D5](#W03-D5))

questions.stem: A patient known to have rectal colonisation with OXA-48-producing K. pneumoniae develops septic shock from pneumonia. Which empirical choice best uses the colonisation information?
options: Ceftolozane-tazobactam
Piperacillin-tazobactam
Meropenem-vaborbactam
Ignore colonisation, as colonisation is not infection
A regimen containing ceftazidime-avibactam
questions.expl: Colonisation ≠ infection (do not treat), but in sepsis it guides the choice of empirical therapy. OXA-48 → ceftazidime-avibactam; vaborbactam does not cover OXA-48, ceftolozane is inactive against carbapenemases. ([W03/D5](#W03-D5), [W02/D3](#W02-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding transmission prevention in the ICU:
options: In MOSAR, rapid PCR screening with isolation significantly reduced acquisition of resistant bacteria.
In REDUCE MRSA, universal decolonisation reduced bloodstream infections from any pathogen by 44 %.
In BUGG, universal glove and gown use significantly reduced the composite of MRSA or VRE acquisition.
In outbreaks and for CRE/CRAB, screening with contact isolation remains part of the multimodal approach (ESCMID 2014).
questions.expl: MOSAR: neither rapid PCR nor conventional screening with isolation further reduced acquisition. BUGG: no difference in the primary outcome (only MRSA alone slightly ↓). ([W03/D5](#W03-D5))

questions.stem: A patient in septic shock on parenteral nutrition has a femoral CVC and suspected CRBSI. Per IDSA 2009, the best initial approach is:
options: Empirical linezolid plus ceftriaxone, keep the catheter
Fluconazole alone
Vancomycin plus Gram-negative coverage, consider an echinocandin, and remove the catheter
Vancomycin alone and keep the catheter until cultures return
Guidewire exchange plus vancomycin
questions.expl: Empirical vancomycin (not linezolid); Gram-negative coverage in critical illness and with a femoral catheter; consider an echinocandin with TPN/femoral catheter; septic shock = indication for removal. ([W03/D1](#W03-D1))

questions.stem: A patient has Hb 10 g/dL, SaO₂ 95 %, PaO₂ 80 mmHg and cardiac output 5 L/min. Using CaO₂ = 1.34 × Hb × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂ (mL/dL), the oxygen delivery is approximately:
options: 65 mL/min
650 mL/min
1300 mL/min
6500 mL/min
480 mL/min

questions.stem: Regarding the haemodynamic profiles of shock (Vincent & De Backer):
options: Hypovolaemic shock: low filling pressures.
Obstructive shock accounted for about 2 % of cases and is rapidly reversible with targeted treatment.
Cardiogenic shock: low cardiac output, high SVR, high filling pressures, low SvO₂.
Septic shock typically has a low SvO₂ even after fluid resuscitation.
questions.expl: Distributive shock typically has a normal/high SvO₂ (which does not exclude tissue hypoxia). ([W04/D1](#W04-D1))

questions.stem: A non-intubated, spontaneously breathing patient with septic shock is in atrial fibrillation. Echocardiography is available. Which test of fluid responsiveness is most appropriate?
options: Passive leg raising, assessing the change in stroke volume (e.g. LVOT VTI) in real time
Pulse pressure variation
Passive leg raising, assessing the change in arterial blood pressure
Respiratory variation of the IVC diameter
End-expiratory occlusion test
questions.expl: PLR works in spontaneous breathing and arrhythmia if CO/SV is measured in real time (threshold ≥ 10 %). PPV does not work in AF and spontaneous breathing; EEO requires intubation; BP alone is insensitive; the IVC is unreliable. ([W04/D2](#W04-D2), [W04/D5](#W04-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding pulse pressure variation (PPV):
options: A tidal volume challenge transiently increases VT from 6 to 8 mL/kg PBW and assesses the absolute increase in PPV.
Michard et al. found that a threshold of 13 % had a sensitivity of 94 % and specificity of 96 %.
De Backer et al. found that with tidal volume < 8 mL/kg, a PPV threshold of 12 % still correctly classified about 90 % of patients.
Spontaneous breathing improves the reliability of PPV.
questions.expl: C: only 51 % with VT < 8 vs 88 % with VT ≥ 8. With spontaneous breathing the AUC is only ~0.68. ([W04/D2](#W04-D2))

questions.stem: A patient with severe septic shock and ARDS is not responding to initial therapy. Which advanced haemodynamic monitoring is suggested by the ESICM 2014 consensus?
options: Transpulmonary thermodilution or a pulmonary artery catheter
Routine pulmonary artery catheter for all patients with shock
No cardiac output monitoring, as it does not change outcome
CVP-guided therapy alone
Any uncalibrated device, whether or not validated in shock
questions.expl: TPTD or PAC in severe shock, especially with ARDS (Level 2, C); no routine PAC (Level 1, A); measure CO/SV in non-responders; less invasive devices only if validated in shock. ([W04/D3](#W04-D3), [W04/D1](#W04-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding transpulmonary thermodilution-derived variables:
options: GEDV = ITTV − PTV.
EVLW = ITTV − ITBV, where ITBV ≈ 1.25 × GEDV.
GEDV is a static preload indicator.
The average of three consecutive cold-bolus measurements is recommended.
questions.expl: GEDV is a **static** preload indicator – it is not used alone to guide fluids (Level 1, B). ([W04/D3](#W04-D3))

questions.stem: A patient in cardiogenic shock after acute myocardial infarction has transpulmonary thermodilution showing EVLWI 14 mL/kg and PVPI 2.1. The best interpretation is:
options: Measurement error, as EVLWI cannot exceed 10 mL/kg
Increased lung water with a hydrostatic mechanism
Normal lung water
Increased lung water due to increased permeability (ARDS pattern)
Hypovolaemia
questions.expl: EVLWI above normal (< 7, upper limit ~10 mL/kg) and PVPI ≤ 3 → hydrostatic (cardiogenic) oedema; PVPI > 3 = permeability oedema. ([W04/D3](#W04-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding venous oxygen saturation and the venous-to-arterial CO₂ difference:
options: With ScvO₂ ≥ 70 % and a gap ≥ 6 mmHg, increasing cardiac output may be considered.
According to the Fick equation for CO₂, P(cv-a)CO₂ is inversely related to cardiac output.
ScvO₂ includes venous blood from the lower body and the coronary sinus.
ScvO₂ < 70 % suggests that oxygen delivery is insufficient for consumption.
questions.expl: ScvO₂ (superior vena cava) does not reflect blood from the lower body and coronary sinus; its trends mostly parallel SvO₂. ([W04/D4](#W04-D4))

questions.stem: Which explanation is most often given for why ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe did not reproduce the benefit of EGDT seen by Rivers?
options: EGDT was harmful in the later trials
Lower baseline mortality because "usual care" had improved (early antibiotics and fluids), plus Rivers being a single-centre study
The later trials used dopamine instead of noradrenaline
The later trials enrolled only patients without hypotension
The later trials did not measure lactate
questions.expl: Early recognition, antibiotics and fluids became standard; a rigid CVP/ScvO₂/Hct protocol adds nothing. PRISM: no subgroup benefited. ([W04/D4](#W04-D4))

questions.stem: Comparing ANDROMEDA-SHOCK (2019) and ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (2025):
options: In ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2, the control group also had CRT assessed every hour.
In ANDROMEDA-SHOCK, 28-day mortality was 34.9 % (CRT) vs 43.4 % (lactate), p = 0.06.
In ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2, the benefit was driven by lower mortality.
Both the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK and the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 interventions lasted 24 hours.
questions.expl: Control in AS-2: CRT only at baseline and after 6 h; mortality 26.5 vs 26.6 %, win ratio 1.16 driven by shorter duration of organ support. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK lasted 8 h, ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 6 h. ([W04/D4](#W04-D4))

questions.stem: A hypotensive patient has a dilated right ventricle (RV/LV end-diastolic area ratio 0.8), a D-shaped LV in short axis, normal RV free wall thickness and a dilated IVC. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Chronic RV pressure overload
Hypovolaemic shock
Cardiac tamponade
Distributive shock
Acute cor pulmonale (obstructive shock, e.g. massive pulmonary embolism)
questions.expl: RV/LV > 0.6 = dilatation (≥ 1 severe) + paradoxical septum (D-shape) = acute cor pulmonale; normal free wall thickness argues against chronic overload (hypertrophy). Fluids are potentially harmful here. ([W04/D5](#W04-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding IVC ultrasound and the 2021 ESICM basic ultrasound consensus:
options: A strong recommendation required agreement of ≥ 84 % of experts.
A dilated, non-collapsing IVC proves that the patient is not fluid responsive.
A small, collapsing IVC supports severe hypovolaemia.
IVC assessment remains reliable during mechanical ventilation with high PEEP and/or low tidal volume.
questions.expl: A dilated non-collapsing IVC is part of the picture of RV failure/tamponade, not proof of non-responsiveness. High PEEP and/or low VT is one of the situations in which IVC assessment fails. ([W04/D5](#W04-D5))

questions.stem: In the study of acute cor pulmonale in moderate-to-severe ARDS (Mekontso Dessap, ICM 2016), which factor was protective?
options: PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg
Pneumonia as the cause of ARDS
Driving pressure ≥ 18 cmH₂O
Prone positioning
PaCO₂ ≥ 48 mmHg
questions.expl: A, B, C and E are risk factors for ACP (prevalence 22 %; severe ACP mortality 57 vs 42 %). ([W04/D5](#W04-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding oxygen delivery targets and inotropes:
options: In Gattinoni's 1995 trial, targeting a supranormal cardiac index did not reduce mortality.
The cardiac index target was achieved in only about 45 % of the supranormal group.
ESICM 2014 recommends an absolute DO₂ target in shock (Level 1, A).
ESICM 2014 recommends against inotropes for isolated cardiac dysfunction without hypoperfusion.
questions.expl: B: 44.9 %. C: Level 1, A **against**. D: Level 1, B. ([W04/D1](#W04-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding MAP targets (integrating ESICM 2014, SSC 2026 and trial data):
options: ESICM 2014 recommends individualising the MAP target, with an initial MAP ≥ 65 mmHg.
ESICM 2014 suggests that a higher MAP may be considered in septic shock with chronic hypertension.
SSC 2026 suggests an initial MAP of 75–80 mmHg in patients aged ≥ 65 years.
In SEPSISPAM, chronically hypertensive patients had significantly lower mortality with the higher target.
questions.expl: B: Level 2, B. C: SSC 2026 suggests **60–65** mmHg in patients aged ≥ 65 (conditional, low). In the chronic hypertension subgroup there was less creatinine doubling and RRT, but no effect on mortality. ([W04/D1](#W04-D1), [W01/D4](#W01-D4))

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock has received several litres of 0.9 % saline: pH 7.29, PaCO₂ 26 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L, Na⁺ 140, Cl⁻ 114 mmol/L, albumin 20 g/L, lactate 4 mmol/L. The best description is:
options: Pure high anion gap metabolic acidosis
Pure normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, because the anion gap of 14 is normal
Metabolic acidosis with coexisting respiratory acidosis
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with coexisting metabolic alkalosis
Mixed high anion gap (after albumin correction) and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, with appropriate respiratory compensation

questions.stem: Plasma: Na⁺ 138, K⁺ 4, Cl⁻ 108, lactate 4 mmol/L (Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ignored); HCO₃⁻ 14 mmol/L; charge of albumin + phosphate (A⁻) 8 mmol/L.
options: Lactate is a weak acid and belongs to ATOT.
The strong ion gap of about 8 mmol/L excludes unmeasured anions other than lactate.
Hypoalbuminaemia in this patient would exert an acidifying effect.
The apparent SID is about 22 mmol/L.
questions.expl: SIDa = (138 + 4) − (108 + 4) = 30; SIDe = 14 + 8 = 22; SIG = 8 → unmeasured anions **in addition** to lactate (lactate is already in SIDa). Lactate is a strong anion; ATOT = albumin and phosphate; hypoalbuminaemia (↓ ATOT) is **alkalinising**. ([W05/D2](#W05-D2))

questions.stem: A previously healthy patient with an opioid overdose has PaCO₂ 70 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 27 mmol/L. Which description and pH are consistent?
options: Acute respiratory acidosis with appropriate acute compensation, pH ≈ 7.21
Primary metabolic alkalosis, pH ≈ 7.45
Chronic compensated respiratory acidosis, pH ≈ 7.32
Acute respiratory acidosis with coexisting metabolic alkalosis, pH ≈ 7.30
Respiratory acidosis with coexisting metabolic acidosis, pH ≈ 7.10
questions.expl: Acute: HCO₃⁻ ↑ by 1 per 10 mmHg → 24 + 3 = 27 (exactly). pH = 6.1 + log(27 / 2.1) = 6.1 + 1.11 ≈ **7.21**. Chronically HCO₃⁻ would be ~34.5. ([W05/D1](#W05-D1))

questions.stem: An ICU patient on a current furosemide infusion, with nasogastric suction and hypoalbuminaemia, has pH 7.52 and HCO₃⁻ 34 mmol/L.
options: Hypokalaemia contributes to the maintenance of metabolic alkalosis.
Severe alkalaemia shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the right.
In Stewart terms, chloride loss increases the strong ion difference.
Current loop diuretic use typically gives urine Cl⁻ > 20 mmol/L.
questions.expl: Alkalaemia shifts the dissociation curve to the **left**. Current diuretics = chloride-resistant (U-Cl⁻ > 20), previous diuretics = chloride-responsive. ([W05/D3](#W05-D3))

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock has pH 7.15, PaCO₂ 35 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L and KDIGO stage 3 AKI. Which statement about sodium bicarbonate is most accurate?
options: It reduces CO₂ production, so minute ventilation can be lowered
SSC 2021 suggests considering it in septic shock with pH ≤ 7.2 and AKI; BICARICU-2 showed no difference in 90-day mortality but less kidney replacement therapy
BICARICU-2 showed a significant reduction in 90-day mortality
It raises ionised calcium
It improves haemodynamics in hypoperfusion-related lactic acidaemia
questions.expl: BICARICU-2: 62.1 vs 61.7 %, KRT 35 vs 50 %. Risks: hypernatraemia, ↓ iCa²⁺, intracellular acidosis from CO₂ (ventilation must be increased). ([W05/D2](#W05-D2))

questions.stem: A patient presents with visual disturbance: Na⁺ 138 mmol/L, glucose 5 mmol/L, urea 7 mmol/L, measured osmolality 320 mOsm/kg, ethanol undetectable, anion gap 30 mmol/L, lactate 1.5, ketones negative.
options: The picture suggests ethylene glycol poisoning, with oxalic acid as the main toxic metabolite.
The osmolal gap is about 32 mOsm/kg.
Haemodialysis is not indicated once fomepizole has been started.
Folate is a recommended cofactor in methanol poisoning.
questions.expl: Visual disturbance points to **methanol** (formic acid). Calculated osmolality = 2 × 138 + 5 + 7 = 288; OG = 320 − 288 = **32**. Dialysis (severe acidosis, visual disturbance, AKI) removes both the parent compound and the metabolites. ([W05/D3](#W05-D3))

questions.stem: A patient with DKA (pH 7.12, HCO₃⁻ 9 mmol/L) has K⁺ 3.2 mmol/L. According to the 2024 consensus, the next step is:
options: Withhold IV fluids until potassium is corrected
Replace potassium and delay insulin until K⁺ is ≥ 3.5 mmol/L
Give an insulin bolus of 0.3 U/kg
Start fixed-rate insulin 0.1 U/kg/h immediately
Give sodium bicarbonate because pH < 7.2
questions.expl: K⁺ < 3.5 → delay insulin and replace K⁺ first. Bicarbonate only if pH < 7.0. ([W05/D3](#W05-D3))

questions.stem: A patient has pH 7.32, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 15 mmol/L, Na⁺ 140, Cl⁻ 92 mmol/L, albumin 40 g/L.
options: The anion gap is 33 mmol/L.
If the patient had chronic compensated respiratory acidosis with a high baseline HCO₃⁻, a ratio > 2 could arise without a true metabolic alkalosis.
The delta ratio is > 2, suggesting a coexisting metabolic alkalosis (e.g. vomiting).
Respiratory compensation is inadequate, indicating an additional respiratory acidosis.
questions.expl: AG = 140 − 107 = 33; delta ratio = 21 / 9 ≈ 2.3; corrected HCO₃⁻ = 15 + 21 = 36 (> 26). Winter 1.5 × 15 + 8 = 30.5 ± 2 → pCO₂ 30 appropriate. ([W05/D1](#W05-D1))

questions.stem: A patient with short bowel syndrome presents with confusion and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Laboratory lactate is normal; ketones and osmolal gap are normal. The most likely cause is:
options: Type A lactic acidosis
Metformin accumulation
Isopropanol ingestion
Normal anion gap acidosis from diarrhoea
D-lactic acidosis
questions.expl: D-lactate from bacterial fermentation; standard analysers measure only L-lactate → an "invisible" HAGMA with encephalopathy. Isopropanol: ketosis without acidosis, ↑ OG. ([W05/D2](#W05-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding saline-induced hyperchloraemic acidosis:
options: In SMART, balanced crystalloids were associated with a higher rate of the composite MAKE30.
It is characterised by a raised anion gap.
0.9 % saline has an SID of zero and dilutes plasma SID.
The urine anion gap is expected to be positive, as in distal RTA.
questions.expl: A: lower with balanced crystalloids – 14.3 vs 15.4 %. B: normal AG. D: renal NH₄⁺ excretion is intact, so the UAG is negative (as in diarrhoea). ([W05/D2](#W05-D2), [W01/D3](#W01-D3))

title: W05 · Saturday – weekly review: Acid–base

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with septic shock: pH 7.22, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 12 mmol/L, Na⁺ 139, Cl⁻ 104 mmol/L, albumin 20 g/L. Which statement is correct?
options: Primary respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis with a coexisting respiratory alkalosis
Normal anion gap acidosis with appropriate compensation
Pure high anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation
High anion gap metabolic acidosis with a coexisting respiratory acidosis
questions.expl:
**Why E:** AG = 139 − (104 + 12) = 23; albumin correction 0.25 × 20 = 5 → corrected AG **28** → HAGMA. Winter's formula: 1.5 × 12 + 8 = 26 ± 2 (24–28); PaCO₂ 30 > 28 → coexisting respiratory acidosis (an inadequate ventilatory response). Check: pH = 6.1 + log(12 / 0.9) = 6.1 + 1.12 ≈ 7.22 ✓. Delta ratio (28 − 12) / (24 − 12) = 1.3 → no further metabolic disorder.

**Why not the others:**
- A – HCO₃⁻ is low and PaCO₂ is below normal, so the primary disorder is metabolic.
- B – a respiratory alkalosis would need a PaCO₂ below 24 mmHg.
- C – the AG is raised (23 uncorrected, 28 corrected).
- D – PaCO₂ is above the Winter range, so compensation is not appropriate.

**Ref:** Figge J et al., Crit Care Med 1998;26:1807–1810; Berend K et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:1434–1445.

questions.stem: Regarding the anion gap and its correction:
options: Modern ion-selective electrode analysers tend to give a lower reference range than the classical 12 ± 4 mmol/L.
Without albumin correction, a hidden gap acidosis is rarely missed in ICU patients.
The anion gap rises in hypoalbuminaemia.
Each 10 g/L fall in albumin lowers the anion gap by about 2.5 mmol/L.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ion-selective electrodes read Cl⁻ higher, so the reference range is ~3–11 mmol/L; each laboratory should use its own range.
- B (False) – hypoalbuminaemia is almost universal in the ICU, and Fencl found that the uncorrected AG missed most hidden gap acidoses.
- C (False) – albumin is the main unmeasured anion, so hypoalbuminaemia **lowers** the AG.
- D (True) – 0.25 × 10 = 2.5 mmol/L (Figge).

**Ref:** Kraut JA, Madias NE, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2007;2:162–174; Fencl V et al., Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2000;162:2246–2251; Figge J et al., Crit Care Med 1998;26:1807–1810.

questions.stem: Plasma: Na⁺ 141, K⁺ 4, Cl⁻ 118, lactate 1 mmol/L (Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ ignored). The apparent SID and its implication are:
options: 22 mmol/L – respiratory acidosis
26 mmol/L – metabolic alkalosis
40 mmol/L – normal
46 mmol/L – metabolic alkalosis
26 mmol/L – metabolic acidosis
questions.expl:
**Why E:** SIDa = (141 + 4) − (118 + 1) = 145 − 119 = **26 mmol/L**. Normal is ~40–42, so the SID is reduced by ~15 → metabolic acidosis, here hyperchloraemic (Na − Cl = 23, also low).

**Why not the others:**
- A – 22 omits K⁺, and the SID is a metabolic, not a respiratory, variable.
- B – the number is right, but a **low** SID means acidosis, not alkalosis.
- C – 40 is the normal SID, not this patient's value.
- D – an SID of 46 would need a much lower chloride; a high SID means alkalosis, which does not fit these values.

**Ref:** Kellum JA, Crit Care 2000;4:6–14.

questions.stem: Which of the following are independent variables determining plasma pH in the Stewart model?
options: Strong ion difference
Base excess
Bicarbonate
Total weak acid concentration (albumin, phosphate)
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the SID (strong cations − strong anions) is one of the three independent variables.
- B (False) – base excess is a derived index of the metabolic component; it reflects changes in SID and ATOT and is not an independent determinant.
- C (False) – HCO₃⁻ is a dependent variable, set by PaCO₂, SID and ATOT.
- D (True) – ATOT (albumin, phosphate) is the third independent variable, alongside PaCO₂.

**Ref:** Kellum JA, Crit Care 2000;4:6–14; Stewart PA, Can J Physiol Pharmacol 1983;61:1444–1461.

questions.stem: A patient has a high anion gap acidosis with AG 26 mmol/L (albumin 40 g/L) and HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L. The delta ratio and interpretation are:
options: 1.7 – pure HAGMA
2.4 – HAGMA with metabolic alkalosis
1.0 – pure HAGMA
0.4 – combined HAGMA and NAGMA
0.2 – pure NAGMA
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Delta ratio = (26 − 12) / (24 − 10) = 14 / 14 = **1.0**. The fall in HCO₃⁻ matches the rise in unmeasured anions, so this is a pure HAGMA; a ratio of ~1 is typical of DKA because ketoanions are lost in the urine.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 1.7 would need an AG of ~36 for this HCO₃⁻ (typical of lactic acidosis).
- B – a ratio > 2 would need an AG of ~46, and the conclusion (metabolic alkalosis) would then differ.
- D – 0.4 would mean an AG of only ~18, i.e. a large NAGMA component.
- E – 0.2 would mean an almost normal AG (~15), i.e. a NAGMA.

**Ref:** Rastegar A, J Am Soc Nephrol 2007;18:2429–2431.

questions.stem: Regarding lactic acidosis:
options: D-lactate is detected by standard lactate analysers.
Thiamine deficiency can cause lactic acidosis.
Type A is defined by the absence of tissue hypoxia or hypoperfusion.
Adrenaline lowers lactate by improving tissue perfusion.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – standard analysers use L-lactate-specific enzymes; D-lactate (short bowel, propylene glycol) needs a dedicated assay.
- B (True) – thiamine is a cofactor of pyruvate dehydrogenase. Deficiency (alcohol, malnutrition, refeeding) diverts pyruvate to lactate, a type B lactic acidosis.
- C (False) – type A means tissue hypoxia or hypoperfusion; type B occurs **without** it.
- D (False) – adrenaline **raises** lactate through β₂-stimulated aerobic glycolysis.

**Ref:** Kraut JA, Madias NE, N Engl J Med 2014;371:2309–2319.

questions.stem: A patient with COPD and chronic hypercapnia (baseline PaCO₂ 65 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 32 mmol/L) is intubated and ventilated to PaCO₂ 40 mmHg. Two hours later: pH 7.53, HCO₃⁻ 32 mmol/L. The best management is:
options: Start hydrochloric acid infusion
Ignore – the alkalosis is harmless
Reduce minute ventilation, targeting the patient's usual PaCO₂
Increase minute ventilation further
Give sodium bicarbonate
questions.expl:
**Why C:** This is post-hypercapnic alkalosis. HCO₃⁻ retained during chronic hypercapnia (32) persists while PaCO₂ has been corrected acutely: pH = 6.1 + log(32 / (0.03 × 40)) = 6.1 + 1.43 = **7.53**. Reducing minute ventilation towards the patient's usual PaCO₂ normalises pH; also correct Cl⁻ and K⁺ deficits.

**Why not the others:**
- A – HCl is invasive and reserved for severe refractory alkalosis; here the cause is the ventilator setting.
- B – alkalaemia causes hypokalaemia, low ionised calcium, arrhythmias, reduced cerebral blood flow and seizures.
- D – lowering PaCO₂ further would worsen the alkalaemia.
- E – bicarbonate would worsen the alkalosis.

**Ref:** Emmett M, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2020;15:1848–1856; Berend K et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:1434–1445.

questions.stem: Regarding chloride and metabolic alkalosis:
options: During active vomiting, urine sodium may be high because of bicarbonaturia.
Urine chloride < 20 mmol/L suggests a chloride-responsive alkalosis.
Chloride-responsive alkalosis is treated with NaCl and KCl.
Hypertension with hypokalaemic alkalosis suggests mineralocorticoid excess.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – filtered HCO₃⁻ exceeding reabsorptive capacity carries Na⁺ (and K⁺) into the urine, so U-Na⁺ is high despite depletion; U-Cl⁻ is the reliable marker.
- B (True) – a U-Cl⁻ < 20 mmol/L reflects avid Cl⁻ retention (vomiting, NG suction, previous diuretics).
- C (True) – Cl⁻ and volume repletion allow the kidney to excrete HCO₃⁻; KCl removes hypokalaemia as a maintenance factor.
- D (True) – mineralocorticoid excess (Conn's, Cushing's, renovascular disease, liquorice) causes hypertension, hypokalaemia and a chloride-resistant alkalosis.

**Ref:** Emmett M, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2020;15:1848–1856.

questions.stem: Na⁺ 140, glucose 10, urea 10 mmol/L; measured osmolality 322 mOsm/kg; blood ethanol 0. AG 28 mmol/L, lactate 1.5, ketones negative. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Isopropanol ingestion
Toxic alcohol ingestion (e.g. ethylene glycol)
Uraemic acidosis
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Lactic acidosis type B
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Calculated osmolality = 2 × 140 + 10 + 10 = 300 mOsm/kg. OG = 322 − 300 = **22** (> 10). Together with an unexplained HAGMA (AG 28, normal lactate, negative ketones), this means methanol or ethylene glycol until proven otherwise → fomepizole and consider haemodialysis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – isopropanol (→ acetone) raises the OG but causes ketosis without a HAGMA.
- C – urea of 10 mmol/L is too modest to explain an AG of 28, and urea is already counted in the calculated osmolality.
- D – ketones are negative and glucose is only 10 mmol/L.
- E – lactate of 1.5 mmol/L is normal.

**Ref:** Kraut JA, Mullins ME, N Engl J Med 2018;378:270–280.

questions.stem: Regarding bicarbonate therapy in severe metabolic acidaemia:
options: Bicarbonate may raise ionised calcium.
BICARICU-2 showed lower 90-day mortality with bicarbonate.
Both trials showed less need for kidney replacement therapy with bicarbonate.
In BICAR-ICU, bicarbonate improved the primary outcome in the prespecified AKIN 2–3 stratum.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – alkalinisation increases calcium binding to albumin and **lowers** ionised calcium; other risks are hypernatraemia, hyperosmolality and CO₂ generation.
- B (False) – BICARICU-2 found no difference in 90-day mortality (62.1 % vs 61.7 %).
- C (True) – BICAR-ICU showed less RRT overall, and BICARICU-2 showed less KRT by day 28 (35 % vs 50 %).
- D (True) – in BICAR-ICU's prespecified AKIN 2–3 stratum, the composite outcome was 70 % vs 82 %.

**EDIC trap:** SSC 2021 suggests considering bicarbonate only for pH ≤ 7.2 with AKI 2–3, not to improve haemodynamics.

**Ref:** Jaber S et al., Lancet 2018;392:31–40; Jung B et al., JAMA 2025 (doi:10.1001/jama.2025.20231).

questions.stem: Which fluid has an in vivo strong ion difference of zero and is most likely to cause hyperchloraemic acidosis?
options: 20 % albumin
0.9 % sodium chloride
4.2 % sodium bicarbonate
Ringer's lactate
Plasma-Lyte 148
questions.expl:
**Why B:** 0.9 % NaCl contains Na⁺ 154 and Cl⁻ 154 mmol/L, so its SID is **0**. Large volumes dilute plasma SID (~40) towards zero, causing a hyperchloraemic, normal-AG acidosis. In SMART, balanced crystalloids reduced MAKE30 (14.3 % vs 15.4 %).

**Why not the others:**
- A – albumin solutions act mainly through ATOT (a weak acid load), not through a zero SID; they are not the classic cause of hyperchloraemia.
- C – 4.2 % NaHCO₃ contains ~500 mmol/L Na⁺ and no Cl⁻, a very high SID that is alkalinising.
- D – Ringer's lactate has an in vivo SID of ~28 once lactate is metabolised.
- E – Plasma-Lyte 148 has an in vivo SID of ~50 once acetate and gluconate are metabolised.

**Ref:** Kellum JA, Crit Care 2000;4:6–14; Semler MW et al. (SMART), N Engl J Med 2018;378:829–839.

questions.stem: A patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor presents unwell after surgery: glucose 9 mmol/L, pH 7.18, HCO₃⁻ 9 mmol/L, β-hydroxybutyrate 5.5 mmol/L. Which statements are correct?
options: Insulin should be withheld because glucose is near-normal.
DKA is excluded because glucose is < 11.1 mmol/L.
This is consistent with euglycaemic DKA.
This DKA is classified as severe.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – insulin is essential to stop ketogenesis; give it with 5–10 % glucose to prevent hypoglycaemia, and stop the SGLT2 inhibitor.
- B (False) – known diabetes meets the glucose criterion whatever the glucose value; this is euglycaemic DKA.
- C (True) – β-OHB ≥ 3.0, pH < 7.3 and HCO₃⁻ < 18 with glucose < 11.1 mmol/L on an SGLT2 inhibitor are typical of euglycaemic DKA (~10 % of cases).
- D (True) – HCO₃⁻ 9 mmol/L (< 10) is enough to classify it as severe.

**Ref:** Umpierrez GE et al., Diabetes Care 2024;47:1257–1275.

questions.stem: Which arterial blood gas is internally inconsistent (likely a sampling or transcription error)?
options: PaCO₂ 40 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 24 mmol/L, pH 7.40
PaCO₂ 60 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 30 mmol/L, pH 7.32
PaCO₂ 20 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 8 mmol/L, pH 7.22
PaCO₂ 30 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 20 mmol/L, pH 7.45
PaCO₂ 48 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 36 mmol/L, pH 7.30
questions.expl:
**Why E:** [H⁺] = 24 × PaCO₂ / HCO₃⁻ = 24 × 48 / 36 = **32 nmol/L** → pH ≈ 7.50. A reported pH of 7.30 corresponds to [H⁺] of 50 nmol/L, so the values cannot all be correct: suspect a sampling or transcription error and repeat the gas.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 24 × 40 / 24 = 40 nmol/L → pH 7.40 ✓.
- B – 24 × 60 / 30 = 48 nmol/L → pH ≈ 7.32 ✓.
- C – 24 × 20 / 8 = 60 nmol/L → pH ≈ 7.22 ✓.
- D – 24 × 30 / 20 = 36 nmol/L → pH ≈ 7.44–7.45 ✓.

**EDIC trap:** between pH 7.20 and 7.50, each 0.01 pH unit ≈ 1 nmol/L of H⁺ in the opposite direction.

**Ref:** Berend K, de Vries AP, Gans RO, N Engl J Med 2014;371:1434–1445.

questions.stem: Regarding mixed acid–base disorders:
options: Salicylate poisoning typically causes respiratory alkalosis plus high anion gap metabolic acidosis.
A normal pH excludes an acid–base disorder.
A delta ratio > 2 may indicate a coexisting metabolic alkalosis.
A PaCO₂ below the Winter prediction indicates an additional respiratory alkalosis.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – salicylates directly stimulate the respiratory centre (respiratory alkalosis) and uncouple oxidative phosphorylation (lactate, ketoacids → HAGMA).
- B (False) – opposing disorders can cancel out (salicylates, sepsis + vomiting); Fencl found a normal BE and HCO₃⁻ in ~1/6 of patients with severe opposing disorders.
- C (True) – HCO₃⁻ has fallen less than the AG has risen, suggesting a coexisting metabolic alkalosis (or a high baseline HCO₃⁻ from chronic hypercapnia).
- D (True) – a PaCO₂ below the expected 1.5 × HCO₃⁻ + 8 ± 2 means an additional respiratory alkalosis; above it, a respiratory acidosis.

**Ref:** Berend K et al., N Engl J Med 2014;371:1434–1445; Rastegar A, J Am Soc Nephrol 2007;18:2429–2431.

questions.stem: A ventilated COPD patient with metabolic alkalosis is considered for acetazolamide. Based on DIABOLO, the best statement is:
options: Acetazolamide increased mortality
Acetazolamide did not significantly reduce the duration of invasive ventilation
Acetazolamide significantly reduced the duration of invasive ventilation
DIABOLO compared acetazolamide with hydrochloric acid
Acetazolamide is contraindicated in metabolic alkalosis
questions.expl:
**Why B:** DIABOLO randomised 380 ventilated COPD patients to acetazolamide or placebo. Median duration of invasive ventilation was 136.5 vs 163 h (p = 0.17, NS). Acetazolamide lowered HCO₃⁻ modestly, but this did not translate into faster liberation; the trial may have been underpowered.

**Why not the others:**
- A – there was no significant difference in mortality.
- C – the reduction in ventilation time was not statistically significant.
- D – the comparator was placebo, not hydrochloric acid.
- E – acetazolamide (which inhibits proximal HCO₃⁻ reabsorption) is used to treat metabolic alkalosis; the caution is hypokalaemia.

**Ref:** Faisy C et al. (DIABOLO), JAMA 2016;315:480–488.

title: W06 · D1 – Hypo- and hypernatraemia: algorithm, rate of correction, ODS

questions.stem: A 45-year-old has a generalised seizure; Na⁺ 116 mmol/L, duration unknown. The most appropriate first treatment according to the European guideline is:
options: 150 mL of 3 % saline IV over 20 minutes, repeated as needed with sodium checks
Fluid restriction to 800 mL/day
0.9 % saline 1 L over 1 hour
Tolvaptan 15 mg orally
3 % saline infusion at 0.5 mL/kg/h, aiming for +8 mmol/L in 24 h
questions.expl:
**Why A:** A seizure is a severe symptom, and the guideline recommends 150 mL of 3 % NaCl IV over 20 min immediately, checking Na⁺ after 20 min and repeating up to twice (3 boluses in total). The aim is a rise of about 5 mmol/L in the first hour, whatever the duration.

**Why not the others:**
- B – fluid restriction raises Na⁺ by only a few mmol/L per day, which is far too slow for a patient who is seizing.
- C – 0.9 % saline raises Na⁺ by < 1 mmol/L per litre and can even lower it in SIAD.
- D – vaptans act slowly and unpredictably and are not recommended for severe symptoms.
- E – a slow infusion delays the urgent 5 mmol/L rise.

**EDIC trap:** treat a hyponatraemia of unknown duration as chronic for the correction limits, but severe symptoms still get boluses.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., ESICM/ESE/ERBP hyponatraemia guideline, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (full version Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47); Baek SH et al. (SALSA), JAMA Intern Med 2021;181:81–92.

questions.stem: Regarding the diagnostic approach to hypotonic hyponatraemia (European guideline):
options: SIAD can be diagnosed while the patient is hypovolaemic.
Urine osmolality ≤ 100 mOsm/kg is typical of SIAD.
Urine sodium ≤ 30 mmol/L suggests a low effective arterial blood volume.
Adrenal insufficiency must be excluded before diagnosing SIAD.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – SIAD requires clinical euvolaemia. Hypovolaemia is itself a non-osmotic stimulus for ADH, so it must be excluded or corrected first.
- B (False) – urine osmolality ≤ 100 mOsm/kg means ADH is suppressed (primary polydipsia, beer potomania, low solute intake); in SIAD it is > 100 mOsm/kg.
- C (True) – urine Na⁺ ≤ 30 mmol/L reflects avid renal Na⁺ retention caused by a low effective arterial volume (extrarenal losses, heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome).
- D (True) – adrenal insufficiency (cortisol deficiency stimulates ADH), hypothyroidism, pituitary and renal insufficiency and recent diuretic use must all be excluded before SIAD is diagnosed.

**EDIC trap:** diuretics raise urine Na⁺ even when the patient is hypovolaemic, so U-Na⁺ > 30 in a patient on a thiazide does not prove SIAD.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., ESICM/ESE/ERBP hyponatraemia guideline, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (full version Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47).

questions.stem: A 60-kg woman (TBW 0.5 × body weight) has Na⁺ 112 mmol/L. Using the Adrogué–Madias formula, 1 L of 3 % saline (Na⁺ 513 mmol/L) would be expected to raise serum Na⁺ by approximately:
options: 18 mmol/L
13 mmol/L
4 mmol/L
25 mmol/L
8 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why B:** TBW = 0.5 × 60 = 30 L. By Adrogué–Madias, ΔNa⁺ = (infusate Na⁺ + K⁺ − serum Na⁺) / (TBW + 1) = (513 + 0 − 112) / (30 + 1) = 401 / 31 ≈ **12.9 mmol/L**. One litre would exceed the 24 h limit even before any aquaresis.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 18 mmol/L would mean dividing 401 by ~22 L instead of TBW + 1 = 31 L, so it overestimates.
- C – 4 mmol/L is roughly the effect of only ~300 mL of 3 % saline (0.3 × 12.9), so it underestimates threefold.
- D – 25 mmol/L would need a TBW of only ~15 L, which nearly doubles the true effect.
- E – 8 mmol/L would need a TBW of ~49 L, i.e. a much heavier patient.

**EDIC trap:** the formula ignores urine output, so with aquaresis the real rise can be much larger. Check Na⁺ every 2–4 h.

**Ref:** Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1581–1589; Spasovski G et al., ESICM/ESE/ERBP hyponatraemia guideline, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (full version Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47).

questions.stem: Regarding correction of chronic hyponatraemia:
options: Hypokalaemia, alcoholism and malnutrition decrease the risk of osmotic demyelination.
Overcorrection should be managed by continuing hypertonic saline at a lower rate.
The rise in Na⁺ should not exceed 20 mmol/L in the first 24 hours.
After the first day, the limit is 8 mmol/L per 24 hours until Na⁺ reaches 130 mmol/L.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – hypokalaemia, alcoholism, malnutrition, advanced liver disease and Na⁺ ≤ 105 mmol/L **increase** the risk of osmotic demyelination; in these patients aim for ≤ 8 mmol/L/24 h.
- B (False) – stop the hypertonic saline and actively re-lower Na⁺ with 10 mL/kg of electrolyte-free water (e.g. 5 % glucose) over 1 h ± desmopressin 2 µg IV (no more often than every 8 h), with close Na⁺ monitoring.
- C (False) – the limit is 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h; a 20 mmol/L rise would be dangerous overcorrection.
- D (True) – after the first day, Na⁺ may rise by ≤ 8 mmol/L in every further 24 h until it reaches 130 mmol/L.

**EDIC trap:** ODS appears 2–6 days after the overcorrection, so a well patient on day 1 does not exclude it.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., ESICM/ESE/ERBP hyponatraemia guideline, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (full version Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47); Sterns RH, N Engl J Med 2015;372:55–65.

questions.stem: A 70-kg man (TBW 0.6 × body weight) has Na⁺ 155 mmol/L. His free water deficit is approximately:
questions.expl:
**Why D:** TBW = 0.6 × 70 = 42 L. Free water deficit = TBW × (Na⁺/140 − 1) = 42 × (155/140 − 1) = 42 × 0.107 ≈ **4.5 L**. This figure leaves out ongoing losses (insensible, urinary, GI), which must be added. Chronic hypernatraemia is traditionally lowered by ≤ 10–12 mmol/L/24 h.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 3.0 L would need a TBW of ~28 L (0.4 × weight), so it underestimates the deficit.
- B – 6.0 L would need a TBW of ~56 L (0.8 × weight), which is physiologically implausible.
- C – 1.5 L is the result of using ECF volume (0.2 × weight = 14 L) instead of total body water.
- E – 7.5 L would match a Na⁺ of ~165 mmol/L in this patient.

**Ref:** Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, Hypernatremia, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1493–1499.

questions.stem: Regarding the SALSA trial:
options: It compared rapid intermittent boluses with slow continuous infusion of hypertonic saline.
Re-lowering therapy was needed more often with rapid intermittent boluses.
Several cases of osmotic demyelination occurred in the bolus group.
Rapid intermittent bolus significantly reduced overcorrection (the primary outcome).
questions.expl:
- A (True) – SALSA randomised 178 Korean patients with moderately severe or severe symptomatic hyponatraemia to rapid intermittent boluses (RIB) or a slow continuous infusion (SCI) of 3 % NaCl.
- B (False) – re-lowering therapy was needed **less** often with RIB (41.4 % vs 57.1 %).
- C (False) – no case of osmotic demyelination occurred in either group.
- D (False) – overcorrection, the primary outcome, did not differ significantly (17.2 % vs 24.2 %); RIB reached the early Na⁺ target more often.

**EDIC trap:** "not superior" does not mean "unsafe". SALSA supports the guideline's bolus strategy.

**Ref:** Baek SH et al., JAMA Intern Med 2021;181:81–92.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man drinking large volumes of beer with poor food intake has Na⁺ 118 mmol/L, serum osmolality 250 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 60 mOsm/kg. The most likely mechanism is:
options: Low solute intake with excess water (beer potomania)
Cerebral salt wasting
SIAD
Primary adrenal insufficiency
Pseudohyponatraemia
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Serum osmolality is 250 mOsm/kg, so the hyponatraemia is hypotonic, and urine osmolality ≤ 100 mOsm/kg means ADH is suppressed. Beer contains little solute, and the kidney can excrete water only with solute: maximal water excretion ≈ daily solute load / minimal U-osm (e.g. 250 mOsm / 50 mOsm/kg ≈ 5 L/day). Beer drunk beyond that volume is retained as free water.

**Why not the others:**
- B – cerebral salt wasting causes hypovolaemia with high urine Na⁺ and concentrated urine (ADH appropriately on).
- C – SIAD requires urine osmolality > 100 mOsm/kg.
- D – primary adrenal insufficiency gives concentrated urine with high urine Na⁺, hypovolaemia and often hyperkalaemia.
- E – pseudohyponatraemia has a normal measured serum osmolality, not 250 mOsm/kg.

**EDIC trap:** once he eats again, solute intake rises and **aquaresis** follows, causing rapid overcorrection. His ODS risk is high (alcohol, malnutrition).

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., ESICM/ESE/ERBP hyponatraemia guideline, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (full version Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47); Sterns RH, N Engl J Med 2015;372:55–65.

questions.stem: Treatment of SIAD with moderate or profound hyponatraemia (no severe symptoms) according to the European guideline:
options: Vasopressin receptor antagonists are recommended in profound hyponatraemia.
Demeclocycline and lithium are recommended against.
Fluid restriction is first-line.
Urea is recommended against.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – the guideline does not recommend vasopressin receptor antagonists in moderate hyponatraemia and recommends **against** them in profound hyponatraemia (risk of overcorrection; tolvaptan is also hepatotoxic).
- B (True) – demeclocycline (nephrotoxic, unpredictable) and lithium are recommended against.
- C (True) – fluid restriction is first-line. It tends to fail when U-osm is > 500 mOsm/kg or (U-Na⁺ + U-K⁺) exceeds serum Na⁺.
- D (False) – urea 0.25–0.50 g/kg/day is a **second-line** option, as is a low-dose loop diuretic with oral NaCl.

**Ref:** Spasovski G et al., ESICM/ESE/ERBP hyponatraemia guideline, Intensive Care Med 2014;40:320–331 (full version Eur J Endocrinol 2014;170:G1–G47).

questions.stem: A patient with DKA has glucose 39.6 mmol/L and measured Na⁺ 125 mmol/L. Using a correction of 1.6 mmol/L per 5.6 mmol/L glucose above 5.6 mmol/L, the corrected Na⁺ is closest to:
options: 145 mmol/L
140 mmol/L
135 mmol/L
130 mmol/L
127 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why C:** (39.6 − 5.6) / 5.6 = 6.07 steps of 5.6 mmol/L; 6.07 × 1.6 = 9.7; 125 + 9.7 ≈ **135 mmol/L**. Glucose is an effective osmole that pulls water out of cells (translocational, hypertonic hyponatraemia). As insulin lowers the glucose, water re-enters cells and Na⁺ should rise towards the corrected value.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 145 mmol/L would need a factor of ~3.3 per 5.6 mmol/L, which overestimates.
- B – 140 mmol/L is the result with Hillier's factor of 2.4 per 5.6 mmol/L, not the 1.6 specified in the stem.
- D – 130 mmol/L adds only about half of the correction.
- E – 127 mmol/L corrects for barely one 5.6 mmol/L step.

**EDIC trap:** a corrected Na⁺ that is high-normal or rising during DKA treatment signals a free water deficit. It is not hypotonic hyponatraemia, so do not restrict water or give hypertonic saline.

**Ref:** Katz MA, N Engl J Med 1973;289:843–844; Hillier TA et al., Am J Med 1999;106:399–403.

questions.stem: Regarding hypernatraemia in the ICU:
options: A rise in urine osmolality after desmopressin suggests central diabetes insipidus.
Polyuria with urine osmolality < 300 mOsm/kg suggests diabetes insipidus.
In a retrospective ICU cohort (Chauhan 2019), rapid correction (> 0.5 mmol/L/h) was associated with higher mortality.
Acute hypernatraemia (< 48 h) can be corrected faster than chronic hypernatraemia.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in central DI the kidney still responds to ADH, so urine osmolality rises markedly after desmopressin; in nephrogenic DI the response is minimal.
- B (True) – in hypernatraemia the urine should be small in volume and maximally concentrated (> 600–800 mOsm/kg). Polyuria with U-osm < 300 mOsm/kg therefore points to DI.
- C (False) – in 449 critically ill adults, correction faster than 0.5 mmol/L/h was **not** associated with higher mortality or with cerebral oedema attributable to the correction.
- D (True) – in acute hypernatraemia (< 48 h) the brain has not yet accumulated organic osmolytes, so faster correction is safe. Chronic hypernatraemia is traditionally lowered by ≤ 10–12 mmol/L/24 h.

**Ref:** Chauhan K et al., Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 2019;14:656–663; Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1493–1499.

questions.stem: A ventilated trauma patient on day 6 receives high-protein enteral nutrition. Na⁺ has risen from 141 to 154 mmol/L over 5 days despite 2.5–3 L/day of urine. Glucose is normal and no mannitol or diuretics are given. Serum urea has risen to 22 mmol/L; urine osmolality is 720 mOsm/kg, urine Na⁺ + K⁺ = 70 mmol/L. The most likely mechanism is:
options: Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus
Urea-induced osmotic diuresis
Central diabetes insipidus
Primary sodium gain from hypertonic fluids
Insensible water loss with appropriate renal water conservation
questions.expl:
**Why B:** U-osm is high and urine volume large, so total solute excretion is ~720 × 2.75 ≈ 2000 mOsm/day (usual load ~600–900). Na⁺ + K⁺ explain only 2 × 70 = 140 of the 720 mOsm/kg, so most of the osmoles are urea from protein feeding and catabolism (serum urea 22 mmol/L). Electrolyte-free water clearance = 2.75 × [1 − 70/154] ≈ **1.5 L/day** of free water lost, which drives the Na⁺ up.

**Why not the others:**
- A – nephrogenic DI gives dilute or isosthenuric urine, not 720 mOsm/kg.
- C – central DI gives hypotonic urine (often < 150–300 mOsm/kg) that concentrates after desmopressin.
- D – no hypertonic fluids were given, and the low urine electrolyte content argues against a sodium load.
- E – appropriate renal water conservation means a small volume of concentrated urine, not 2.5–3 L/day.

**EDIC trap:** use the **electrolyte-free** water clearance (urine Na⁺ + K⁺), not total free water clearance. Treat with free water and review the protein load.

**Ref:** Lindner G et al., Nephrol Dial Transplant 2012;27:962–967.

questions.stem: Hypernatraemia with a normal or high urine output:
options: In central diabetes insipidus urine osmolality is inappropriately low and increases after desmopressin.
In the polyuric phase of AKI urine osmolality is typically close to plasma osmolality.
After high-dose furosemide, a urine osmolality close to plasma osmolality proves nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
Osmotic diuresis from mannitol or glucose produces urine with an osmolality above plasma.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – without ADH the urine stays hypotonic despite a high plasma osmolality (e.g. after brain death, TBI or pituitary surgery), and it concentrates after desmopressin.
- B (True) – recovering tubules cannot rebuild the medullary gradient, so the urine is isosthenuric (~280–320 mOsm/kg) and copious.
- C (False) – loop diuretics wash out the medullary concentration gradient, so the kidney cannot concentrate urine whatever the ADH level. Reassess after the drug effect has worn off.
- D (True) – the unreabsorbed solute drags water with it. The urine is iso- to hypertonic, but the large volume and low electrolyte content still cause a net loss of free water.

**EDIC trap:** in a hypernatraemic patient, a "normal" urine output is never appropriate. The expected response is a small volume of maximally concentrated urine.

**Ref:** Lindner G et al., Nephrol Dial Transplant 2012;27:962–967; Adrogué HJ, Madias NE, N Engl J Med 2000;342:1493–1499.

open.q: A 65-year-old malnourished alcoholic woman is admitted with vomiting and a seizure; Na⁺ 108 mmol/L, duration unknown. Outline your management over the first 48 hours.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Severe symptoms (seizure, vomiting) → 150 mL 3 % NaCl IV over 20 min, check Na⁺ after 20 min, repeat up to 3 boluses; target +5 mmol/L in the first hour (regardless of acuity).
- Unknown duration → treat as chronic; she has several ODS risk factors (Na⁺ near 105, alcoholism, malnutrition, possible hypokalaemia/liver disease) → cautious limit ~8 mmol/L/24 h.
- Absolute limits: ≤ 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h, ≤ 8 mmol/L per further 24 h until Na⁺ 130.
- Frequent Na⁺ checks (every 2–4 h initially) and urine output monitoring; the Adrogué–Madias formula ignores aquaresis.
- Anticipate aquaresis once the ADH stimulus resolves (volume repletion after vomiting, nausea settling, restored solute intake).
- If overcorrected: 10 mL/kg free water (5 % glucose) over 1 h ± desmopressin 2 µg IV (not more often than every 8 h).
- Diagnostic work-up in parallel: serum/urine osmolality, urine Na⁺, volume status, exclude adrenal/thyroid insufficiency; correct K⁺.

open.q: An 80-kg elderly man after neurosurgery has Na⁺ 160 mmol/L, polyuria and urine osmolality 150 mOsm/kg. Calculate his free water deficit and outline diagnosis and treatment.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Polyuria + urine osmolality < 300 → diabetes insipidus; after neurosurgery most likely central.
- Desmopressin test: a rise in urine osmolality confirms central DI (nephrogenic causes: lithium, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia).
- TBW = 0.5 × 80 = 40 L; deficit = 40 × (160/140 − 1) ≈ 5.7 L.
- 1 L of 5 % glucose lowers Na⁺ by (0 − 160) / 41 ≈ 3.9 mmol/L; ~2.6 L is needed to lower Na⁺ by 10 mmol/L/24 h, plus ongoing (urinary) losses.
- Acute hypernatraemia (< 48 h, DI after neurosurgery) can be corrected faster; for chronic, traditionally ≤ 10–12 mmol/L/24 h.
- Chauhan (CJASN 2019): faster correction (> 0.5 mmol/L/h) was not associated with higher mortality or cerebral oedema; evidence for the limit in adults is weak.
- Frequent Na⁺ monitoring; treat with desmopressin plus free water.

title: W06 · D2 – Potassium and magnesium: hyperkalaemia, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia

questions.stem: A haemodialysis patient has K⁺ 7.3 mmol/L with broad QRS complexes. The first drug to give is:
options: Calcium chloride 10 % 10 mL IV
Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g orally
Furosemide 80 mg IV
Nebulised salbutamol 10 mg
Insulin 10 units with 25 g glucose
questions.expl:
**Why A:** K⁺ 7.3 mmol/L with broad QRS complexes is severe hyperkalaemia (≥ 6.5 mmol/L) with ECG changes. ERC 2025 starts by protecting the heart with 10 mL 10 % CaCl₂ (≈ 6.8 mmol Ca²⁺) IV over 5 min, or 30 mL 10 % Ca gluconate. Calcium stabilises the myocardial membrane within minutes and lasts ~30–60 min, but it does not lower K⁺. Shifting therapies follow, then urgent dialysis, which is the definitive removal in this patient.

**Why not the others:**
- B – SZC removes K⁺ through the gut over hours, so it gives no immediate protection to the myocardium.
- C – furosemide needs residual renal function, which a haemodialysis patient usually lacks.
- D – salbutamol is an adjunct that shifts K⁺; it does not stabilise the membrane, and many dialysis patients respond poorly.
- E – insulin–glucose is the fastest K⁺-lowering drug (onset ~15–30 min), but with ECG changes it comes after calcium.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: Regarding insulin–glucose for hyperkalaemia (ERC 2025):
options: If pre-treatment glucose is < 7 mmol/L, a 10 % glucose infusion at 50 mL/h for 5 hours is suggested.
Nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg can be added.
Insulin removes potassium from the body.
The dose is 25 units of soluble insulin with 10 g glucose IV.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ERC 2025: if pre-treatment glucose is < 7 mmol/L, follow the bolus with 10 % glucose at 50 mL/h for 5 h (25 g) to prevent delayed hypoglycaemia.
- B (True) – nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg adds to the effect of insulin but is not sufficient on its own.
- C (False) – insulin stimulates Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and only **shifts** K⁺ into cells. Total body K⁺ is unchanged, so K⁺ rebounds unless it is removed (SZC, diuretic, dialysis).
- D (False) – the dose is 10 units of soluble insulin with **25 g** glucose IV (= 50 mL 50 %, 125 mL 20 % or 250 mL 10 %).

**EDIC trap:** hypoglycaemia is the most common complication, especially with low baseline glucose and renal failure (slower insulin clearance). Monitor glucose for several hours.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: You need to give 25 g of glucose and only 20 % glucose is available. The required volume is:
options: 250 mL
50 mL
100 mL
200 mL
125 mL
questions.expl:
**Why E:** 20 % glucose = 20 g per 100 mL = 0.2 g/mL, so 25 g / 0.2 g/mL = **125 mL**. The same 25 g dose is 50 mL of 50 % or 250 mL of 10 % glucose. This is the glucose given with 10 units of insulin for hyperkalaemia.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 250 mL is the volume needed with 10 % glucose.
- B – 50 mL is the volume needed with 50 % glucose.
- C – 100 mL of 20 % glucose provides only 20 g.
- D – 200 mL of 20 % glucose provides 40 g.

**EDIC trap:** 50 % glucose is very irritant to veins. Diluted solutions are kinder to peripheral veins but add volume.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: Regarding calcium in hyperkalaemia:
options: In hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest, calcium and sodium bicarbonate should not be given together through the same line without flushing.
10 mL of 10 % calcium gluconate contains roughly three times more calcium than 10 mL of 10 % calcium chloride.
Calcium lowers the serum potassium concentration.
Its membrane-stabilising effect lasts about 24 hours, so a single dose suffices.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – calcium and bicarbonate precipitate as CaCO₃, so give them through separate lines or flush in between. In hyperkalaemic arrest ERC 2025 recommends 10 mL 10 % CaCl₂ plus 50 mmol NaHCO₃.
- B (False) – the reverse is true: 10 mL 10 % CaCl₂ contains ≈ 6.8 mmol Ca²⁺ and 10 mL 10 % gluconate ≈ 2.2 mmol, so ~30 mL of gluconate is needed for an equivalent dose.
- C (False) – calcium restores the gap between resting and threshold membrane potential and leaves the serum K⁺ unchanged.
- D (False) – the effect lasts only ~30–60 min. Repeat the dose if ECG changes persist, and always add shifting and removal therapy.

**EDIC trap:** CaCl₂ is more irritant on extravasation, so give it through a large or central vein.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: A patient on furosemide and long-term omeprazole has K⁺ 2.9 mmol/L that does not improve despite 3 days of IV KCl. The most likely contributing factor is:
options: Metabolic acidosis
Hypercalcaemia
Hypophosphataemia
Hyponatraemia
Hypomagnesaemia
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Loop diuretics (renal Mg²⁺ loss) and long-term PPIs (impaired intestinal absorption via TRPM6/7) both cause magnesium deficiency. Low intracellular Mg²⁺ releases its normal block of the ROMK channels in the collecting duct, so the kidney keeps wasting K⁺. KCl stays ineffective until Mg²⁺ is replaced (e.g. MgSO₄ 2 g ≈ 8 mmol IV, then an infusion).

**Why not the others:**
- A – metabolic acidosis shifts K⁺ out of cells and raises serum K⁺; furosemide usually causes alkalosis.
- B – hypercalcaemia is not a recognised cause of KCl-refractory hypokalaemia in this setting, and loop diuretics tend to lower calcium.
- C – hypophosphataemia often coexists (refeeding, alkalosis) but does not block K⁺ repletion.
- D – hyponatraemia does not cause renal K⁺ wasting.

**EDIC trap:** a normal serum Mg²⁺ does not exclude depletion (< 1 % is in serum), so replace empirically if hypokalaemia is refractory.

**Ref:** Gennari FJ, N Engl J Med 1998;339:451–458; Huang CL, Kuo E, J Am Soc Nephrol 2007;18:2649–2652.

questions.stem: ECG features of hypokalaemia include:
options: ST-segment depression
U waves
T-wave flattening or inversion
Prolonged QT(U) interval with risk of torsades de pointes
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ST-segment depression is a typical repolarisation change of hypokalaemia.
- B (True) – U waves (most prominent in V2–V3) reflect delayed repolarisation and grow as K⁺ falls.
- C (True) – the T wave flattens or inverts, and it may merge with the U wave.
- D (True) – the QT(U) interval lengthens and predisposes to torsades de pointes, especially with hypomagnesaemia, digoxin or QT-prolonging drugs.

**EDIC trap:** peaked T waves, a prolonged PR and a broad QRS point to **hyperkalaemia**. Correlation of the ECG with the K⁺ level is poor in both directions.

**Ref:** Gennari FJ, N Engl J Med 1998;339:451–458; ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: In cardiac arrest attributed to severe hypokalaemia, ERC 2025 suggests:
options: Potassium is contraindicated during CPR
KCl 100 mmol as a bolus
KCl 40 mmol over 1 hour
Oral potassium after ROSC only
KCl 20 mmol IV over 2–3 minutes, followed by 10 mmol over 2 minutes
questions.expl:
**Why E:** ERC 2025 recommends KCl **20 mmol IV/IO over 2–3 min, then 10 mmol over 2 min** for hypokalaemic cardiac arrest, followed by an infusion adjusted to repeated K⁺ measurements, with any magnesium deficit corrected at the same time. A rapid potassium bolus is justified only during arrest, where the rhythm is already lethal. Outside arrest, peripheral rates are kept to ~10 mmol/h.

**Why not the others:**
- A – severe hypokalaemia is a reversible cause of arrest (one of the "4 Hs"), and correcting it is part of ALS.
- B – a 100 mmol bolus would cause fatal hyperkalaemia.
- C – 40 mmol over 1 h is too slow during arrest; it is a monitored central-line replacement rate.
- D – waiting until ROSC leaves the cause untreated, and oral potassium is impossible during CPR.

**Ref:** ERC Guidelines 2025: Special Circumstances in Resuscitation, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110753.

questions.stem: Recognised causes of hyperkalaemia include:
options: Metabolic alkalosis
Succinylcholine in a patient with a 2-week-old spinal cord injury
Pseudohyperkalaemia from marked thrombocytosis
Furosemide
questions.expl:
- A (False) – alkalosis shifts K⁺ into cells and increases kaliuresis, which causes **hypo**kalaemia. It is mineral (hyperchloraemic) acidosis that raises K⁺.
- B (True) – denervation up-regulates extrajunctional (including α7) acetylcholine receptors from about 24–72 h after injury, lasting for months. Succinylcholine then causes massive K⁺ efflux and a risk of arrest.
- C (True) – platelets release K⁺ during clotting in a serum tube. A heparinised plasma or whole-blood sample (blood gas analyser) shows the true value.
- D (False) – loop diuretics increase distal Na⁺ delivery and flow, which causes kaliuresis and hypokalaemia. K⁺-sparing diuretics, ACEi/ARB and trimethoprim cause hyperkalaemia.

**Ref:** Martyn JAJ, Richtsfeld M, Anesthesiology 2006;104:158–169; Clase CM et al. (KDIGO), Kidney Int 2020;97:42–61.

questions.stem: A patient with torsades de pointes receives 2 g of magnesium sulphate (MgSO₄·7H₂O). This corresponds to approximately:
options: 2 mmol Mg²⁺
8 mmol Mg²⁺
4 mmol Mg²⁺
20 mmol Mg²⁺
16 mmol Mg²⁺
questions.expl:
**Why B:** MgSO₄·7H₂O has a molar mass of ≈ 246 g/mol, so 1 g ≈ 4.06 mmol Mg²⁺ and 2 g = 2000 / 246 ≈ **8 mmol** (= 16 mEq, because Mg²⁺ is divalent). In torsades de pointes, 2 g IV is given whatever the serum magnesium level.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 2 mmol treats grams as millimoles.
- C – 4 mmol corresponds to 1 g, not 2 g.
- D – 20 mmol is about 5 g of MgSO₄·7H₂O.
- E – 16 is the value in mEq, not mmol.

**EDIC trap:** check whether a question uses mmol or mEq. For a divalent ion, mEq = 2 × mmol.

**Ref:** Soar J et al., ERC Guidelines 2025 Adult Advanced Life Support, Resuscitation 2025;215(Suppl 1):110769.

questions.stem: Regarding magnesium:
options: A normal serum magnesium reliably excludes total body magnesium deficiency.
Severe hypermagnesaemia can cause loss of deep tendon reflexes and respiratory depression.
Hypomagnesaemia may cause hypocalcaemia by impairing PTH secretion and action.
Long-term proton pump inhibitor use can cause hypomagnesaemia.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – < 1 % of total body magnesium is in serum (most is in bone and cells), so a normal serum level does not exclude a deficit.
- B (True) – Mg²⁺ reduces acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction. Deep tendon reflexes disappear at ~3.5–5 mmol/L, followed by respiratory depression, hypotension, bradycardia and heart block. Treat with IV calcium, diuresis and dialysis.
- C (True) – hypomagnesaemia impairs PTH secretion and causes end-organ resistance to PTH, so the hypocalcaemia is refractory until Mg²⁺ is corrected.
- D (True) – long-term PPIs reduce active intestinal Mg²⁺ absorption (TRPM6/7), and the level recovers after the drug is stopped.

**Ref:** Hess MW et al., Aliment Pharmacol Ther 2012;36:405–413; Gennari FJ, N Engl J Med 1998;339:451–458.

open.q: A patient with AKI on an ACE inhibitor and trimethoprim has K⁺ 7.0 mmol/L with peaked T waves and a widened QRS. Outline your management step by step, including doses, and explain the role of each drug.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Severe hyperkalaemia (≥ 6.5 mmol/L, ERC 2025) with ECG changes = urgent treatment; exclude pseudohyperkalaemia only if it does not delay therapy (blood gas analyser sample).
- Protect the heart: 10 mL 10 % CaCl₂ IV over 5 min (or 30 mL 10 % Ca gluconate over 10 min); stabilises the membrane, does not lower K⁺; short effect (~30–60 min) → repeat if ECG changes persist.
- Shift K⁺ into cells: insulin 10 U + glucose 25 g IV (onset ~15–30 min); if pre-treatment glucose < 7 mmol/L, follow with 10 % glucose 50 mL/h for 5 h; monitor for hypoglycaemia.
- Add nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg (additive, insufficient alone).
- Remove K⁺: SZC 10 g orally, loop diuretic if passing urine, dialysis if refractory; insulin/salbutamol only shift K⁺ → rebound.
- Monitor K⁺ and glucose.
- Prevent: stop ACE inhibitor and trimethoprim (ENaC blockade), treat the AKI cause.

open.q: Explain why hypokalaemia may be refractory to potassium replacement in an ICU patient and how you would correct it safely.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ~98 % of K⁺ is intracellular, so a small fall in serum K⁺ reflects a large total deficit (hundreds of mmol).
- Hypomagnesaemia (diuretics, long-term PPIs, alcohol, refeeding, CRRT…) releases ROMK inhibition → renal K⁺ wasting; without Mg²⁺ correction hypokalaemia remains refractory.
- Serum Mg poorly reflects stores (< 1 % in serum) – a normal level does not exclude deficiency.
- Ongoing shift into cells (insulin, β₂-agonists/adrenaline, alkalosis, refeeding) or ongoing losses (diuretics, mineralocorticoids, amphotericin B) also contribute.
- Give MgSO₄ (2 g ≈ 8 mmol IV, then infusion) alongside KCl.
- IV KCl peripherally up to ~10 mmol/h, higher rates centrally only with ECG monitoring; dilute in glucose-free solution.
- Monitor ECG (U waves, QT(U)) and stop QT-prolonging drugs.

title: W06 · D3 – Calcium and phosphate, refeeding syndrome

questions.stem: Total calcium 1.84 mmol/L, albumin 22 g/L. Using the formula Ca + 0.02 × (40 − albumin), the corrected calcium is:
options: 2.20 mmol/L
1.98 mmol/L
2.10 mmol/L
2.36 mmol/L
2.48 mmol/L
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Corrected Ca = 1.84 + 0.02 × (40 − 22) = 1.84 + 0.02 × 18 = 1.84 + 0.36 = **2.20 mmol/L**. The value looks normal, but in critically ill patients the formula agrees poorly with ionised calcium because of pH changes, complexing anions and hypoalbuminaemia. Measure iCa²⁺ directly.

**Why not the others:**
- B – 1.98 adds only 0.14, as if the albumin deficit were 7 g/L instead of 18 g/L.
- C – 2.10 adds only 0.26 (an arithmetic slip).
- D – 2.36 comes from adding 0.36 to 2.00 instead of to the measured 1.84.
- E – 2.48 would need an albumin of only 8 g/L.

**EDIC trap:** a "normal" corrected calcium can hide true ionised hypocalcaemia.

**Ref:** Aberegg SK, Ionized calcium in the ICU, Chest 2016;149:846–855.

questions.stem: Regarding ionised calcium:
options: Alkalosis decreases ionised calcium.
Albumin-corrected calcium accurately predicts ionised calcium in critically ill patients.
A total/ionised calcium ratio > 2.5 during citrate CRRT suggests citrate accumulation.
About 90 % of plasma calcium is ionised.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – alkalosis increases the negative charge on albumin, so more Ca²⁺ is bound and iCa²⁺ falls (hyperventilation tetany). Acidosis has the opposite effect.
- B (False) – albumin-corrected calcium agrees poorly with iCa²⁺ in the ICU (altered pH, citrate/lactate/phosphate complexes, hypoalbuminaemia), so measure iCa²⁺.
- C (True) – citrate–calcium complexes raise total Ca while iCa²⁺ falls. A total/ionised ratio > 2.5 together with a worsening high-AG acidosis indicates citrate accumulation (liver failure, shock).
- D (False) – about 45–50 % of plasma calcium is ionised, ~40 % is protein-bound and ~10 % is complexed.

**Ref:** Aberegg SK, Ionized calcium in the ICU, Chest 2016;149:846–855; Schneider AG et al., Crit Care 2017;21:281.

questions.stem: In the refeeding syndrome trial by Doig et al. (2015), protocolised caloric restriction in critically ill adults with refeeding hypophosphataemia:
options: Increased mortality
Consisted of stopping all nutrition for 5 days
Was tested only in patients with anorexia nervosa
Significantly increased the primary outcome of days alive after ICU discharge
Did not significantly change the primary outcome but improved 60-day survival
