**Ref:** Mebazaa A et al., STRONG-HF, Lancet 2022;400:1938–1952; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: Regarding inotropes and vasopressors in cardiogenic shock:
options: Milrinone acts independently of beta-adrenergic receptors.
Dobutamine's effect may be attenuated by beta-blockade.
Inotropes have been shown to improve long-term survival.
Milrinone accumulates in renal failure.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – milrinone inhibits PDE-3 and raises cAMP downstream of the β-receptor, so it works despite β-blockade. It is an inodilator that lowers both PVR and SVR.
- B (True) – dobutamine is a β1-agonist, and competitive β-blockade blunts its effect, so higher doses are needed.
- C (False) – no inotrope has been shown to improve long-term survival, and prolonged use is associated with harm (arrhythmias, ischaemia). They are bridging drugs.
- D (True) – milrinone is renally excreted and accumulates in renal failure, causing hypotension and arrhythmias, so reduce the dose.

**EDIC trap:** inodilators (milrinone, levosimendan) often need norepinephrine to maintain MAP.

**Ref:** Mathew R et al., N Engl J Med 2021;385:516–525; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: According to ESC 2026, non-invasive positive pressure ventilation in decompensated HF is suggested in patients with:
options: Only when PaCO₂ exceeds 8 kPa
Cardiogenic shock with SBP < 70 mmHg as first-line therapy
Only after failure of high-flow nasal oxygen
Respiratory distress (RR > 25/min, SpO₂ < 90 %), started early
Any dyspnoea, regardless of oxygenation
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ESC 2026 (table 9) suggests NIV in patients with respiratory distress (RR > 25/min, SpO₂ < 90%), started early to reduce the risk of intubation (IIa, B2). Positive pressure improves oxygenation and work of breathing and lowers LV preload and afterload.

**Why not the others:**
- A – there is no PaCO₂ threshold; hypoxaemic, normocapnic patients also benefit.
- B – in severe CS, positive pressure can worsen venous return and hypotension, and intubation is often needed instead.
- C – there is no requirement to try high-flow nasal oxygen first.
- E – NIV is not for dyspnoea alone; oxygen is given only if SpO₂ < 90% or PaO₂ < 60 mmHg (I, C).

**EDIC trap:** intubate if respiratory failure persists or progresses despite oxygen or NIV (I, C).

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457; Gray A et al., N Engl J Med 2008;359:142–151.

questions.stem: Regarding the SURVIVE and SOAP II trials:
options: SOAP II showed significantly lower overall 28-day mortality with dopamine.
SURVIVE compared levosimendan with dobutamine.
SOAP II found more arrhythmic events with dopamine than norepinephrine.
Levosimendan produced a greater reduction in BNP.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – 28-day mortality was 52.5% with dopamine vs 48.5% with norepinephrine (NS), and dopamine was associated with higher mortality in the CS subgroup.
- B (True) – SURVIVE compared levosimendan with dobutamine in 1327 patients with ADHF who needed inotropic support.
- C (True) – arrhythmias occurred in 24.1% vs 12.4%, mostly AF, and more patients stopped dopamine because of them.
- D (True) – levosimendan lowered BNP more, but caused more AF and hypokalaemia and did not improve survival.

**EDIC trap:** a greater fall in a biomarker does not mean better survival.

**Ref:** De Backer D et al., SOAP II, N Engl J Med 2010;362:779–789; Mebazaa A et al., SURVIVE, JAMA 2007;297:1883–1891.

open.q: A 72-year-old woman presents with acute pulmonary oedema, BP 190/105 mmHg, RR 32/min and SpO₂ 86%. Outline your management according to ESC 2026 and the supporting evidence.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Recognise APO: mainly fluid redistribution with ↑ afterload, not total volume overload.
- O₂ for SpO₂ < 90% (I, C); early NIV (CPAP or NIPPV) for RR > 25/min and SpO₂ < 90% (IIa, B2).
- 3CPO: NIV did not reduce mortality but improved dyspnoea, acidosis and hypercapnia faster; CPAP = NIPPV.
- IV vasodilators (nitrates) since SBP > 110 mmHg (IIb, C) – fewer intubations; caution with severe AS/RV infarction.
- IV loop diuretic if fluid overloaded (I, A) – but fewer diuretics needed than in left-sided DHF.
- No routine opioids (III, C).
- Intubate if respiratory failure persists/progresses despite O₂ or NIV (I, C).

open.q: Compare dobutamine, milrinone and levosimendan and explain how you would choose between them in a hypoperfused patient on chronic beta-blocker therapy.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Dobutamine: β1 agonist; arrhythmias, ischaemia; effect attenuated by β-blockade.
- Milrinone: PDE-3 inhibitor acting independently of β-receptors; inodilator, ↓ PVR; hypotension; accumulates in renal failure.
- Levosimendan: Ca²⁺ sensitisation of troponin C + K-ATP opening; long-acting metabolite; hypotension, hypokalaemia, AF.
- DOREMI: milrinone = dobutamine (composite 49 vs 54%, NS); SURVIVE: levosimendan = dobutamine (180-d mortality 26 vs 28%).
- ESC 2026: levosimendan or PDE-3 inhibitor may be preferred over dobutamine in patients on β-blockers.
- Inodilators often need norepinephrine to counter hypotension.
- Inotropes do not improve survival – use for SBP < 90 with hypoperfusion (IIb, C), lowest dose, shortest time.

title: W07 · D5 – Right heart failure and pulmonary hypertension in the ICU

questions.stem: According to the 2022 ESC/ERS guidelines, pre-capillary pulmonary hypertension is defined as:
options: mPAP ≥ 25 mmHg, PAWP ≤ 15 mmHg, PVR ≥ 3 WU
sPAP > 40 mmHg on echocardiography
mPAP > 30 mmHg irrespective of PAWP
mPAP > 20 mmHg, PAWP ≤ 15 mmHg, PVR > 2 WU
mPAP > 20 mmHg, PAWP > 15 mmHg, PVR ≤ 2 WU
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ESC/ERS 2022 defines PH as mPAP > 20 mmHg at rest on right heart catheterisation. Pre-capillary PH also requires PAWP ≤ 15 mmHg and PVR > 2 WU. These thresholds were lowered from mPAP ≥ 25 mmHg and PVR > 3 WU on the basis of the upper limit of normal in healthy subjects.

**Why not the others:**
- A – this is the older (2015-era) definition.
- B – echocardiography estimates the probability of PH (e.g. peak TR velocity > 2.8 m/s) but cannot define it; diagnosis requires RHC.
- C – no such threshold exists, and PAWP is needed to separate pre- from post-capillary PH.
- E – this is isolated post-capillary PH (IpcPH).

**Ref:** Humbert M et al., 2022 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618–3731.

questions.stem: Regarding ventricular interdependence:
options: Volume loading of a failing, dilated RV reliably increases cardiac output.
It can reduce left ventricular filling and stroke volume despite normal LV contractility.
Systemic hypotension may worsen RV function by reducing RV coronary perfusion.
A pressure-overloaded right ventricle shifts the septum towards the left ventricle.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – volume loading a dilated, failing RV raises wall tension, worsens TR and pushes the septum to the left, compressing the LV. CO may **fall**, and most patients need a negative balance.
- B (True) – diastolic interdependence (shared septum, stiff pericardium) reduces LV compliance and filling, so stroke volume falls despite normal LV contractility. PCWP may even be falsely high.
- C (True) – RV coronary perfusion pressure ≈ aortic pressure − RV pressure. Hypotension causes RV ischaemia, which closes the vicious circle.
- D (True) – leftward septal shift gives paradoxical septal motion and a D-shaped LV in the short axis.

**EDIC trap:** in acute RV failure, fluids "to raise CO" are mostly ineffective and potentially harmful.

**Ref:** Vieillard-Baron A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:774–790.

questions.stem: Which factor was NOT part of the risk score for acute cor pulmonale in ARDS (Mekontso Dessap, ICM 2016)?
options: PaCO₂ ≥ 48 mmHg
Age > 65 years
Pneumonia as the cause of ARDS
PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg
Driving pressure ≥ 18 cmH₂O
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In 752 patients with moderate/severe ARDS on protective ventilation, acute cor pulmonale occurred in ~22%. Four independent risk factors formed the score: pneumonia as the cause of ARDS, driving pressure ≥ 18 cmH₂O, PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg and PaCO₂ ≥ 48 mmHg. ACP prevalence rose steeply with each point, and severe ACP was associated with higher mortality. Age was not part of the score.

**Why not the others:**
- A – PaCO₂ ≥ 48 mmHg is in the score; hypercapnia raises PVR.
- C – pneumonia is in the score (direct lung and vascular injury, hypoxic vasoconstriction).
- D – PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 mmHg is in the score.
- E – driving pressure ≥ 18 cmH₂O is in the score and is the main modifiable factor.

**Ref:** Mekontso Dessap A et al., Intensive Care Med 2016;42:862–870.

questions.stem: Regarding inhaled nitric oxide:
options: It acts predominantly in ventilated lung units, improving V/Q matching.
It causes marked systemic hypotension.
It can be stopped abruptly without risk of rebound pulmonary hypertension.
It improves survival in ARDS.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – iNO reaches only ventilated alveoli and dilates the vessels supplying them. This lowers PVR and redirects flow towards ventilated units, improving V/Q matching.
- B (False) – it is rapidly bound and inactivated by haemoglobin (forming methaemoglobin and nitrate), so it has negligible systemic effect.
- C (False) – abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound PH, hypoxaemia and RV collapse, so wean gradually.
- D (False) – in ARDS, iNO improves oxygenation only transiently and does not improve survival (it may increase AKI). It is not used routinely.

**EDIC trap:** in severe LV dysfunction, iNO can worsen pulmonary oedema by increasing flow into a high-pressure LA.

**Ref:** Gebistorf F et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;(6):CD002787; Vieillard-Baron A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:774–790.

questions.stem: A patient with known pulmonary arterial hypertension is admitted with pneumonia, BP 82/50 mmHg, CVP 18 mmHg, lactate 3.5 mmol/L and a dilated RV with D-sign. The most appropriate initial haemodynamic intervention is:
options: Urgent intubation to reduce work of breathing
1 L crystalloid bolus
Norepinephrine to restore systemic pressure, with consideration of an inotrope
Intravenous nitroglycerin
Beta-blocker to control heart rate
questions.expl:
**Why C:** This is decompensated PAH with shock (BP 82/50 mmHg, lactate 3.5 mmol/L), a high CVP and a D-sign. The priority is to restore systemic pressure, which preserves RV coronary perfusion and breaks the vicious circle. ESC/ERS 2022 advises keeping MAP > 60 mmHg with norepinephrine or vasopressin, adding an inotrope for low output, treating the trigger and aiming for a negative balance.

**Why not the others:**
- A – intubation (induction plus positive pressure) carries a high risk of circulatory collapse and should be avoided whenever possible.
- B – with CVP 18 mmHg and a dilated RV, more fluid worsens septal shift and LV underfilling.
- D – IV nitroglycerin is a systemic vasodilator that lowers BP and RV perfusion.
- E – with a fixed RV stroke volume, CO depends on heart rate, so a β-blocker would lower output.

**Ref:** Humbert M et al., 2022 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618–3731; Hoeper MM, Granton J, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2011;184:1114–1124.

questions.stem: According to the ESC/ERS 2022 guidelines on ICU management of PAH with right heart failure:
options: Intubation should be avoided whenever possible.
Most patients require a positive fluid balance.
VA-ECMO is never used in PAH.
Norepinephrine or vasopressin may be required for persistent hypotension.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – intubation in severe PH/RV failure carries a high risk of collapse and death. If it is unavoidable, start a vasopressor before a haemodynamically gentle induction.
- B (False) – most patients need a **negative** balance (diuretics, possibly RRT or ultrafiltration) to reduce RV dilatation and TR.
- C (False) – VA-ECMO is used as a bridge to transplantation in irreversible failure, or to recovery when the trigger is reversible, decided case by case.
- D (True) – norepinephrine or vasopressin is used for persistent hypotension. Vasopressin raises SVR with little effect on PVR.

**Ref:** Humbert M et al., 2022 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618–3731; Hoeper MM, Granton J, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2011;184:1114–1124.

questions.stem: In a mechanically ventilated patient, pulmonary vascular resistance is lowest at:
options: Lung volumes associated with atelectasis
Maximal PEEP
Functional residual capacity
Total lung capacity
Residual volume
questions.expl:
**Why C:** PVR is the sum of the resistances of alveolar vessels, which are compressed as the lungs inflate, and extra-alveolar vessels, which narrow at low volumes as radial traction is lost and hypoxic vasoconstriction sets in. The result is a "U"-shaped curve with its lowest point at FRC.

**Why not the others:**
- A – in atelectasis, extra-alveolar vessels collapse and hypoxic vasoconstriction raises PVR.
- B – maximal PEEP overdistends the alveoli and compresses alveolar capillaries, raising PVR and RV afterload.
- D – at TLC, compression of alveolar vessels is maximal.
- E – at residual volume, extra-alveolar vessels narrow and hypoxic vasoconstriction increases PVR.

**EDIC trap:** both too little and too much PEEP harm the RV, so titrate it and check the RV on echo.

**Ref:** Vieillard-Baron A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:774–790; Hoeper MM, Granton J, Am J Respir Crit Care Med 2011;184:1114–1124.

questions.stem: "RV-protective" ventilation in ARDS includes:
options: Maximising PEEP to the highest tolerated level
Avoiding hypercapnia
Prone positioning
Limiting driving pressure
questions.expl:
- A (False) – excessive PEEP overdistends alveoli, compresses alveolar vessels and raises PVR and RV afterload. Titrate PEEP to recruit without overdistension.
- B (True) – hypercapnia and acidosis cause pulmonary vasoconstriction; target PaCO₂ < 48 mmHg (~6.4 kPa).
- C (True) – prone positioning recruits lung, lowers driving pressure and PaCO₂, and relieves acute cor pulmonale.
- D (True) – driving pressure ≥ 18 cmH₂O is an ACP risk factor, so keep it < 18 cmH₂O and limit plateau pressure.

**EDIC trap:** for refractory ACP, VV-ECMO allows ultra-protective ventilation and correction of hypercapnia.

**Ref:** Mekontso Dessap A et al., Intensive Care Med 2016;42:862–870; Vieillard-Baron A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:774–790.

questions.stem: Which echocardiographic finding is most typical of RV pressure overload?
options: Paradoxical septal motion with a D-shaped LV in short axis
Small RV with hyperdynamic LV
Isolated LV apical akinesia
Collapsible inferior vena cava
Mitral valve systolic anterior motion
questions.expl:
**Why A:** In RV pressure overload, RV pressure approaches or exceeds LV pressure, which flattens the septum (most at end-systole). This produces a D-shaped LV in the parasternal short axis with paradoxical septal motion. Other findings are RV/LV > 1 in the apical 4-chamber view, low TAPSE and a dilated, non-collapsing IVC.

**Why not the others:**
- B – a small RV with a hyperdynamic LV suggests hypovolaemia.
- C – isolated apical akinesia suggests LAD infarction or takotsubo.
- D – RV failure with high RAP gives a dilated IVC with little respiratory variation.
- E – SAM of the mitral valve indicates dynamic LVOT obstruction (HCM, hypovolaemia, inotropes, takotsubo).

**EDIC trap:** septal flattening mainly in diastole suggests RV **volume** overload.

**Ref:** Vieillard-Baron A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:774–790; Humbert M et al., 2022 ESC/ERS PH Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618–3731.

questions.stem: Regarding acute right ventricular failure in the ICU:
options: Venous congestion does not affect liver or kidney function.
The right ventricle tolerates acute increases in afterload better than volume load.
Pulmonary embolism and RV infarction should be excluded in right-sided decompensated HF.
Hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acidosis increase pulmonary vascular resistance.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – venous congestion causes congestive hepatopathy (↑ bilirubin, transaminases) and congestive nephropathy, because high renal venous pressure lowers renal perfusion pressure.
- B (False) – the opposite is true: the thin-walled RV tolerates volume well but an acute rise in afterload (e.g. PE) poorly, and acutely it cannot generate a high mPAP.
- C (True) – ESC 2026: in decompensated right-sided HF, exclude PE and RV infarction, which have specific reperfusion treatments.
- D (True) – hypoxaemia, hypercapnia and acidosis all raise PVR, so correcting them is central to RV-protective care.

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457; Vieillard-Baron A et al., Intensive Care Med 2018;44:774–790.

open.q: A patient with known PAH is admitted with pneumonia, BP 82/50 mmHg, CVP 18 mmHg, lactate 3.5 mmol/L and a dilated RV with D-sign. Outline your management and explain the physiological rationale.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Vicious circle: ↑ RV afterload → dilatation, TR → ↓ LV filling → hypotension → ↓ RV coronary perfusion → ischaemia.
- Treat the trigger (pneumonia – antibiotics; check arrhythmia, anaemia, interrupted PAH therapy).
- Restore systemic pressure – MAP > 60 mmHg with norepinephrine or vasopressin (vasopressin raises SVR without marked rise in PVR).
- Avoid fluid boluses – dilated RV compresses the LV; most need negative balance (diuretics, RRT/ultrafiltration).
- Inotrope for low output (dobutamine, milrinone; levosimendan alternative), with vasopressor if inodilator causes hypotension.
- Reduce RV afterload: correct hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, acidosis; inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (iNO, inhaled prostacyclins).
- Maintain sinus rhythm/AV synchrony; avoid intubation if possible (if needed: vasopressor running before induction, gentle induction).
- Consider VA-ECMO as a bridge to transplantation or recovery.

open.q: A ventilated ARDS patient has driving pressure 20 cmH₂O, PaCO₂ 55 mmHg and a D-sign on echo. Explain why the RV is failing and describe RV-protective ventilation.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Acute cor pulmonale occurs in ~22% of moderate/severe ARDS; this patient has risk factors (DP ≥ 18, PaCO₂ ≥ 48).
- Positive pressure ↑ RV afterload and ↓ preload; hypercapnia and acidosis ↑ PVR.
- PVR–lung volume relationship is U-shaped – lowest at FRC; atelectasis and hyperinflation both raise PVR.
- Limit plateau and driving pressure (target < 18 cmH₂O).
- Keep PaCO₂ < 48 mmHg; correct hypoxaemia.
- Titrate PEEP – enough to recruit, avoid overdistension; do not simply increase PEEP or give fluids.
- Prone positioning unloads the RV; consider VV-ECMO for refractory ACP; vasopressor to maintain RV perfusion.

title: W07 · Saturday – weekly review: Cardio I

questions.stem: A 61-year-old man with anterior STEMI has BP 88/56 mmHg and HR 112/min, warm extremities, normal mentation, urine output 1 mL/kg/h and lactate 1.4 mmol/L. His SCAI SHOCK stage is:
options: C
A
E
B
D
questions.expl:
**Why D:** The patient is hypotensive (88/56 mmHg) and tachycardic (112/min) but well perfused: warm extremities, normal mentation, urine output 1 mL/kg/h and lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Haemodynamic instability without hypoperfusion is SCAI stage B (Beginning), which is option D.

**Why not the others:**
- A – stage C needs hypoperfusion (lactate ≥ 2, cold periphery, oliguria) that requires intervention.
- B – stage A (At risk) has no haemodynamic instability, but this patient is hypotensive and tachycardic.
- C – stage E means collapse, CPR or ECMO, or lactate ≥ 8 mmol/L.
- E – stage D means hypoperfusion that worsens despite initial therapy.

**EDIC trap:** stage B is a warning stage with a high risk of progression; reassess perfusion often.

**Ref:** Naidu SS et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2022;79:933–946.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman is in AMI-related cardiogenic shock with three-vessel disease. Regarding revascularisation:
options: Emergency CABG has no role, even if coronary anatomy is unsuitable for PCI.
All significant lesions should be treated during the index procedure.
CULPRIT-SHOCK showed a lower 30-day rate of death or RRT with culprit-only PCI.
Immediate coronary angiography with PCI of the infarct-related artery is recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – emergency CABG is recommended in AMI-CS when the coronary anatomy is unsuitable for PCI.
- B (False) – immediate multivessel PCI increased death/RRT in CULPRIT-SHOCK, and routine immediate non-IRA PCI in CS is III, B. Non-culprit lesions are staged.
- C (True) – 45.9% vs 55.4% (RR 0.83), driven by mortality (43.3% vs 51.6%) and sustained at 1 year.
- D (True) – immediate angiography with PCI of the infarct-related artery is class I, based on the SHOCK trial (lower 6-month mortality).

**Ref:** Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826; Thiele H et al., N Engl J Med 2017;377:2419–2432.

questions.stem: Five days after an inferior STEMI treated late, a patient becomes hypotensive with a new harsh holosystolic murmur. PAC shows SpO₂ 62 % in the right atrium and 84 % in the pulmonary artery. The diagnosis is:
options: Acute mitral regurgitation
Ventricular septal rupture
Free wall rupture
Pulmonary embolism
Right ventricular infarction
questions.expl:
**Why B:** O₂ saturation rises from 62% in the RA to 84% in the PA, a step-up of > 20%. That means oxygenated blood is entering the right heart between the RA and the PA, i.e. a left-to-right shunt at ventricular level: ventricular septal rupture. Together with a new harsh holosystolic murmur and shock 5 days after a late-treated inferior MI (basal septum, worse prognosis), the diagnosis is clear. Confirm with colour-Doppler echo, bridge with IABP/MCS, then close.

**Why not the others:**
- A – acute MR causes large v waves without a saturation step-up, and its murmur is often soft.
- C – free wall rupture causes tamponade or PEA, with no murmur or step-up.
- D – PE causes no shunt, so saturation does not rise from RA to PA.
- E – RV infarction causes high RAP and clear lungs, with no murmur or step-up.

**Ref:** Damluji AA et al., Circulation 2021;144:e16–e35.

questions.stem: Regarding mechanical circulatory support trials in infarct-related cardiogenic shock:
options: Both ECLS-SHOCK and DanGer Shock showed more bleeding complications with the device.
ECLS-SHOCK showed no reduction in 30-day mortality with early routine VA-ECMO.
DanGer Shock showed lower 180-day mortality with a microaxial flow pump in STEMI-related shock.
IABP-SHOCK II showed no reduction in 30-day mortality with IABP.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ECLS-SHOCK: BARC 3–5 bleeding 23.4% vs 9.6%. DanGer Shock: moderate or severe bleeding 21.8% vs 11.9%.
- B (True) – 30-day mortality was 47.8% vs 49.0% (RR 0.98), with more bleeding and vascular complications.
- C (True) – 180-day mortality was 45.8% vs 58.5% (HR 0.74) in STEMI-CS with LVEF < 45%, excluding comatose OHCA survivors.
- D (True) – 30-day mortality was 39.7% vs 41.3% (RR 0.96), with no difference at 6 years either.

**EDIC trap:** only DanGer Shock was positive, in a highly selected population and at the cost of more complications.

**Ref:** Thiele H et al., N Engl J Med 2012;367:1287–1296 and 2023;389:1286–1297; Møller JE et al., N Engl J Med 2024;390:1382–1393.

questions.stem: A patient on peripheral femoral VA-ECMO for refractory cardiogenic shock develops progressive pulmonary oedema. The arterial line shows a flat trace without pulsatility, and echo shows a closed aortic valve with spontaneous contrast in the LV. The most appropriate next step is:
options: Increase ECMO flow to maximum
Convert to VV-ECMO immediately
Give a fluid bolus
Increase PEEP to 20 cmH₂O and continue unchanged
Start an inotrope and consider LV unloading (IABP or microaxial pump)
questions.expl:
**Why E:** A flat arterial trace, a closed aortic valve, spontaneous contrast in the LV and worsening pulmonary oedema indicate LV distension, caused by the afterload that retrograde flow imposes on peripheral VA-ECMO. The steps are an inotrope to open the valve, ECMO flow reduced to the minimum that maintains perfusion, afterload reduction and, if distension persists, LV unloading with an IABP, microaxial pump ("ECPELLA") or an LA vent. This is urgent because of the risk of thrombus.

**Why not the others:**
- A – higher flow raises afterload further and worsens distension.
- B – VV-ECMO gives no circulatory support in refractory CS.
- C – fluid increases preload and worsens distension.
- D – PEEP may ease the oedema but does not address the cause, and leaving things unchanged allows thrombus to form.

**Ref:** Lorusso R et al., ELSO VA-ECMO interim guidelines, ASAIO J 2021;67:827–844; Kim MC et al., Circulation 2023;148:1570–1581.

questions.stem: A patient on femoral VA-ECMO with severe lung injury has a recovering left ventricle. Regarding differential (Harlequin) hypoxaemia:
options: Increasing FiO₂ on the oxygenator corrects cerebral hypoxaemia.
Conversion to V-AV ECMO is a possible solution.
Oxygenation should be monitored from a femoral arterial line.
The upper body, including the brain and coronaries, may be perfused by poorly oxygenated blood.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – oxygenator FiO₂ affects only ECMO blood, which already goes to the lower body. The upper body receives native cardiac output from the failing lungs.
- B (True) – in V-AV ECMO, an additional return cannula in the internal jugular vein sends oxygenated blood through the RA, lungs and LV to the aortic root. Other options are optimising ventilation or changing the cannulation site.
- C (False) – monitor from the **right radial** artery (ABG, right-hand SpO₂) and with cerebral NIRS. Femoral blood mainly reflects the ECMO circuit.
- D (True) – depending on the mixing zone, the coronaries, carotids and right subclavian artery receive poorly oxygenated native output.

**Ref:** Lorusso R et al., ELSO VA-ECMO interim guidelines, ASAIO J 2021;67:827–844.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on long-term bisoprolol is admitted with low-output heart failure (SBP 92 mmHg, cold extremities, lactate 3 mmol/L) and remains hypoperfused after cautious fluids. According to ESC 2026, which inotrope may be preferred over dobutamine?
options: Isoprenaline
Dopamine
Vasopressin
Phenylephrine
Levosimendan or a PDE-3 inhibitor
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Long-term β-blockade (bisoprolol) blunts β1-agonists such as dobutamine. Levosimendan (troponin C sensitisation plus K-ATP vasodilation) and PDE-3 inhibitors such as milrinone (cAMP rise downstream of the receptor) work independently of the β-receptor, and ESC 2026 notes they may be preferred. Both are inodilators, so with SBP 92 mmHg norepinephrine is often needed and a bolus is usually omitted.

**Why not the others:**
- A – isoprenaline is a non-selective β-agonist that β-blockade blunts just as much, and it causes tachycardia and vasodilation.
- B – dopamine also depends on the β-receptor and caused more arrhythmias, with higher mortality in the CS subgroup of SOAP II.
- C – vasopressin is a vasopressor with no inotropic effect.
- D – phenylephrine is a pure α1-agonist that raises afterload and can lower CO.

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457; Mebazaa A et al., JAMA 2007;297:1883–1891.

questions.stem: Regarding trials of inotropes:
options: In SURVIVE, 180-day mortality did not differ significantly.
DOREMI compared milrinone with dobutamine in cardiogenic shock.
SURVIVE compared levosimendan with dobutamine in acute decompensated heart failure.
DOREMI found a significant mortality benefit with milrinone.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – 180-day mortality was 26% vs 28% (HR 0.91), not significant.
- B (True) – DOREMI was a double-blind trial in 192 CS patients (SCAI B–E).
- C (True) – SURVIVE enrolled 1327 patients with ADHF who needed inotropic support.
- D (False) – in-hospital mortality was 37% vs 43% (RR 0.85, NS), and the primary composite was 49% vs 54% (NS).

**EDIC trap:** no inotrope has shown a survival benefit over another; choose according to the haemodynamic profile and β-blocker use.

**Ref:** Mathew R et al., N Engl J Med 2021;385:516–525; Mebazaa A et al., JAMA 2007;297:1883–1891.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman presents with acute pulmonary oedema, BP 200/110 mmHg, RR 34/min, SpO₂ 84 %, pH 7.24, PaCO₂ 7.5 kPa, alert and cooperative. The best initial respiratory support is:
options: Heliox
Non-invasive ventilation (CPAP or NIPPV)
Intravenous morphine and oxygen
Immediate intubation
Low-flow oxygen 2 L/min only
questions.expl:
**Why B:** This is hypertensive APO with hypoxaemia, tachypnoea and respiratory acidosis (pH 7.24, PaCO₂ 7.5 kPa) in an alert, cooperative patient, so NIV (CPAP or NIPPV) is indicated. In 3CPO, NIV corrected acidosis, hypercapnia and dyspnoea faster than oxygen, and CPAP and NIPPV were equivalent. ESC 2026 suggests early NIV (IIa, B2). Add IV nitrates for the hypertension, and intubate if NIV fails.

**Why not the others:**
- A – heliox has no role in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
- C – routine morphine is III, C and risks respiratory depression in a hypercapnic patient.
- D – an alert, cooperative patient deserves an NIV trial; intubation is for NIV failure, coma or exhaustion.
- E – low-flow oxygen is inadequate with SpO₂ 84% and does not reduce work of breathing.

**Ref:** Gray A et al., N Engl J Med 2008;359:142–151; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

questions.stem: Regarding the 2026 ESC heart failure guidelines:
options: The term "decompensated heart failure" replaces "acute heart failure".
HFmrEF remains a separate category.
Vasopressors, preferably norepinephrine, may be considered in cardiogenic shock.
Intensive rapid up-titration of foundational therapy before and after discharge is recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – "decompensated HF" replaces "acute HF", because many patients deteriorate gradually rather than suddenly.
- B (False) – HFmrEF was abolished: LVEF < 50% is HFrEF and ≥ 50% is HFpEF.
- C (True) – norepinephrine is the preferred vasopressor (IIb, C); dopamine causes more arrhythmias.
- D (True) – rapid up-titration of foundational therapy is I, B2, based on STRONG-HF (death or HF readmission at 180 days 15.2% vs 23.3%).

**Ref:** Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457; Mebazaa A et al., Lancet 2022;400:1938–1952.

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS from pneumonia has driving pressure 19 cmH₂O, PaO₂/FiO₂ 110 mmHg and PaCO₂ 52 mmHg (7 kPa). Echo shows a dilated RV with paradoxical septal motion. Which measure is most likely to help the right ventricle?
options: Fluid bolus of 1 L
Increase PEEP to maximal tolerated values
Start a beta-blocker
Prone positioning with reduction of driving pressure and PaCO₂
Permissive hypercapnia with PaCO₂ target 8 kPa
questions.expl:
**Why D:** All four ACP risk factors are present: pneumonia, driving pressure ≥ 18 (19 cmH₂O), PaO₂/FiO₂ < 150 (110 mmHg) and PaCO₂ ≥ 48 (52 mmHg). A dilated RV with paradoxical septal motion confirms acute cor pulmonale. Prone positioning recruits lung, lowers driving pressure and PaCO₂ and unloads the RV; combine it with a lower tidal volume and correction of hypercapnia (e.g. less dead space). Consider VV-ECMO if this is not enough.

**Why not the others:**
- A – fluids worsen RV dilatation and septal shift.
- B – maximal PEEP overdistends the lung and raises PVR.
- C – a β-blocker lowers contractility and heart rate, and so CO in RV failure.
- E – a PaCO₂ of 8 kPa (60 mmHg) worsens pulmonary vasoconstriction; the target is < 48 mmHg (~6.4 kPa).

**Ref:** Mekontso Dessap A et al., Intensive Care Med 2016;42:862–870; Guérin C et al., PROSEVA, N Engl J Med 2013;368:2159–2168.

questions.stem: Regarding pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure:
options: In PAH with right heart failure, intubation should be avoided whenever possible.
Group 2 PH is associated with lung disease and/or hypoxia.
Pulmonary hypertension is defined by mPAP > 20 mmHg (ESC/ERS 2022).
Isolated post-capillary PH has PAWP > 15 mmHg and PVR > 2 WU.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESC/ERS 2022 advises avoiding intubation whenever possible. If it is unavoidable, start a vasopressor before induction.
- B (False) – group 2 is left heart disease (the most common group); lung disease and/or hypoxia is group 3.
- C (True) – PH is defined as mPAP > 20 mmHg at rest on right heart catheterisation (previously ≥ 25 mmHg).
- D (False) – isolated post-capillary PH has PAWP > 15 mmHg and PVR ≤ 2 WU. A PVR > 2 WU defines combined post- and pre-capillary PH.

**Ref:** Humbert M et al., Eur Heart J 2022;43:3618–3731.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old with inferior STEMI is hypotensive (82/50 mmHg) with distended neck veins and clear lungs. ST elevation is present in V4R. Which initial treatment should be avoided?
options: Temporary pacing for complete AV block
Cautious fluid challenge
Primary PCI of the right coronary artery
Dobutamine if hypoperfusion persists
Intravenous nitrates
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Inferior STEMI with hypotension, raised JVP, clear lungs and ST elevation in V4R is RV infarction. The ischaemic RV depends on preload, so nitrates (and diuretics), which dilate veins, can cause profound hypotension and should be avoided.

**Why not the others:**
- A – AV block is common with proximal RCA occlusion; pacing (ideally AV-sequential) restores rate and atrial kick.
- B – a cautious fluid challenge is reasonable if the patient is not volume-overloaded; avoid large volumes.
- C – primary PCI of the RCA is the key treatment of the cause.
- D – dobutamine supports RV contractility if hypoperfusion persists after preload is optimised.

**EDIC trap:** record right-sided leads in every inferior STEMI before giving nitrates.

**Ref:** Byrne RA et al., 2023 ESC ACS Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3720–3826.

questions.stem: Regarding diagnostics in cardiogenic shock:
options: ESICM 2025 considers echocardiography the first-line tool to determine the type of shock.
Mixed venous saturation is typically low.
Large v waves on PCWP tracing suggest acute mitral regurgitation.
A lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L is required for SCAI stage B.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESICM 2025 recommends echocardiography as the first-line tool to identify the type of shock.
- B (True) – low CO increases O₂ extraction, so SvO₂ is typically low (unlike septic shock).
- C (True) – large v waves reflect regurgitant flow into a non-compliant LA. They are suggestive, not specific (also seen in VSR or a stiff LA).
- D (False) – stage B has **normal** lactate; lactate ≥ 2 mmol/L with hypoperfusion is stage C.

**Ref:** Monnet X et al., Intensive Care Med 2025;51:1971–2012; Naidu SS et al., J Am Coll Cardiol 2022;79:933–946.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old with anterior STEMI and cardiogenic shock (LVEF 25 %, lactate 5 mmol/L) is awake and was not resuscitated. He remains hypoperfused despite norepinephrine after primary PCI. According to ESC 2026, which option has class IIa support?
options: Dopamine as first-line vasopressor
No mechanical support should be considered
Routine VA-ECMO for all AMI-CS
Microaxial flow pump
Routine IABP
questions.expl:
**Why D:** An awake, non-resuscitated patient with anterior STEMI-CS, LVEF 25% and lactate 5 mmol/L despite norepinephrine after PCI matches the DanGer Shock population (180-day mortality 45.8% vs 58.5%). ESC 2026 gives a microaxial flow pump IIa, B1 in selected STEMI-CS with LV dysfunction and no risk of hypoxic brain injury. Weigh this against bleeding, limb ischaemia and RRT, and involve the shock team (I, C).

**Why not the others:**
- A – dopamine causes more arrhythmias; norepinephrine is the preferred vasopressor (IIb, C).
- B – this patient fits the only population with a proven mortality benefit from MCS.
- C – routine VA-ECMO in unselected AMI-CS is III, B1 (ECLS-SHOCK).
- E – routine IABP is III, B1 (IABP-SHOCK II).

**Ref:** Møller JE et al., N Engl J Med 2024;390:1382–1393; Køber L et al., 2026 ESC HF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2026;47:5346–5457.

title: W08 · D1 – Arrhythmias in the ICU: AF, VT/electrical storm, bradyarrhythmias

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with septic shock on noradrenaline develops new atrial fibrillation at 165/min. BP falls to 70/40 mmHg with rising lactate despite adequate filling. According to ERC 2025, the most appropriate immediate step is:
options: IV digoxin loading
Synchronised cardioversion with an initial shock at maximum defibrillator output
Synchronised cardioversion starting at 50 J with stepwise escalation
Wait 48 hours for spontaneous conversion
IV diltiazem bolus
questions.expl:
**Why B:** AF with shock, ischaemia or acute heart failure is an indication for emergency synchronised electrical cardioversion (ESC 2024, class I C). ERC 2025 changed the energy advice for AF: the first synchronised shock should be delivered at **maximum defibrillator output** instead of escalating, because the first-shock success is higher and repeated shocks are avoided. If it fails, give amiodarone 300 mg IV and shock again.

**Why not the others:**
- A – digoxin acts slowly (hours) and does not treat shock caused by the arrhythmia.
- C – a low start with stepwise escalation is the old approach; ERC 2025 recommends maximum energy for AF (70–120 J is for flutter/SVT).
- D – "wait-and-see" within 48 h is only for haemodynamically stable patients.
- E – diltiazem is negatively inotropic and a vasodilator, so it would worsen the hypotension.

**Ref:** Soar J et al., ERC Guidelines 2025 Adult ALS, Resuscitation 2025;215:110769; Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414.

questions.stem: Regarding rate control of atrial fibrillation according to the 2024 ESC guidelines:
options: Lenient rate control with a resting heart rate < 110/min should be considered as the initial target.
Diltiazem and verapamil should be avoided when LVEF is ≤ 40 %.
Digoxin can be used irrespective of left ventricular ejection fraction.
In haemodynamic instability, IV amiodarone, digoxin, esmolol or landiolol may be considered.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESC 2024 recommends lenient rate control (resting HR < 110/min) as the initial target (IIa B), based on RACE II.
- B (True) – non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are negatively inotropic and can cause decompensation in HFrEF, so they are used only if LVEF > 40%.
- C (True) – digoxin (like beta-blockers) can be used at any LVEF; it is slower and less effective at high sympathetic tone, but it does not lower blood pressure.
- D (True) – in haemodynamic instability or severely reduced LVEF, IV amiodarone, digoxin, esmolol or landiolol may be considered (IIb B).

**EDIC trap:** All four are true – a K′ item can have four true statements.

**Ref:** Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414; Van Gelder IC et al. (RACE II), N Engl J Med 2010;362:1363–1373.

questions.stem: In the STRESS-L trial of landiolol in septic shock with heart rate ≥ 95/min:
options: There was no improvement in organ failure and the trial was stopped early with a possible signal of harm
Landiolol significantly reduced 28-day mortality
Landiolol significantly reduced the mean SOFA score
Landiolol was compared with esmolol
Only patients with atrial fibrillation were enrolled
questions.expl:
**Why A:** STRESS-L (126 adults with septic shock, noradrenaline > 0.1 µg/kg/min for > 24 h, HR ≥ 95/min) randomised landiolol titrated to HR 80–94/min vs standard care. Mean SOFA over 14 days did not differ (8.8 vs 8.1). The trial was stopped early because benefit was unlikely; 28-day mortality was 37.1% vs 25.4% and 90-day mortality 43.5% vs 28.6% (not significant), a possible signal of harm.

**Why not the others:**
- B – 28-day mortality was numerically **higher** with landiolol, not lower.
- C – there was no difference in mean SOFA score, the primary outcome.
- D – the comparator was standard care, not esmolol.
- E – most patients had sinus tachycardia; the entry criterion was heart rate, not AF.

**EDIC trap:** Do not confuse STRESS-L with Morelli's single-centre esmolol trial (JAMA 2013), which suggested benefit.

**Ref:** Whitehouse T et al. (STRESS-L), JAMA 2023;330:1641–1652.

questions.stem: Concerning anticoagulation and cardioversion in atrial fibrillation (ESC 2024):
options: The CHA₂DS₂-VA score adds one point for female sex.
A score of ≥ 2 is an indicator to start oral anticoagulation.
Early cardioversion without anticoagulation or TOE is acceptable if AF has lasted up to 72 hours.
Atrial fibrillation triggered by a reversible precipitant never requires long-term anticoagulation.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – CHA₂DS₂-**VA** (ESC 2024) dropped female sex; it is no longer counted as a risk factor.
- B (True) – a score ≥ 2 means oral anticoagulation is recommended (I C); a score of 1 means it should be considered (IIa C).
- C (False) – the threshold in ESC 2024 is **24 h**: early cardioversion without anticoagulation or TOE is not recommended if AF has lasted > 24 h (III C).
- D (False) – AF triggered by a reversible precipitant (e.g. sepsis, surgery) often recurs; long-term OAC should be **considered** in patients at increased thromboembolic risk (IIa C).

**EDIC trap:** Older sources use 48 h and CHA₂DS₂-VASc – ESC 2024 uses 24 h and CHA₂DS₂-VA.

**Ref:** Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old woman with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (LVEF 25 %) has haemodynamically stable recent-onset AF. Pharmacological cardioversion is requested. The most appropriate agent is:
options: Vernakalant
Verapamil
Flecainide
Propafenone
Amiodarone
questions.expl:
**Why E:** In structural heart disease – HFrEF, coronary artery disease or severe LVH – IV amiodarone is the recommended agent for pharmacological cardioversion (ESC 2024, I A). Its effect is delayed (often 8–12 h or more), but it is safe in a low-EF heart and also slows the ventricular rate in the meantime. Watch for hypotension, bradycardia and QT prolongation with IV use.

**Why not the others:**
- A – vernakalant is contraindicated in HFrEF, recent ACS and severe aortic stenosis.
- B – verapamil is a rate-control drug, not a cardioversion drug, and is contraindicated with LVEF ≤ 40%.
- C – flecainide (class IC) is contraindicated in CAD and HFrEF because it is proarrhythmic in a scarred ventricle (CAST).
- D – propafenone (class IC) has the same contraindications as flecainide.

**Ref:** Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414.

questions.stem: Regarding electrical storm (ESC 2022):
options: It is defined as ≥ 3 episodes of sustained ventricular arrhythmia within 7 days, each requiring intervention.
Catheter ablation is contraindicated during electrical storm.
Sedation is part of the initial management.
A non-selective beta-blocker such as propranolol combined with amiodarone is commonly used.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – electrical storm is ≥ 3 episodes of sustained ventricular arrhythmia within **24 hours**, separated by ≥ 5 min, each needing intervention (e.g. ICD shock or ATP).
- B (False) – catheter ablation is a key treatment of storm and is preferred in incessant monomorphic VT.
- C (True) – sedation breaks the cycle of shocks, fear and sympathetic drive; deep sedation or intubation is used if the storm is refractory.
- D (True) – non-selective beta-blockade (propranolol) plus amiodarone is the most common drug combination; landiolol is an option for amiodarone-resistant VT.

**EDIC trap:** "7 days" is a wrong definition; the window is 24 h.

**Ref:** Zeppenfeld K et al., 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997–4126.

questions.stem: A patient on haloperidol and ciprofloxacin with QTc 590 ms develops recurrent runs of torsade de pointes. Serum magnesium is normal. The first-line drug is:
options: Adenosine
Intravenous magnesium sulfate
Procainamide
Sotalol
Amiodarone
questions.expl:
**Why B:** This is drug-induced long-QT torsade de pointes (haloperidol + ciprofloxacin, QTc 590 ms). IV magnesium sulfate (e.g. 2 g) stops and prevents recurrences even when serum magnesium is normal, probably by blocking early afterdepolarisations. Also correct K⁺ to high-normal and stop the QT-prolonging drugs; for recurrences raise the heart rate with isoprenaline or overdrive pacing.

**Why not the others:**
- A – adenosine is for re-entrant SVT and has no role in TdP.
- C – procainamide (class IA) prolongs the QT interval and can worsen TdP.
- D – sotalol has class III action and is itself a common cause of TdP.
- E – amiodarone prolongs QT further and is avoided in long-QT TdP.

**EDIC trap:** Unstable or pulseless TdP needs an unsynchronised shock (defibrillation).

**Ref:** Zeppenfeld K et al., 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997–4126.

questions.stem: Bradycardia with adverse features (ERC 2025):
options: Transcutaneous pacing can be used as a bridge to transvenous pacing.
The initial atropine dose is 500 µg IV, repeated up to a total of 3 mg.
Isoprenaline or adrenaline are second-line options when atropine fails.
Atropine is the drug of choice after heart transplantation.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – transcutaneous pacing is a bridge when drugs fail and transvenous pacing is not yet available.
- B (True) – ERC 2025: atropine 500 µg IV, repeated every 3–5 min up to a total of 3 mg.
- C (True) – if atropine is ineffective, isoprenaline (start 5 µg/min) or adrenaline 2–10 µg/min are second-line drugs; aminophylline and glucagon are used in specific situations.
- D (False) – after heart transplantation the heart is denervated, so atropine does not work and can cause paradoxical high-degree AV block; aminophylline is the alternative.

**EDIC trap:** Atropine is also unlikely to work in high-degree AV block with broad QRS (block below the His bundle) – go to pacing.

**Ref:** Soar J et al., ERC Guidelines 2025 Adult ALS, Resuscitation 2025;215:110769; Glikson M et al., 2021 ESC Pacing Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2021;42:3427–3520.

questions.stem: In a large cohort of patients hospitalised with severe sepsis (Walkey, JAMA 2011), new-onset atrial fibrillation was associated with:
options: No difference in stroke
Higher in-hospital stroke and mortality
A protective effect of anticoagulation on mortality
Lower in-hospital mortality
Reduced length of stay
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In over 49,000 patients with severe sepsis, new-onset AF occurred in 5.9%. It was associated with more in-hospital ischaemic stroke (2.6% vs 0.6%) and higher in-hospital mortality (56% vs 39%). This is an observational association – NOAF is a marker of illness severity, not proven to cause the outcomes.

**Why not the others:**
- A – stroke was about four times more frequent with NOAF.
- C – the study did not show a protective effect of anticoagulation; ICU data do not support routine therapeutic anticoagulation in acute sepsis.
- D – mortality was higher, not lower.
- E – NOAF is associated with a longer, not shorter, stay.

**Ref:** Walkey AJ et al., JAMA 2011;306:2248–2254; Wetterslev M et al., Intensive Care Med 2019;45:928–938.

questions.stem: Regarding sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia (ESC 2022):
options: In PROCAMIO, amiodarone terminated more tachycardias than procainamide.
Haemodynamic instability is an indication for IV amiodarone before any attempt at cardioversion.
A haemodynamically tolerated VT may be left untreated if blood pressure is normal.
Procainamide should be avoided in severe heart failure and acute myocardial infarction.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – in PROCAMIO, IV **procainamide** terminated more tolerated wide-QRS tachycardias and caused fewer major cardiac adverse events than amiodarone.
- B (False) – unstable SMVT needs **immediate synchronised cardioversion**; drugs come after or if the shock fails.
- C (False) – even haemodynamically tolerated SMVT should be promptly terminated (cardioversion, antiarrhythmics or pacing), because it can deteriorate.
- D (True) – procainamide is negatively inotropic and hypotensive; avoid it in severe HF, acute MI and end-stage renal failure (active metabolite NAPA accumulates).

**Ref:** Ortiz M et al. (PROCAMIO), Eur Heart J 2017;38:1329–1335; Zeppenfeld K et al., 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997–4126.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old woman is in the ICU 2 days after a large intracerebral haemorrhage. She receives haloperidol for agitation and clarithromycin for pneumonia. K⁺ 3.1 mmol/L, Mg²⁺ 0.55 mmol/L, QTc 610 ms; she has repeated self-terminating runs of polymorphic VT with "twisting" QRS axis, each preceded by a pause, and is haemodynamically stable between runs. Which combination is most appropriate?
options: Procainamide 10–15 mg/kg IV
Adenosine 6 mg IV to clarify the rhythm
Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV, potassium to high-normal, stop haloperidol and clarithromycin; isoprenaline or overdrive pacing if runs recur
Amiodarone 300 mg IV, then infusion
Synchronised cardioversion at 120 J and then sotalol
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Pause-dependent polymorphic VT with a twisting axis and QTc 610 ms is torsade de pointes. There are several additive causes: QT-prolonging drugs (haloperidol, clarithromycin), hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and acute brain injury. Treatment is IV magnesium 2 g (works even at normal levels), K⁺ to high-normal (~4.5–5 mmol/L), stopping the drugs, and raising the heart rate (isoprenaline or overdrive pacing) to shorten QT if runs recur.

**Why not the others:**
- A – procainamide prolongs QT and can worsen TdP.
- B – adenosine is for re-entrant SVT; the rhythm here is already clear.
- D – amiodarone prolongs QT further.
- E – the patient is stable between self-terminating runs, and sotalol is a QT-prolonging drug.

**EDIC trap:** If TdP becomes pulseless or unstable, defibrillate (unsynchronised) – synchronisation often fails.

**Ref:** Zeppenfeld K et al., 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997–4126.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old man has repeated runs of polymorphic VT/VF on the day after primary PCI for an anterior STEMI. According to the 2022 ESC guidelines:
options: IV lidocaine may be considered if beta-blockers and amiodarone are ineffective or amiodarone is contraindicated.
An IV beta-blocker is recommended for recurrent polymorphic VT/VF unless contraindicated.
Routine prophylactic antiarrhythmic drugs other than beta-blockers are recommended after ACS to prevent VT.
Repeat urgent coronary angiography should be considered if ongoing ischaemia (e.g. stent thrombosis) is suspected.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – IV lidocaine may be considered (IIb) if beta-blockers and amiodarone fail or amiodarone is contraindicated; IV amiodarone itself is IIa.
- B (True) – IV beta-blockers are recommended (class I) for recurrent polymorphic VT/VF in STEMI, as they reduce sympathetic drive and ischaemia.
- C (False) – routine prophylactic antiarrhythmic drugs other than beta-blockers are **not** recommended after ACS (class III).
- D (True) – residual ischaemia (e.g. stent thrombosis) is the main driver of polymorphic VT/VF after MI; urgent repeat angiography/revascularisation and K⁺/Mg²⁺ repletion are class I.

**EDIC trap:** Polymorphic VT in ACS is ischaemic, not long-QT – the answer is revascularisation and beta-blockers, not magnesium alone.

**Ref:** Zeppenfeld K et al., 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997–4126 (Table 22, Figure 14).

open.q: A 70-year-old ventilated patient with septic shock on norepinephrine develops new AF at 140/min with stable blood pressure. Outline your management, including anticoagulation.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Haemodynamically stable – no immediate cardioversion; NOAF is a marker of severity.
- Treat triggers first: sepsis source control, volume status (hypovolaemia or overload), catecholamine dose, hypoxaemia/hypercapnia, acidosis, K⁺ and Mg²⁺, CVC tip in the RA.
- Wait-and-see within 48 h is reasonable (IIa B) – up to 83% revert spontaneously after treating the cause.
- Rate control target < 110/min; BB or digoxin; diltiazem/verapamil only if LVEF > 40%; with instability or low EF consider amiodarone, digoxin, esmolol or landiolol (IIb).
- Do not routinely beta-block compensatory sinus tachycardia (STRESS-L: no benefit, signal of harm).
- If becomes unstable: synchronised cardioversion with maximum energy (ERC 2025), then amiodarone 300 mg if it fails.
- Anticoagulation: CHA₂DS₂-VA; in acute sepsis benefit/risk unclear, no routine therapeutic anticoagulation; no elective cardioversion without OAC/TOE if AF > 24 h.
- After discharge consider long-term OAC in patients at increased risk (IIa C).

open.q: A patient with an ICD receives five shocks for monomorphic VT within 6 hours. Outline your management of this electrical storm.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Meets the definition: ≥ 3 sustained ventricular arrhythmia episodes in 24 h, separated by ≥ 5 min, each requiring intervention.
- Unstable VT → immediate synchronised cardioversion (unsynchronised if synchronisation fails).
- Sedation to break the shock–fear–sympathetic cycle; deep sedation/intubation if refractory.
- Non-selective BB (propranolol) + amiodarone; landiolol for amiodarone-resistant VT; procainamide an option (PROCAMIO) except in severe HF, acute MI, end-stage renal failure.
- Correct K⁺ and Mg²⁺, look for ischaemia (urgent angiography if suspected), stop proarrhythmic drugs.
- Catheter ablation – preferred for incessant monomorphic VT.
- MCS for stabilisation (prophylactic before ablation better than rescue).

title: W08 · D2 – Pulmonary embolism: risk stratification, thrombolysis, catheters, ECMO, PERT

questions.stem: A 60-year-old woman with confirmed PE has BP 118/70 mmHg, HR 112/min, sPESI 2, RV/LV ratio 1.3 on CT and elevated troponin. According to ESC 2019 she is classified as:
options: High risk
Intermediate-low risk
Intermediate-high risk
Low risk
Cannot be classified without PESI class
questions.expl:
**Why C:** She is normotensive (no arrest, shock or persistent hypotension), so she is not high risk. sPESI ≥ 1 puts her above low risk, and she has **both** RV dysfunction (RV/LV ratio ≥ 1.0 on CT) **and** a raised troponin – that combination defines intermediate-high risk. These patients get anticoagulation, close monitoring and rescue reperfusion if they deteriorate.

**Why not the others:**
- A – high risk needs haemodynamic instability; BP 118/70 is normal.
- B – intermediate-low risk means only one or neither of RV dysfunction and troponin is positive.
- D – low risk requires sPESI 0 and no RV dysfunction or biomarker rise.
- E – sPESI can be used instead of PESI class (sPESI ≥ 1 is equivalent to PESI III–V).

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603.

questions.stem: Regarding the PEITHO trial:
options: Tenecteplase did not significantly reduce the composite of death or haemodynamic decompensation within 7 days.
It enrolled hypotensive patients (SBP < 90 mmHg) with RV dysfunction.
Tenecteplase significantly reduced 30-day mortality.
Stroke, mostly haemorrhagic, was more frequent with tenecteplase.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – tenecteplase significantly **reduced** the primary composite of death or haemodynamic decompensation within 7 days (2.6% vs 5.6%; OR 0.44).
- B (False) – PEITHO enrolled 1006 **normotensive** intermediate-risk patients with RV dysfunction and a positive troponin.
- C (False) – 30-day mortality did not differ significantly (2.4% vs 3.2%); the benefit came from fewer decompensations.
- D (True) – stroke was 2.4% vs 0.2%, mostly haemorrhagic, and major extracranial bleeding 6.3% vs 1.2%.

**EDIC trap:** PEITHO is positive for the primary end-point but negative for mortality – so thrombolysis in intermediate-high risk is rescue, not routine (ESC 2019 I B).

**Ref:** Meyer G et al. (PEITHO), N Engl J Med 2014;370:1402–1411.

questions.stem: Which of the following meets the ESC 2019 definition of haemodynamic instability in PE?
options: Elevated lactate with normal blood pressure
SBP 95 mmHg with heart rate 120/min
RV/LV ratio > 1.0 on CT
SBP drop of 30 mmHg for 10 minutes
SBP < 90 mmHg for more than 15 minutes not explained by arrhythmia, hypovolaemia or sepsis
questions.expl:
**Why E:** ESC 2019 defines haemodynamic instability in PE as one of three: cardiac arrest, obstructive shock (SBP < 90 mmHg or vasopressors needed, plus end-organ hypoperfusion), or persistent hypotension. Persistent hypotension means SBP < 90 mmHg or a drop ≥ 40 mmHg for **> 15 min**, not caused by new arrhythmia, hypovolaemia or sepsis. Any one of these makes the PE high risk.

**Why not the others:**
- A – raised lactate without hypotension is not one of the ESC criteria (it is used in the AHA/ACC 2026 categories).
- B – SBP 95 mmHg is above the 90 mmHg threshold; tachycardia alone is not instability.
- C – RV/LV ratio > 1.0 is RV dysfunction, which counts for intermediate risk.
- D – the drop must be ≥ 40 mmHg and last > 15 min.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603.

questions.stem: Haemodynamic management of a patient with high-risk PE:
options: Large fluid boluses (> 2 L) are recommended to support the RV.
Dobutamine may be used in low cardiac output.
Induction of anaesthesia and positive pressure ventilation can precipitate cardiovascular collapse.
Noradrenaline is contraindicated because it raises pulmonary vascular resistance.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – the failing RV is overfilled easily; ESC 2019 limits fluids to **≤ 500 mL**, as more worsens septal shift and LV filling.
- B (True) – dobutamine (2–20 µg/kg/min) may be used for low cardiac output; it can worsen hypotension, so combine it with noradrenaline if needed.
- C (True) – induction causes vasodilation and less preload, and positive pressure raises RV afterload, which can cause collapse; AHA/ACC 2026 calls avoidable intubation harmful in categories C–E.
- D (False) – noradrenaline is the vasopressor of choice; it restores systemic pressure and RV coronary perfusion.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603; Creager MA et al., 2026 AHA/ACC PE Guideline, Circulation 2026;153:e977–e1051.

questions.stem: A patient with intermediate-high risk PE on LMWH becomes hypotensive (SBP 80 mmHg) on day 2. There is no contraindication to fibrinolysis. The best next step according to ESC 2019 is:
options: Continue LMWH and add noradrenaline only
Switch to a DOAC
Administer 2 L of crystalloid
Insert an inferior vena cava filter
Rescue systemic thrombolysis
questions.expl:
**Why E:** Her PE is now high risk (SBP 80 mmHg) on anticoagulation. ESC 2019 recommends rescue systemic thrombolysis for haemodynamic deterioration (class I B); PEITHO showed most decompensations occur in the first days. Surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment are alternatives (IIa) if thrombolysis is contraindicated or the centre has the expertise.

**Why not the others:**
- A – noradrenaline is supportive, but on its own it does not remove the clot.
- B – changing the anticoagulant does not treat obstructive shock; UFH is preferred if reperfusion is planned.
- C – 2 L of fluid would worsen RV dilatation; the maximum is ≤ 500 mL.
- D – an IVC filter does not treat the existing clot; it is for patients who cannot be anticoagulated.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603.

questions.stem: Regarding catheter-directed therapy trials:
options: PEERLESS compared large-bore mechanical thrombectomy with catheter-directed thrombolysis.
HI-PEITHO showed a significant reduction in all-cause mortality.
PRAGUE-26 reduced the 7-day composite mainly through fewer cardiorespiratory decompensations.
HI-PEITHO compared ultrasound-facilitated catheter-directed thrombolysis plus anticoagulation with anticoagulation alone.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – PEERLESS (550 intermediate-risk patients) compared large-bore mechanical thrombectomy with CDT; the win ratio favoured thrombectomy (less deterioration/bailout, fewer ICU stays).
- B (False) – HI-PEITHO showed no difference in mortality; the 7-day composite (4.0% vs 10.3%) was reduced by fewer decompensations.
- C (True) – PRAGUE-26 cut the 7-day composite from 6.8% to 0.7%, mainly through fewer cardiorespiratory decompensations; there were 2 intracranial haemorrhages with CDT.
- D (True) – HI-PEITHO compared ultrasound-facilitated CDT (low-dose alteplase) plus anticoagulation with anticoagulation alone.

**EDIC trap:** Catheter-directed therapy has not yet been shown to reduce mortality.

**Ref:** PEERLESS, Circulation 2025;151:260–273; Rosenfield K et al. (HI-PEITHO), N Engl J Med 2026; Kroupa J et al. (PRAGUE-26), N Engl J Med 2026.

questions.stem: The approved systemic alteplase regimen for high-risk PE is:
options: 50 mg bolus followed by 50 mg over 12 hours
1 mg/h for 24 hours
10 mg bolus only
0.9 mg/kg over 60 minutes, max 90 mg
100 mg over 2 hours
questions.expl:
**Why E:** The approved systemic regimen for high-risk PE is alteplase **100 mg IV over 2 hours** (ESC 2019). The benefit is greatest when given within 48 h of symptom onset, but it can still help when symptoms have lasted 6–14 days. In cardiac arrest or extreme instability, an off-label accelerated regimen of 0.6 mg/kg over 15 min (max 50 mg) is used.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a 50 mg bolus followed by 50 mg over 12 h is not a standard PE regimen.
- B – 1 mg/h is the type of low-dose infusion used in catheter-directed thrombolysis, not systemic treatment.
- C – a 10 mg bolus alone is far below an effective systemic thrombolytic dose.
- D – 0.9 mg/kg over 60 min (max 90 mg) is the regimen for acute ischaemic stroke.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603.

questions.stem: Regarding VA-ECMO and PERT in PE:
options: ESC 2019 states that ECMO may be considered in refractory circulatory collapse or cardiac arrest.
ECMO in PE is supported by large randomised trials.
ECMO in PE is associated with a low rate of complications.
The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline recommends PERT activation for categories C–E.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESC 2019: VA-ECMO may be considered (IIb C) in refractory circulatory collapse or cardiac arrest, together with surgical embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment.
- B (False) – there are no randomised trials of ECMO in PE; the evidence is from observational series.
- C (False) – complications are frequent, especially bleeding and limb or vascular ischaemia.
- D (True) – AHA/ACC 2026 recommends PERT activation (class 1) for categories C–E; ESC 2019 gave a multidisciplinary team IIa C.

**EDIC trap:** VA-ECMO is a bridge (it unloads the RV and keeps perfusion) – it is not reperfusion therapy itself.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603; Creager MA et al., 2026 AHA/ACC PE Guideline, Circulation 2026;153:e977–e1051.

questions.stem: In the 2026 AHA/ACC acute PE classification, a normotensive patient with signs of shock and end-organ dysfunction (normotensive shock) belongs to category:
options: C3
C1
E2
B
D
questions.expl:
**Why E:** The 2026 AHA/ACC guideline replaces "massive/submassive" with categories A–E. Category **D** means incipient cardiopulmonary failure; D2 is normotensive shock (signs of hypoperfusion and organ dysfunction, e.g. raised lactate, with normal BP). Category E is overt failure: E1 persistent hypotension/cardiogenic shock, E2 refractory shock or cardiac arrest. In D1–D2, systemic thrombolysis, CDT or thrombectomy may be considered.

**Why not the others:**
- A – C3 is a raised severity score with RV dysfunction and biomarkers, but no hypoperfusion.
- B – C1 is a raised severity score with no RV or biomarker abnormality.
- C – E2 is refractory shock or cardiac arrest.
- D – B is symptomatic PE with a low severity score (sPESI 0).

**Ref:** Creager MA et al., 2026 AHA/ACC PE Guideline, Circulation 2026;153:e977–e1051.

questions.stem: Anticoagulation in acute PE:
options: Unfractionated heparin is preferred when creatinine clearance is ≤ 30 mL/min.
LMWH is generally preferred over unfractionated heparin.
Unfractionated heparin is preferred in haemodynamically unstable patients who may need reperfusion.
Routine IVC filter placement in anticoagulated patients is recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – LMWH and fondaparinux are renally cleared and accumulate, so UFH is preferred if CrCl ≤ 30 mL/min.
- B (True) – LMWH (or fondaparinux) is preferred over UFH in most patients: it has a predictable dose response, less HIT and needs no aPTT monitoring (AHA/ACC 2026 class 1).
- C (True) – in haemodynamic instability UFH is preferred because it has a short half-life and can be reversed with protamine if thrombolysis or a procedure is needed.
- D (False) – a routine IVC filter in an anticoagulated patient is harmful (AHA/ACC 2026); filters are for patients who cannot be anticoagulated.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603; Creager MA et al., 2026 AHA/ACC PE Guideline, Circulation 2026;153:e977–e1051.

open.q: A 60-year-old woman with confirmed PE is normotensive with HR 112/min, sPESI 2, RV/LV ratio 1.3 and elevated troponin. Classify her risk and outline your management, including what you would do if she deteriorates.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ESC 2019: intermediate-high risk (no instability, sPESI ≥ 1, RV dysfunction and positive troponin); AHA/ACC 2026 category C or higher – measure lactate.
- Anticoagulation – LMWH preferred over UFH (UFH if reperfusion likely or CrCl ≤ 30 mL/min).
- No routine primary systemic thrombolysis – PEITHO: ↓ decompensation (2.6 vs 5.6%) but no mortality benefit and ↑ major bleeding/haemorrhagic stroke.
- Close monitoring; activate PERT (AHA/ACC 2026 Class 1 for C–E).
- If haemodynamic deterioration: rescue systemic thrombolysis (I B); embolectomy or catheter-directed treatment as alternatives (IIa).
- Catheter-directed therapy may reduce early decompensation in selected patients with additional severity signs (HI-PEITHO, PRAGUE-26) – no proven mortality benefit.
- Haemodynamic support: fluids ≤ 500 mL, norepinephrine, dobutamine for low output; avoid intubation where possible.
- Refractory collapse/arrest: VA-ECMO as a bridge (IIb C) or ECPR.

open.q: Explain why PEITHO and the 2026 catheter-directed trials (HI-PEITHO, PRAGUE-26) are interpreted differently despite all reducing early decompensation.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- All three targeted intermediate-high-risk PE and reduced early (7-day) decompensation-driven composites.
- PEITHO used full-dose systemic tenecteplase: major extracranial bleeding 6.3 vs 1.2%, stroke 2.4 vs 0.2% (mostly haemorrhagic).
- PEITHO: no reduction in 7-d or 30-d mortality → routine systemic thrombolysis not recommended.
- CDT uses a lower thrombolytic dose delivered into the thrombus, aiming for less bleeding.
- HI-PEITHO: 4.0 vs 10.3%, no significant difference in major bleeding, no intracranial haemorrhage.
- PRAGUE-26: 0.7 vs 6.8%, major bleeding 1.4 vs 2.2% (NS), but 2 intracranial haemorrhages with CDT.
- None showed a mortality benefit; selection, availability and centre expertise (PERT) determine use.

title: W08 · D3 – Acute aortic dissection and cardiac tamponade

questions.stem: CT angiography shows an intimal flap originating in the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery, with retrograde extension into the ascending aorta. This is classified as:
options: DeBakey III
Penetrating aortic ulcer
Stanford B, because the entry is in the descending aorta
Intramural haematoma
Stanford A
questions.expl:
**Why E:** The Stanford classification depends only on whether the **ascending aorta** is involved, not on where the entry tear is. A retrograde dissection from a descending-aorta entry into the ascending aorta is therefore type A. It carries the same risks (rupture, tamponade, coronary involvement, acute AR) and needs emergency surgery; the frozen elephant trunk technique is used when the primary entry is in the descending aorta.

**Why not the others:**
- A – DeBakey III is limited to the descending aorta; this flap reaches the ascending aorta.
- B – a PAU is an ulcer in an atherosclerotic plaque, not a flap that extends along the aorta.
- C – Stanford B means the ascending aorta is **not** involved, wherever the entry is.
- D – an IMH has no intimal flap or false-lumen flow.

**EDIC trap:** Stanford A = DeBakey I + II.

**Ref:** Mazzolai L et al., 2024 ESC Guidelines on peripheral arterial and aortic diseases, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538–3700.

questions.stem: Regarding initial medical therapy of acute aortic dissection (ESC 2024):
options: Opioids should be avoided because they mask ongoing pain from extension of the dissection.
IV labetalol or esmolol are first-line agents.
A vasodilator should be started before beta-blockade to lower BP quickly.
The target is systolic BP < 120 mmHg and heart rate ≤ 60/min.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – adequate IV opioid analgesia is part of management, because pain drives sympathetic tone and raises BP and HR.
- B (True) – IV labetalol is the first choice and esmolol an alternative; non-dihydropyridine CCBs are used if beta-blockers are contraindicated.
- C (False) – a vasodilator is added only **after** rate control; on its own it causes reflex tachycardia, which increases dP/dt and wall shear stress.
- D (True) – the target is SBP < 120 mmHg and HR ≤ 60/min to reduce dP/dt; a higher BP may be accepted if there is malperfusion.

**EDIC trap:** "Rate first, then pressure."

**Ref:** Mazzolai L et al., 2024 ESC Guidelines on peripheral arterial and aortic diseases, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538–3700; Williams B et al., 2018 ESC/ESH Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2018;39:3021–3104.

questions.stem: A haemodynamically unstable patient in the emergency department is suspected to have acute aortic dissection; CT is not immediately possible. The most appropriate imaging is:
options: Aortography
Chest radiograph
MRI angiography
Transoesophageal echocardiography
D-dimer measurement
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ECG-gated CT angiography is the method of choice (sensitivity ~100%, specificity ~98%), but when the patient is unstable or CT is unavailable, ESC 2024 recommends TOE. It can be done at the bedside or in theatre and shows the flap, entry tear, aortic regurgitation, pericardial effusion and coronary involvement. TTE is a first look only, and a negative TTE does not exclude dissection.

**Why not the others:**
- A – invasive aortography is obsolete for diagnosis and needs transfer to a cath lab.
- B – a chest radiograph is often normal and cannot confirm or exclude dissection.
- C – MRI is accurate, but has limited acute availability and is unsuitable for unstable patients.
- E – D-dimer is a lab test used with ADD-RS in low-probability patients, not imaging.

**Ref:** Mazzolai L et al., 2024 ESC Guidelines on peripheral arterial and aortic diseases, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538–3700.

questions.stem: Which are features of complicated type B aortic dissection that favour TEVAR?
options: Rupture or impending rupture
Rapid aortic expansion
Refractory pain or refractory hypertension
Malperfusion
questions.expl:
- A (True) – rupture or impending rupture (e.g. periaortic haematoma, haemothorax) is the most serious complication and needs urgent TEVAR.
- B (True) – rapid aortic expansion shows the false lumen is unstable and is an indication for intervention.
- C (True) – refractory pain or refractory hypertension despite full medical therapy suggests the dissection is progressing.
- D (True) – malperfusion of the limbs, gut, kidneys or spinal cord makes the dissection complicated; TEVAR covers the entry and re-expands the true lumen.

**EDIC trap:** Uncomplicated type B is treated medically, but TEVAR may be considered when there are high-risk features and suitable anatomy.

**Ref:** Mazzolai L et al., 2024 ESC Guidelines on peripheral arterial and aortic diseases, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538–3700.

questions.stem: The approximate mortality of untreated acute type A dissection in the first 48 hours is:
options: 10 % per hour
1–2 % per hour
Mortality is similar to treated type B dissection
5 % in total
0.1 % per hour
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Untreated acute type A dissection has a mortality of about 50% in the first 48 hours, i.e. roughly **1–2% per hour** (IRAD data). Death is caused by rupture into the pericardium (tamponade), acute aortic regurgitation, coronary malperfusion or stroke. For this reason ESC 2024 recommends immediate surgery, and age alone is not a contraindication.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 10% per hour would mean almost all patients die within a day, which overstates the risk.
- C – untreated type A has a much higher mortality than treated type B dissection.
- D – 5% in total is far too low.
- E – 0.1% per hour is far too low.

**EDIC trap:** Mesenteric malperfusion raises mortality to 65–95%.

**Ref:** Mazzolai L et al., 2024 ESC Guidelines on peripheral arterial and aortic diseases, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538–3700; Hagan PG et al. (IRAD), JAMA 2000;283:897–903.

questions.stem: Echocardiographic findings supporting cardiac tamponade:
options: Small inferior vena cava collapsing > 50 % with inspiration
Diastolic right ventricular collapse
Absence of respiratory variation of mitral and tricuspid inflow
Right atrial collapse
questions.expl:
- A (False) – in tamponade the IVC is **dilated and non-collapsing** (plethora), because right atrial pressure is high; a small collapsing IVC makes tamponade unlikely.
- B (True) – diastolic RV collapse is more specific than RA collapse for tamponade.
- C (False) – tamponade causes **exaggerated** respiratory variation of mitral and tricuspid inflow, due to ventricular interdependence (the echo version of pulsus paradoxus).
- D (True) – RA collapse (systolic) is the earliest and most sensitive sign, especially if it lasts more than one third of the cardiac cycle.

**Ref:** Schulz-Menger J et al., 2025 ESC Guidelines for myocarditis and pericarditis, Eur Heart J 2025;46:3952–4041.

questions.stem: A patient with acute type A dissection develops haemopericardium with SBP 60 mmHg in the emergency department; the operating room will be ready in 30 minutes. The most appropriate approach is:
options: Complete pericardial drainage aiming for SBP 140 mmHg
Transfer for TEVAR
Intubation and high PEEP before any drainage
IV nitroprusside to reduce shear stress
Controlled pericardial drainage of small volumes aiming for SBP around 90 mmHg as a bridge to surgery
questions.expl:
**Why E:** The definitive treatment of haemopericardium in type A dissection is emergency aortic surgery. If collapse is imminent before theatre, controlled drainage of small volumes can be used as a bridge. In Hayashi's series (18 patients), repeated small aspirations (mean ~40 mL) through a pigtail, aiming for SBP ~90 mmHg, raised SBP from ~64 to ~95 mmHg; all patients reached surgery without drainage complications.

**Why not the others:**
- A – complete drainage and a high BP target can restart bleeding and extend the dissection.
- B – TEVAR is for type B; type A needs open surgery.
- C – induction and positive pressure reduce venous return in tamponade and can cause arrest.
- D – nitroprusside in a patient with SBP 60 mmHg would worsen shock.

**EDIC trap:** The goal is a bridge to theatre, not normotension.

**Ref:** Hayashi T et al., Circulation 2012;126(11 Suppl 1):S97–S101; Mazzolai L et al., 2024 ESC Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538–3700.

questions.stem: Clinical signs of cardiac tamponade include:
options: Electrical alternans
Widened pulse pressure with bounding pulses
Pulsus paradoxus > 10 mmHg
Distended jugular veins
questions.expl:
- A (True) – electrical alternans (beat-to-beat change in QRS amplitude) comes from the heart "swinging" in a large effusion, often with low voltage.
- B (False) – tamponade causes a **narrow** pulse pressure because stroke volume is low; a wide pulse pressure with bounding pulses suggests aortic regurgitation.
- C (True) – pulsus paradoxus (inspiratory SBP fall > 10 mmHg) is caused by ventricular interdependence.
- D (True) – distended jugular veins are part of Beck's triad, together with hypotension and muffled heart sounds.

**EDIC trap:** In hypovolaemic or low-pressure tamponade (e.g. haemorrhage), JVD may be absent.

**Ref:** Schulz-Menger J et al., 2025 ESC Guidelines for myocarditis and pericarditis, Eur Heart J 2025;46:3952–4041.

questions.stem: According to the 2025 ESC pericardial guidelines, a definite tamponade triage score indicating immediate pericardiocentesis is:
options: Effusion > 10 mm in end-diastole
> 2 points
> 4 points
> 6 points from at least two categories
Any circumferential effusion
questions.expl:
**Why D:** The ESC triage score (expert consensus) adds points for aetiology, clinical features and imaging. A score **> 6 points**, from at least two categories, indicates immediate pericardiocentesis. Examples: LA collapse 2 points, RV collapse 1.5, IVC plethora 1.5, large circumferential effusion 3, pulsus paradoxus > 10 mmHg 2, orthopnoea 3. Lower scores allow drainage to be delayed (up to 12–48 h) if the patient is stable.

**Why not the others:**
- A – > 10 mm is a moderate effusion; size alone does not decide.
- B – > 2 points is far below the threshold.
- C – > 4 points is below the threshold.
- E – a circumferential effusion gives points but does not by itself mean tamponade.

**Ref:** Schulz-Menger J et al., 2025 ESC Guidelines for myocarditis and pericarditis, Eur Heart J 2025;46:3952–4041; Ristić AD et al., Eur Heart J 2014;35:2279–2284.

questions.stem: Regarding pericardial drainage (ESC 2025):
options: Pericardiocentesis should be guided by echocardiography, CT or fluoroscopy.
Needle pericardiocentesis alone is preferred over surgical drainage for purulent effusion.
A large effusion is defined as > 10 mm in end-diastole.
Diuretics are a useful first step in tamponade to reduce effusion volume.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – image guidance (echo, CT or fluoroscopy) makes pericardiocentesis safer and is class I C.
- B (False) – for purulent effusion, **surgical** drainage is preferred (I C), as pus is thick and loculated; surgery is also used if a percutaneous approach is not possible.
- C (False) – a large effusion is > 20 mm in end-diastole; 10–20 mm is moderate and < 10 mm is small.
- D (False) – the patient is preload-dependent; diuretics (and vasodilators) lower filling and can cause collapse.

**EDIC trap:** Avoid induction and positive pressure before drainage if possible.

**Ref:** Schulz-Menger J et al., 2025 ESC Guidelines for myocarditis and pericarditis, Eur Heart J 2025;46:3952–4041.

open.q: A 64-year-old hypertensive man presents with sudden tearing chest pain radiating to the back, BP 190/100 mmHg and HR 105/min. Outline your diagnostic approach and initial medical management.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Suspect AAS; ADD-RS + D-dimer helps only at low pre-test probability (< 500 ng/mL makes dissection unlikely).
- ECG-gated CT angiography neck to pelvis is the method of choice (sensitivity 100%, specificity 98%); TOE if unstable or CT unavailable; negative TTE does not exclude.
- Arterial line (ideally right radial), ICU, careful IV opioid analgesia.
- Targets SBP < 120 mmHg and HR ≤ 60/min to reduce dP/dt.
- Rate first: IV labetalol or esmolol (non-dihydropyridine CCB if BB contraindicated).
