- Vasodilator (nitroprusside, nitroglycerin, nicardipine) only after rate control – avoid reflex tachycardia.
- Classify: Stanford A → immediate surgery (1–2%/h mortality untreated); B uncomplicated → medical, complicated → TEVAR.
- Tolerate higher BP in malperfusion; treat hypotension as a warning sign (tamponade, rupture, AR, MI).

open.q: Explain the pathophysiology of cardiac tamponade and why management of haemopericardium in type A dissection differs from tamponade of other causes.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Raised intrapericardial pressure exceeds chamber filling pressure → right chamber collapse, ventricular interdependence, ↓ LV filling and output.
- Rate of accumulation matters more than volume – small acute haemopericardium can cause tamponade.
- Patient is preload- and HR-dependent: avoid diuretics and vasodilators, fluids cautiously; induction and positive pressure may cause collapse – drain before intubation if possible.
- Usual treatment: image-guided pericardiocentesis (I C); surgical drainage if not feasible or purulent.
- In type A dissection, definitive treatment is emergency aortic surgery.
- Uncontrolled full drainage may raise BP and increase aortic bleeding.
- Controlled drainage of small volumes (mean ~40 mL) targeting SBP ~90 mmHg as a bridge (Hayashi 2012: SBP ~64 → ~95 mmHg, all reached surgery).

title: W08 · D4 – Hypertensive crises: emergency vs urgency, drugs, target reductions

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man has BP 230/130 mmHg, headache and no evidence of acute organ damage (normal neurology, ECG, troponin, creatinine, fundoscopy). The most appropriate management is:
options: ICU admission and IV nitroprusside
Oral antihypertensive therapy and close outpatient follow-up
IV labetalol to reduce MAP by 25 % within 1 hour
IV esmolol targeting SBP < 120 mmHg
Sublingual nifedipine
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Without acute hypertension-mediated organ damage this is a hypertensive **urgency**, however high the number. ESC 2024 recommends oral treatment (e.g. low-dose ACE inhibitor/ARB, or a short-acting beta-blocker), gradual reduction over 24–48 h and early outpatient review. In chronic hypertension, autoregulation of the brain, kidneys and heart is shifted to the right, so a fast fall can cause ischaemia.

**Why not the others:**
- A – ICU and IV nitroprusside are for emergencies with organ damage.
- C – a 25% MAP reduction within 1 h is an emergency target (e.g. encephalopathy), not for urgency.
- D – SBP < 120 mmHg with esmolol is the target for aortic dissection only.
- E – sublingual nifedipine causes an unpredictable, sudden fall in BP and has been linked to stroke and MI.

**EDIC trap:** Organ damage decides, not the absolute BP value.

**Ref:** McEvoy JW et al., 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3912–4018.

questions.stem: Regarding hypertensive emergency (ESC 2024):
options: Patients should be screened for secondary hypertension after the acute event.
Short half-life IV drugs are preferred.
Rapid normalisation of BP is the goal in most cases.
It is defined by BP ≥ 180/110 mmHg with acute hypertension-mediated organ damage.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – after stabilisation, patients should be screened for secondary causes (e.g. renovascular disease, primary aldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma), because they remain at high CV risk.
- B (True) – short half-life, titratable IV drugs (e.g. labetalol, nicardipine, clevidipine, esmolol) with an arterial line allow control and avoid overshoot.
- C (False) – rapid or excessive lowering is not recommended; most emergencies aim for MAP −20–25%, with exceptions such as aortic dissection, pulmonary oedema and ACS.
- D (True) – ESC 2024 defines a hypertensive emergency as BP ≥ 180/110 mmHg with acute HMOD, which usually needs IV treatment in a monitored bed.

**Ref:** McEvoy JW et al., 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3912–4018; Williams B et al., 2018 ESC/ESH Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2018;39:3021–3104.

questions.stem: A patient with malignant hypertension (grade IV retinopathy, AKI) should have BP lowered:
options: With IV furosemide as first-line therapy
Only if creatinine continues to rise
By 20–25 % of MAP over several hours
By 50 % of MAP immediately
To < 120/80 mmHg within 1 hour
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Malignant hypertension (extreme BP with acute microangiopathy, e.g. grade IV retinopathy, AKI, often TMA) is an emergency, but autoregulation is shifted to the right. ESC/ESH 2018 recommends reducing MAP by 20–25% over **several hours**. First-line is IV labetalol; alternatives are nicardipine, nitroprusside or urapidil.

**Why not the others:**
- A – patients are often volume-depleted from pressure natriuresis; diuretics are only for fluid overload.
- B – the organ damage is already there; waiting for creatinine to rise more delays treatment.
- D – a 50% fall in MAP straight away risks ischaemia of the brain, kidneys and heart.
- E – normalising BP within 1 h is dangerous outside aortic dissection.

**Ref:** Williams B et al., 2018 ESC/ESH Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2018;39:3021–3104; McEvoy JW et al., 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3912–4018.

questions.stem: Match situations with ESC/ESH targets:
options: Hypertensive encephalopathy: reduce MAP by 20–25 % immediately.
Acute aortic dissection: SBP < 120 mmHg and HR < 60/min immediately.
Severe pre-eclampsia: SBP < 120 mmHg and DBP < 80 mmHg.
Acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema: SBP < 100 mmHg immediately.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – in hypertensive encephalopathy, MAP is reduced by 20–25% immediately; first-line drugs are labetalol or nicardipine.
- B (True) – in aortic dissection, SBP < 120 mmHg and HR < 60/min are the targets, reached immediately to reduce dP/dt (esmolol plus a vasodilator).
- C (False) – in severe pre-eclampsia the target is SBP < 160 and DBP < 105 mmHg; lowering further can reduce placental perfusion.
- D (False) – in acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema the target is SBP < 140 mmHg (nitroglycerin or nitroprusside plus a loop diuretic).

**EDIC trap:** Only dissection is "fast and very low"; 120 mmHg is not a general target.

**Ref:** Williams B et al., 2018 ESC/ESH Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2018;39:3021–3104 (Table 31).

questions.stem: In the ATACH-2 trial of intracerebral haemorrhage, intensive SBP lowering to 110–139 mmHg compared with 140–179 mmHg resulted in:
options: Significantly lower death or disability
No difference in death or disability and more renal adverse events
Increased intracranial rebleeding
Reduced haematoma expansion and lower mortality
Lower renal adverse events
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ATACH-2 randomised 1000 patients with ICH and SBP ≥ 180 mmHg within 4.5 h to SBP 110–139 vs 140–179 mmHg for 24 h, using IV nicardipine. Death or disability (mRS 4–6) at 3 months did not differ (38.7% vs 37.7%), and the trial was stopped for futility. Renal adverse events within 7 days were more common with intensive lowering (9.0% vs 4.0%).

**Why not the others:**
- A – the primary outcome was not different.
- C – rebleeding was not increased by intensive lowering.
- D – any small effect on haematoma expansion did not translate into lower mortality.
- E – renal adverse events were **more** frequent, not less.

**EDIC trap:** ESC 2024 therefore aims for SBP 140–160 mmHg, not < 140.

**Ref:** Qureshi AI et al. (ATACH-2), N Engl J Med 2016;375:1033–1043.

questions.stem: Blood pressure management in acute ischaemic stroke (ESC 2024):
options: Before thrombolysis, BP should be < 220/120 mmHg.
In patients without reperfusion and BP < 220/110 mmHg, routine immediate lowering is recommended.
In ENCHANTED2/MT, an SBP target < 120 mmHg after thrombectomy improved functional outcome.
After reperfusion, BP should be kept < 180/105 mmHg for at least 24 hours.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – BP must be < **185/110** mmHg before thrombolysis; < 220/120 is the threshold for treating patients not getting reperfusion.
- B (False) – without reperfusion, BP is not lowered unless it is ≥ 220/110 mmHg, and then by only ~15% over 24 h (IIa C), as penumbral perfusion depends on BP.
- C (False) – in ENCHANTED2/MT, SBP < 120 mmHg after thrombectomy gave a **worse** functional outcome (common OR 1.37) and more early neurological deterioration; the trial stopped early.
- D (True) – after thrombolysis or thrombectomy, BP is kept < 180/105 mmHg for at least 24 h (IIa B).

**Ref:** McEvoy JW et al., 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3912–4018; Yang P et al. (ENCHANTED2/MT), Lancet 2022;400:1585–1596.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with BP 210/120 mmHg, tachycardia and sweating after cocaine use. Which drug should be avoided as monotherapy?
options: Propranolol
Benzodiazepine
Nitroglycerin
Phentolamine
Nicardipine
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Cocaine causes intense sympathetic stimulation with α- and β-adrenergic effects. A non-selective beta-blocker like propranolol, given alone, removes β₂-mediated vasodilation and leaves α-vasoconstriction unopposed, which can worsen hypertension and coronary vasospasm. The same reasoning applies to phaeochromocytoma crisis. First-line treatment is a benzodiazepine, then an α-blocker or vasodilator.

**Why not the others:**
- B – benzodiazepines reduce central sympathetic outflow and are first-line.
- C – nitroglycerin is a vasodilator that also relieves coronary vasospasm.
- D – phentolamine (α-blocker) treats the α-mediated vasoconstriction directly.
- E – nicardipine is a vasodilator that can safely lower BP here.

**EDIC trap:** Labetalol (α + β) is listed as an option in phaeochromocytoma, but its β effect is stronger – α-blockade should come first.

**Ref:** McEvoy JW et al., 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3912–4018.

questions.stem: Regarding IV antihypertensive drugs:
options: Nicardipine is a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker.
Labetalol is a pure β₁-selective blocker.
Esmolol has a long duration of action (4–6 h).
Nitroprusside can cause cyanide/thiocyanate accumulation, especially in renal or hepatic failure.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – nicardipine is an IV dihydropyridine CCB (onset 5–15 min); a caution is liver failure.
- B (False) – labetalol blocks both α₁ and β receptors (β effect stronger); it is not β₁-selective.
- C (False) – esmolol is ultra-short-acting (onset 1–2 min, duration 10–30 min) because red-cell esterases break it down, so it is easy to titrate.
- D (True) – nitroprusside releases cyanide, which is converted to thiocyanate; both accumulate with high doses or long infusions, especially in liver or renal failure.

**EDIC trap:** Urapidil and enalaprilat last 4–6 h – they are not esmolol's duration.

**Ref:** Williams B et al., 2018 ESC/ESH Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2018;39:3021–3104 (Table 32).

questions.stem: According to ESC 2024, in acute intracerebral haemorrhage with SBP 230 mmHg, which statement is correct?
options: The target is SBP 180–200 mmHg
IV hydralazine is first-line
BP should not be treated in the first 24 hours
SBP should be lowered to < 120 mmHg within 1 hour
Lowering SBP by more than 70 mmHg within 1 hour is not recommended
questions.expl:
**Why E:** ESC 2024 advises against lowering SBP by more than 70 mmHg within 1 hour when SBP is ≥ 220 mmHg (III B). Such a fall is associated with AKI and early neurological deterioration. The aim is SBP 140–160 mmHg within 6 h of onset (IIa A), reached with titratable IV drugs.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 180–200 mmHg is too high; the target is 140–160 mmHg.
- B – hydralazine is unpredictable and not first-line; titratable drugs such as labetalol, nicardipine or urapidil are preferred.
- C – early lowering (within 6 h) is recommended, as INTERACT2 suggested a functional benefit.
- D – SBP < 120 within 1 h is far too aggressive; ATACH-2 showed no benefit below 140 and more renal harm.

**Ref:** McEvoy JW et al., 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3912–4018; Anderson CS et al. (INTERACT2), N Engl J Med 2013;368:2355–2365.

questions.stem: Severe pre-eclampsia with hypertensive crisis (ESC 2024):
options: IV nitroglycerin is contraindicated if pulmonary oedema is present.
IV labetalol or nicardipine plus magnesium sulphate is recommended.
The target is SBP < 160 mmHg and DBP < 105 mmHg within 150–180 minutes.
Loop diuretics are first-line because plasma volume is increased.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – IV nitroglycerin is **recommended** (I C) when pre-eclampsia or eclampsia is complicated by pulmonary oedema.
- B (True) – IV labetalol or nicardipine plus MgSO₄ (to prevent seizures) is recommended (I C); definitive treatment is delivery.
- C (True) – the target is SBP < 160 and DBP < 105 mmHg within 150–180 min; if not controlled in 360 min on two drugs, consult an intensivist.
- D (False) – plasma volume is **reduced** in pre-eclampsia, so diuretics are inappropriate (except for pulmonary oedema).

**EDIC trap:** MgSO₄ with nifedipine can cause marked hypotension.

**Ref:** McEvoy JW et al., 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3912–4018.

open.q: Explain the difference between a hypertensive emergency and urgency, and why BP targets differ between malignant hypertension, aortic dissection and acute ischaemic stroke.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Emergency = BP ≥ 180/110 with acute HMOD → IV titratable drugs, monitored bed; urgency = no HMOD → oral therapy, outpatient follow-up.
- Organ damage decides, not the absolute BP value.
- Chronic hypertension shifts autoregulation to the right – rapid/excessive lowering causes ischaemia (stroke, AKI, MI).
- Malignant hypertension: MAP −20–25% over several hours (labetalol first line).
- Aortic dissection: exception – immediately SBP < 120 and HR < 60 (esmolol + vasodilator) to reduce shear stress.
- Ischaemic stroke: do not lower unless extreme; < 185/110 before thrombolysis, < 180/105 for 24 h after reperfusion; ~15% reduction over 24 h if ≥ 220/110 without reperfusion.
- ENCHANTED2/MT: SBP < 120 after thrombectomy worsened outcome.

open.q: A patient with acute ICH has SBP 230 mmHg. Outline your BP management and explain how INTERACT2 and ATACH-2 inform it.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- ESC 2024: lower within 6 h to SBP 140–160 mmHg (IIa A).
- Avoid a fall > 70 mmHg within 1 h when SBP ≥ 220 (III B) – risk of AKI and early neurological deterioration.
- Use short half-life titratable IV drugs with arterial line monitoring.
- INTERACT2: SBP < 140 within 1 h vs < 180 – primary outcome 52.0 vs 55.6% (NS), ordinal mRS favoured intensive arm, no excess harm.
- ATACH-2: SBP 110–139 vs 140–179 – no difference (38.7 vs 37.7%), stopped for futility, more renal adverse events (9.0 vs 4.0%).
- Conclusion: moderate lowering is reasonable, very aggressive lowering brings no benefit and some harm.

title: W08 · D5 – Valvular heart disease in the critically ill and infective endocarditis

questions.stem: A 78-year-old in cardiogenic shock has a calcified aortic valve with AVA 0.7 cm², mean gradient 26 mmHg and LVEF 25 %. Which statement is correct?
options: Severe AS is excluded because the mean gradient is < 40 mmHg
Balloon valvuloplasty is the preferred definitive therapy
This may be low-flow, low-gradient severe AS; the low gradient reflects low flow
An IABP is contraindicated
The patient should receive high-dose nitroprusside
questions.expl:
**Why C:** The transvalvular gradient depends on flow. With LVEF 25% and shock, a truly severe valve (AVA 0.7 cm²) may generate only 26 mmHg – this is low-flow, low-gradient AS (SVi ≤ 35 mL/m²). Dobutamine stress echo separates truly severe from pseudo-severe AS: a rise in stroke volume ≥ 20% shows contractile reserve. In decompensated severe AS, early valve intervention (usually TAVI) is the only way to reverse the low output.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the 40 mmHg threshold applies only with normal flow; AVA ≤ 1 cm² still points to severe AS.
- B – balloon valvuloplasty is only a rare bridge to TAVI/SAVR, not definitive therapy.
- D – an IABP is contraindicated in significant AR, not in AS.
- E – high-dose vasodilators cause hypotension against a fixed obstruction and lower coronary perfusion.

**Ref:** Praz F et al., 2025 ESC/EACTS Valvular Heart Disease Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding perioperative/ICU management of severe aortic stenosis:
options: Hypotension is generally well tolerated and does not need prompt treatment.
Loss of atrial contraction (AF) is usually well tolerated.
Tachycardia is well tolerated because it increases cardiac output.
Arterial vasodilators are first-line for hypotension.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – hypotension reduces coronary perfusion of the hypertrophied LV, causing ischaemia and a downward spiral; treat it promptly with a vasopressor (noradrenaline, phenylephrine).
- B (False) – the stiff LV depends on the atrial kick for filling, so AF is often poorly tolerated; restore sinus rhythm.
- C (False) – tachycardia shortens diastole, which reduces both LV filling and coronary perfusion and causes ischaemia.
- D (False) – arterial vasodilators lower BP without raising flow across a fixed obstruction; they should be avoided.

**EDIC trap:** A K′ item can have four false statements.

**Ref:** Praz F et al., 2025 ESC/EACTS Valvular Heart Disease Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2025.

questions.stem: Three days after an inferior MI, a patient develops sudden pulmonary oedema and shock. A murmur is barely audible. TTE shows a flail posterior mitral leaflet. The best bridging management before urgent surgery is:
options: Systemic thrombolysis
IABP is contraindicated; give high-dose beta-blocker
Afterload reduction (e.g., nitroprusside if BP allows), inotropes, diuretics and consider IABP
Pure alpha-agonist to raise afterload
Large fluid boluses
questions.expl:
**Why C:** A flail posterior leaflet after inferior MI suggests rupture of the posteromedial papillary muscle, which has a single blood supply. In acute MR the small, stiff LA causes a sudden rise in pressure, leading to pulmonary oedema and shock. Lowering afterload (nitroprusside if BP allows, or an IABP) increases forward flow and reduces the regurgitant fraction. Inotropes and diuretics bridge the patient to urgent surgery, usually valve replacement.

**Why not the others:**
- A – thrombolysis does not treat a mechanical complication and increases bleeding risk at surgery.
- B – an IABP helps in MR; a high-dose beta-blocker would worsen cardiogenic shock.
- D – raising afterload increases the regurgitant fraction and lowers forward output.
- E – the LA pressure is already high, and large fluid boluses would worsen pulmonary oedema.

**EDIC trap:** In acute MR the murmur may be soft or absent; an eccentric jet is underestimated on TTE, so use TOE.

**Ref:** Praz F et al., 2025 ESC/EACTS Valvular Heart Disease Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2025.

questions.stem: Acute severe aortic regurgitation:
options: An intra-aortic balloon pump is contraindicated.
Classic peripheral signs of chronic AR (wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses) are usually prominent.
Bradycardia increases regurgitant volume.
It can usually be managed medically without surgery.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – an IABP inflates in diastole and increases the regurgitant volume, so it is contraindicated in significant AR.
- B (False) – in acute AR the peripheral signs of chronic AR are usually absent; the LV is not dilated, LVEDP rises quickly and the murmur is short and soft.
- C (True) – bradycardia lengthens diastole and increases regurgitation; a relative tachycardia is compensatory, so beta-blockers are used with caution.
- D (False) – acute severe AR (e.g. from endocarditis or type A dissection) usually needs immediate surgery; vasodilators and inotropes are only a bridge.

**EDIC trap:** IABP helps in acute MR and ventricular septal rupture, but is contraindicated in AR and aortic dissection.

**Ref:** Praz F et al., 2025 ESC/EACTS Valvular Heart Disease Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2025.

questions.stem: According to ESC 2023, emergency surgery (within 24 h) for infective endocarditis is indicated in:
options: Vegetation 12 mm without embolism or valve dysfunction
Splenic infarction
Positive blood cultures for 48 hours
Severe aortic regurgitation causing refractory pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock
Streptococcal native valve IE responding to antibiotics
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ESC 2023 lists emergency surgery (within 24 h) for aortic or mitral NVE/PVE with severe regurgitation, obstruction or a fistula that causes refractory pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock. Without surgery these patients die from heart failure, which is the most common cause of death in IE. Other indications (abscess, large vegetations with embolism) are urgent, within 3–5 days.

**Why not the others:**
- A – a 12-mm vegetation alone, without embolism or another indication, does not need emergency surgery.
- B – a splenic infarct alone is not an emergency indication; vegetation size and recurrence decide.
- C – uncontrolled infection is defined by bacteraemia persisting > 1 week despite proper antibiotics, and it is an urgent indication.
- E – a streptococcal NVE responding to antibiotics does not need surgery.

**Ref:** Delgado V et al., 2023 ESC Endocarditis Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948–4042.

questions.stem: Which are indications for urgent surgery (within 3–5 days) in left-sided IE according to ESC 2023?
options: Aortic root abscess
New atrioventricular block
Vegetation ≥ 10 mm after an embolic episode despite appropriate antibiotics
Fever persisting for 24 hours after starting antibiotics
questions.expl:
- A (True) – an aortic root abscess shows locally uncontrolled infection, which needs urgent surgery.
- B (True) – a new AV block suggests the infection has spread to the conduction tissue (often a perivalvular abscess), which is an urgent indication.
- C (True) – a vegetation ≥ 10 mm after at least one embolic episode despite antibiotics is an urgent indication to prevent further emboli.
- D (False) – fever often lasts several days on antibiotics; only bacteraemia persisting > 1 week despite proper treatment counts as uncontrolled infection.

**EDIC trap:** Embolism prevention is the third indication, together with heart failure and uncontrolled infection.

**Ref:** Delgado V et al., 2023 ESC Endocarditis Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948–4042.

questions.stem: In the EASE trial (early surgery within 48 h vs conventional treatment in left-sided IE with large vegetations), early surgery:
options: Included patients with vegetations < 5 mm
Increased perioperative mortality
Reduced the composite of in-hospital death or embolic events at 6 weeks, mainly by preventing emboli
Reduced 6-month all-cause mortality significantly
Was tested only in prosthetic valve endocarditis
questions.expl:
**Why C:** EASE randomised 76 patients with left-sided IE, severe valve disease and vegetations > 10 mm to surgery within 48 h or conventional treatment. In-hospital death or embolic events at 6 weeks fell from 23% to 3%, mainly because early surgery prevented emboli. Six-month all-cause mortality did not differ significantly (3% vs 5%).

**Why not the others:**
- A – patients needed vegetations > 10 mm.
- B – early surgery did not increase perioperative mortality.
- D – the difference in 6-month mortality was not significant.
- E – the trial was in native valve IE, not prosthetic valve IE.

**EDIC trap:** This trial supports ESC 2023's urgent surgery for vegetation ≥ 10 mm with embolism or another indication.

**Ref:** Kang DH et al. (EASE), N Engl J Med 2012;366:2466–2473.

questions.stem: Regarding antibiotic therapy of IE (ESC 2023, POET):
options: In POET, partial oral therapy was inferior to continued IV therapy in stable patients.
Switching to oral therapy requires TEE showing no progression of local complications.
Rifampicin is used for IE involving foreign material such as prosthetic valves.
Aminoglycosides are recommended for staphylococcal native valve IE.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – in POET, partial oral therapy was **non-inferior** to continued IV therapy (composite 9.0% vs 12.1%).
- B (True) – ESC 2023 requires TOE showing no progression of local complications before the oral switch (after ≥ 10 days of IV treatment in stable patients).
- C (True) – rifampicin is used in IE with foreign material (prosthetic valves), as it acts against biofilm.
- D (False) – aminoglycosides are not recommended in staphylococcal NVE; they add nephrotoxicity without clinical benefit.

**EDIC trap:** POET included streptococci, *E. faecalis*, *S. aureus* and CoNS – not only "easy" pathogens.

**Ref:** Iversen K et al. (POET), N Engl J Med 2019;380:415–424; Delgado V et al., 2023 ESC Endocarditis Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948–4042.

questions.stem: A patient with mitral valve IE, a 14-mm vegetation, severe MR with heart failure and a small ischaemic stroke without haemorrhage on CT. Regarding surgery timing:
options: Complete 6 weeks of antibiotics first
Delay surgery at least 4 weeks because of the stroke
Surgery should not be delayed because of the ischaemic stroke
Perform TAVI instead
Surgery is contraindicated after any stroke
questions.expl:
**Why C:** This patient has strong indications for surgery: heart failure from severe MR and a large (14 mm) vegetation with embolism. ESC 2023 recommends that surgery is **not delayed** after a TIA or ischaemic stroke without haemorrhage, because the risk of neurological worsening during cardiopulmonary bypass is low and the risk of more emboli and heart failure is high. Coma or significant haemorrhage on imaging changes this.

**Why not the others:**
- A – waiting 6 weeks exposes her to more emboli and worsening heart failure.
- B – a ≥ 4-week delay is considered only after significant intracranial haemorrhage.
- D – TAVI is an aortic procedure and is not used for active mitral IE.
- E – stroke is not an absolute contraindication; decisions are made individually.

**Ref:** Delgado V et al., 2023 ESC Endocarditis Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948–4042.

questions.stem: Regarding infective endocarditis management (ESC 2023):
options: ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT has no role in possible prosthetic valve IE.
Fungal IE is an indication for surgery.
Right-sided IE never requires surgery.
Definite CIED-related IE requires complete system extraction.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – ¹⁸F-FDG PET/CT is recommended in possible prosthetic valve IE and is a major Duke-ESC criterion.
- B (True) – fungal IE is an indication for surgery (urgent or non-urgent, depending on haemodynamics), as antifungals alone rarely clear it.
- C (False) – right-sided IE may need surgery: severe TR with RV dysfunction, recurrent PE requiring ventilation, vegetations > 20 mm, or left-sided involvement.
- D (True) – definite CIED-related IE requires complete system extraction without delay, plus antibiotics.

**Ref:** Delgado V et al., 2023 ESC Endocarditis Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948–4042.

open.q: Compare the ICU haemodynamic management of acute severe mitral regurgitation and acute severe aortic regurgitation, including the role of IABP and heart rate.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Both: non-dilated chamber cannot accommodate sudden volume → pulmonary oedema and shock; murmurs may be soft/short; TOE often needed.
- MR: afterload reduction (nitroprusside if BP allows) increases forward flow and reduces regurgitant fraction; inotropes and diuretics.
- MR: IABP can be used (exceptionally) to reduce afterload; definitive treatment urgent surgery or transcatheter therapy (repair/replacement, TEER).
- AR: IABP contraindicated – diastolic augmentation increases regurgitation.
- AR: bradycardia harmful (longer diastole = more regurgitation); relative tachycardia compensatory; caution with β-blockers.
- AR: vasodilators and inotropes as bridge; immediate surgery usually required (IE, type A dissection).

open.q: A patient with left-sided native valve IE has severe aortic regurgitation, a 12-mm vegetation and progressive dyspnoea. Outline the indications and timing of surgery according to ESC 2023, and the evidence from EASE.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Three main indications: heart failure, uncontrolled infection, prevention of embolism; decided by the Endocarditis Team.
- Emergency (< 24 h) if refractory pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock.
- Urgent (3–5 days) for HF from severe valve dysfunction, abscess/pseudoaneurysm/fistula/new AV block, or vegetation ≥ 10 mm after embolism (or with another indication).
- Imaging: TTE then TOE; CT angiography if echo inconclusive; brain/whole-body imaging if symptomatic.
- EASE: surgery within 48 h for severe valve disease + vegetation > 10 mm reduced in-hospital death/embolism at 6 weeks (3 vs 23%), driven by emboli; 6-month mortality NS.
- Ischaemic stroke without haemorrhage does not delay surgery; significant ICH → consider delay ≥ 4 weeks.
- Antibiotics continue (NVE 2–6 weeks); no aminoglycosides in staphylococcal NVE.

title: W08 · Saturday – weekly review: Cardio II

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman on day 3 of septic shock (noradrenaline 0.3 µg/kg/min) develops AF at 150/min. BP is stable at MAP 68 mmHg, LVEF 30 %. Potassium 3.2 mmol/L. The most appropriate initial approach is:
options: IV verapamil
Immediate full anticoagulation with UFH
Correct potassium/magnesium and treat sepsis; if rate control is needed, consider IV amiodarone
Elective cardioversion after 3 weeks of anticoagulation
IV flecainide for pharmacological cardioversion
questions.expl:
**Why C:** New-onset AF in septic shock is usually driven by triggers: sepsis, catecholamines, hypokalaemia/hypomagnesaemia, fluid status. Up to 83% revert within 48 h once these are treated (ESC 2024). She is stable, so start with K⁺/Mg²⁺ correction and sepsis control. With LVEF 30%, IV amiodarone (or digoxin, esmolol, landiolol – IIb B) is a suitable rate-control option.

**Why not the others:**
- A – verapamil is negatively inotropic and contraindicated with LVEF ≤ 40%.
- B – the benefit of therapeutic anticoagulation for NOAF in acute sepsis is unclear and bleeding risk is high; it is not routine.
- D – elective cardioversion after 3 weeks of OAC is outpatient planning, not initial ICU management.
- E – flecainide is contraindicated in structural heart disease and low EF.

**Ref:** Van Gelder IC et al., 2024 ESC AF Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3314–3414; Drikite L et al., Crit Care 2021;25 (systematic scoping review).

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy and ICD receives 5 appropriate shocks for monomorphic VT within 6 hours.
options: Mechanical circulatory support has no role in electrical storm.
This meets the definition of electrical storm.
Propranolol combined with amiodarone is a commonly used regimen.
Sedation is appropriate early management.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – mechanical circulatory support may be considered (ESC 2022) to stabilise refractory storm; prophylactic use before ablation did better than rescue use.
- B (True) – electrical storm is ≥ 3 episodes of sustained VA within 24 h, separated by ≥ 5 min, each needing intervention; 5 shocks in 6 h meets this.
- C (True) – a non-selective beta-blocker (propranolol) plus amiodarone is the most common combination.
- D (True) – sedation breaks the cycle of shocks, fear and sympathetic drive, and is part of early management.

**EDIC trap:** Catheter ablation is preferred for incessant monomorphic VT – it is not contraindicated during storm.

**Ref:** Zeppenfeld K et al., 2022 ESC Guidelines for ventricular arrhythmias, Eur Heart J 2022;43:3997–4126.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old with traumatic cervical spinal cord injury has recurrent symptomatic bradycardia to 30/min during tracheal suctioning, unresponsive to atropine. Besides pacing, which drug is specifically suggested by ERC 2025 in this setting?
options: Digoxin
Aminophylline
Adenosine
Amiodarone
Metoprolol
questions.expl:
**Why B:** In cervical spinal cord injury, the loss of sympathetic outflow leaves vagal tone unopposed, so suctioning can cause severe bradycardia or asystole. ERC 2025 suggests aminophylline 100–200 mg slow IV in spinal cord injury and after heart transplantation, when atropine is ineffective. It works by adenosine-receptor antagonism; pacing remains the definitive option.

**Why not the others:**
- A – digoxin increases vagal tone and slows AV conduction.
- C – adenosine causes transient AV block and would worsen the bradycardia.
- D – amiodarone slows the sinus node and AV conduction.
- E – metoprolol is a beta-blocker and would worsen bradycardia.

**EDIC trap:** In bradycardia caused by beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers, the specific drug is glucagon.

**Ref:** Soar J et al., ERC Guidelines 2025 Adult ALS, Resuscitation 2025;215:110769.

questions.stem: A 64-year-old with PE has SBP 105 mmHg, HR 118/min, RV/LV ratio 1.4 on CT, elevated troponin and sPESI 1.
options: Close monitoring with rescue reperfusion on deterioration is appropriate.
ESC 2019 classifies this as intermediate-high risk.
In PEITHO, thrombolysis in this population did not increase major extracranial bleeding.
Routine full-dose systemic thrombolysis is recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – intermediate-high risk PE is managed with anticoagulation, close monitoring and rescue reperfusion if the patient deteriorates (ESC 2019 I B).
- B (True) – normotension + sPESI ≥ 1 + RV dysfunction (RV/LV 1.4) **and** a raised troponin = intermediate-high risk.
- C (False) – in PEITHO, tenecteplase increased major extracranial bleeding (6.3% vs 1.2%) and stroke (2.4% vs 0.2%).
- D (False) – routine primary systemic thrombolysis is not recommended in intermediate- or low-risk PE (class III); it reduced decompensation but not mortality.

**EDIC trap:** SBP 105 mmHg is above the instability threshold (< 90 mmHg for > 15 min), so this is not high risk.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603; Meyer G et al. (PEITHO), N Engl J Med 2014;370:1402–1411.

questions.stem: A patient with massive PE suffers cardiac arrest in the CT suite. Which systemic thrombolytic regimen is typically used in this situation (off-label)?
options: Urokinase 4400 IU/kg/h for 12 hours only
Alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours
Alteplase 0.6 mg/kg over 15 minutes (maximum 50 mg)
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg intracatheter
Streptokinase 100 000 IU/h for 24 hours
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In cardiac arrest from PE there is no time for a 2-hour infusion. An accelerated alteplase regimen of 0.6 mg/kg over 15 min (maximum 50 mg) is used off-label (ESC 2019). ERC guidance is to continue CPR for 60–90 min after giving a thrombolytic before stopping.

**Why not the others:**
- A – urokinase over 12 h is far too slow in cardiac arrest.
- B – alteplase 100 mg over 2 h is the approved regimen for haemodynamically unstable PE without arrest.
- D – intracatheter dosing needs a catheter laboratory and is not suitable during CPR.
- E – streptokinase over 24 h is far too slow and is rarely used now.

**EDIC trap:** In an available team, ECPR (VA-ECMO) can also be considered in PE-related arrest.

**Ref:** Konstantinides SV et al., 2019 ESC PE Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2020;41:543–603; Soar J et al., ERC Guidelines 2025 Adult ALS, Resuscitation 2025;215:110769.

questions.stem: Regarding catheter-directed therapy in intermediate-high risk PE (2025–2026 trials):
options: PRAGUE-26 compared large-bore mechanical thrombectomy with anticoagulation alone.
In HI-PEITHO, the benefit was mainly driven by fewer deaths.
Both trials demonstrated a significant reduction in all-cause mortality.
PEERLESS showed lower ICU utilisation with mechanical thrombectomy compared with catheter-directed thrombolysis.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – PRAGUE-26 tested conventional catheter-directed **thrombolysis** (alteplase) plus anticoagulation against anticoagulation alone; thrombectomy was the PEERLESS intervention.
- B (False) – in HI-PEITHO (7-day composite 4.0% vs 10.3%) the benefit came mainly from fewer cardiorespiratory decompensations, not deaths.
- C (False) – neither trial showed a significant reduction in all-cause mortality.
- D (True) – in PEERLESS, large-bore mechanical thrombectomy had far fewer ICU stays than CDT (41.6% vs 98.6%) and less deterioration/bailout.

**EDIC trap:** Catheter-directed therapy prevents early decompensation; a mortality benefit has not yet been shown.

**Ref:** Kroupa J et al. (PRAGUE-26), N Engl J Med 2026; Rosenfield K et al. (HI-PEITHO), N Engl J Med 2026; PEERLESS, Circulation 2025;151:260–273.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old presents with tearing chest pain, BP 175/100 mmHg, HR 105/min. CT shows type B dissection without malperfusion. The best initial drug strategy is:
options: No BP lowering to avoid spinal ischaemia
Oral amlodipine
IV nitroprusside alone
IV labetalol or esmolol first, then add a vasodilator if SBP remains > 120 mmHg
IV hydralazine
questions.expl:
**Why D:** Medical therapy for all acute aortic syndromes aims to reduce dP/dt and wall stress: HR ≤ 60/min and SBP < 120 mmHg (ESC 2024). A beta-blocker is given first – IV labetalol, or esmolol – with good analgesia. A vasodilator (nitroprusside, nitroglycerin, nicardipine) is added only once the rate is controlled. Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically.

**Why not the others:**
- A – BP lowering is the core treatment; a higher BP is accepted only with malperfusion.
- B – oral amlodipine is slow, not titratable, and does not control heart rate.
- C – nitroprusside alone causes reflex tachycardia, which increases shear stress.
- E – hydralazine is unpredictable and also causes reflex tachycardia.

**Ref:** Mazzolai L et al., 2024 ESC Guidelines on peripheral arterial and aortic diseases, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538–3700.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old with lung cancer has dyspnoea, HR 125/min, BP 85/60 mmHg, pulsus paradoxus 18 mmHg and a 28-mm circumferential pericardial effusion.
options: Right atrial and right ventricular diastolic collapse support tamponade.
Malignancy is the most common cause of tamponade.
Imaging-guided pericardiocentesis is recommended.
Early intubation with positive pressure ventilation before drainage is the safest approach.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – RA collapse (earliest, sensitive) and diastolic RV collapse (more specific) are key echo signs of tamponade, along with IVC plethora.
- B (True) – in ESC 2025, malignancy is the most common cause of tamponade, ahead of iatrogenic/trauma, pericarditis and TB.
- C (True) – echo-, CT- or fluoroscopy-guided pericardiocentesis is recommended (I C); surgical drainage is used for purulent effusion or when percutaneous drainage is not possible.
- D (False) – induction and positive pressure reduce venous return and can cause collapse; if possible, drain before intubation.

**EDIC trap:** Avoid diuretics and vasodilators; the patient is preload- and HR-dependent.

**Ref:** Schulz-Menger J et al., 2025 ESC Guidelines for myocarditis and pericarditis, Eur Heart J 2025;46:3952–4041.

questions.stem: In a patient with acute type A aortic dissection, which statement is correct?
options: Age > 80 years is an absolute contraindication to surgery
Medical therapy is equivalent to surgery
Immediate surgical repair is recommended; untreated mortality is about 1–2 % per hour early
TEVAR is the first-line treatment
Surgery should be delayed until BP is normal for 48 hours
questions.expl:
**Why C:** Untreated acute type A dissection has ~50% mortality in the first 48 h, about 1–2% per hour, from rupture, tamponade, acute AR or coronary malperfusion. ESC 2024 recommends immediate surgical repair. Age alone is not a contraindication; malperfusion (e.g. mesenteric) worsens the prognosis but does not rule out surgery.

**Why not the others:**
- A – age > 80 years is not an absolute contraindication.
- B – medical therapy alone has a much higher mortality than surgery in type A.
- D – TEVAR is first-line for complicated type B, not type A.
- E – delaying surgery for 48 h exposes the patient to the highest-risk period.

**Ref:** Mazzolai L et al., 2024 ESC Guidelines on peripheral arterial and aortic diseases, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3538–3700.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old woman at 34 weeks' gestation has BP 176/112 mmHg, headache and proteinuria.
options: The target is SBP < 140 and DBP < 90 mmHg within the first hour.
Furosemide is preferred to reduce plasma volume.
IV labetalol or nicardipine plus magnesium sulphate is recommended.
If BP is uncontrolled after 360 min on two drugs, critical care consultation is recommended.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – the target in severe pre-eclampsia is SBP < 160 and DBP < 105 mmHg within 150–180 min; lowering further risks placental hypoperfusion.
- B (False) – plasma volume is already reduced in pre-eclampsia, so diuretics are inappropriate (except for pulmonary oedema).
- C (True) – IV labetalol or nicardipine plus MgSO₄ for seizure prevention is recommended (I C).
- D (True) – if BP is not controlled after 360 min on two drugs, critical care should be consulted.

**EDIC trap:** In pulmonary oedema complicating pre-eclampsia, IV nitroglycerin is the drug (I C); delivery is the definitive treatment.

**Ref:** McEvoy JW et al., 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3912–4018.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old has acute spontaneous intracerebral haemorrhage, GCS 14, SBP 210 mmHg, 2 hours after onset. According to ESC 2024 the most appropriate BP target is:
options: No treatment unless SBP > 240 mmHg
SBP 140–160 mmHg, lowered within 6 hours
SBP < 185 mmHg only before thrombolysis
SBP < 110 mmHg within 1 hour
Reduce MAP by 50 % immediately
questions.expl:
**Why B:** ESC 2024 recommends that immediate BP lowering to SBP 140–160 mmHg within 6 h of onset should be considered (IIa A). INTERACT2 (target < 140 within 1 h) showed a borderline functional benefit on ordinal analysis. ATACH-2 found no benefit from 110–139 mmHg and more renal adverse events, so the target is not lower.

**Why not the others:**
- A – waiting until SBP > 240 mmHg is not recommended; early lowering is advised.
- C – < 185/110 mmHg is the pre-thrombolysis target in ischaemic stroke; thrombolysis is contraindicated in ICH.
- D – SBP < 110 mmHg within 1 h is too aggressive; this was not beneficial and caused more AKI.
- E – a 50% MAP fall risks cerebral and renal ischaemia.

**EDIC trap:** With SBP ≥ 220 mmHg, do not lower by > 70 mmHg within 1 h (III B).

**Ref:** McEvoy JW et al., 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3912–4018; Qureshi AI et al. (ATACH-2), N Engl J Med 2016;375:1033–1043.

questions.stem: A 63-year-old has BP 240/140 mmHg, papilloedema with retinal haemorrhages, creatinine 290 µmol/L (previously normal) and schistocytes on the blood film.
options: Labetalol is a first-line option.
Normalisation of BP within the first hour should be avoided.
This is malignant hypertension.
MAP should be reduced by about 20–25 % over several hours.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – IV labetalol is first-line for malignant hypertension (alternatives nicardipine, nitroprusside, urapidil).
- B (True) – autoregulation is shifted to the right, so rapid normalisation risks cerebral, renal and coronary ischaemia.
- C (True) – extreme BP with acute microangiopathy (grade IV retinopathy, AKI, schistocytes from thrombotic microangiopathy) is malignant hypertension.
- D (True) – ESC/ESH 2018: reduce MAP by 20–25% over several hours.

**EDIC trap:** TMA with schistocytes and AKI can mimic TTP/aHUS; check ADAMTS13 if it does not settle with BP control.

**Ref:** Williams B et al., 2018 ESC/ESH Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2018;39:3021–3104; McEvoy JW et al., 2024 ESC Hypertension Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2024;45:3912–4018.

questions.stem: A patient with aortic valve endocarditis (S. aureus) develops a new PR prolongation progressing to second-degree AV block. TEE shows a periannular abscess. Haemodynamics are stable. According to ESC 2023, surgery should be:
options: Elective after completing antibiotics
Performed only if a stroke occurs
Urgent (within 3–5 days)
Replaced by percutaneous drainage
Not indicated; continue antibiotics for 6 weeks
questions.expl:
**Why C:** A periannular abscess with new, progressing AV block shows locally uncontrolled infection spreading into the conduction tissue. ESC 2023 lists this as an indication for **urgent** surgery (within 3–5 days). Antibiotics alone rarely clear an abscess, and the block can progress to complete heart block. Emergency surgery (< 24 h) is kept for refractory pulmonary oedema or shock.

**Why not the others:**
- A – waiting until antibiotics are completed lets the abscess spread (fistula, pseudoaneurysm, complete block).
- B – stroke is not what makes surgery necessary here; uncontrolled infection is.
- D – there is no percutaneous drainage for a periannular abscess; it needs surgical debridement.
- E – an abscess is a clear indication for surgery.

**EDIC trap:** Repeat the ECG regularly in aortic IE – a new or longer PR interval suggests a root abscess.

**Ref:** Delgado V et al., 2023 ESC Endocarditis Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948–4042.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with known severe aortic stenosis requires emergency laparotomy and becomes hypotensive after induction.
options: High-gradient severe AS is characterised by mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg, Vmax ≥ 4 m/s and AVA ≤ 1 cm².
Tachycardia should be avoided.
Noradrenaline or phenylephrine is appropriate to restore diastolic pressure.
Balloon aortic valvuloplasty is the routine first-line treatment of decompensated AS.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – ESC 2025 high-gradient severe AS: mean gradient ≥ 40 mmHg, Vmax ≥ 4.0 m/s and AVA ≤ 1 cm² (≤ 0.6 cm²/m²).
- B (True) – tachycardia shortens diastole, reducing LV filling and coronary perfusion of the hypertrophied LV.
- C (True) – a vasopressor such as noradrenaline or phenylephrine restores diastolic pressure and coronary perfusion; fluids are given with caution.
- D (False) – balloon valvuloplasty has been largely replaced by TAVI in decompensated AS; it is only rarely used as a bridge.

**EDIC trap:** In low-flow states, a gradient < 40 mmHg does not exclude severe AS.

**Ref:** Praz F et al., 2025 ESC/EACTS Valvular Heart Disease Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2025.

questions.stem: A patient with acute severe aortic regurgitation from endocarditis is in cardiogenic shock awaiting surgery. Which intervention is contraindicated?
options: Intra-aortic balloon pump
Emergency surgery
Nitroprusside with careful monitoring
Dobutamine
Avoiding bradycardia
questions.expl:
**Why A:** An IABP inflates in diastole, which raises aortic diastolic pressure and increases the regurgitant volume into the non-dilated LV. It is therefore contraindicated in significant AR (and in aortic dissection). Acute severe AR with cardiogenic shock from endocarditis needs emergency surgery (within 24 h). Vasodilators and inotropes are used as a bridge.

**Why not the others:**
- B – emergency surgery is the definitive treatment.
- C – nitroprusside lowers afterload and regurgitation, so it is a suitable bridge if BP allows.
- D – dobutamine supports contractility and raises heart rate, which shortens diastole.
- E – avoiding bradycardia is correct, as a longer diastole increases regurgitation.

**EDIC trap:** IABP helps in acute MR and ventricular septal rupture, but not in AR.

**Ref:** Praz F et al., 2025 ESC/EACTS Valvular Heart Disease Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2025; Delgado V et al., 2023 ESC Endocarditis Guidelines, Eur Heart J 2023;44:3948–4042.

title: W09 · D1 – ALS according to ERC 2025

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man in the ED develops ventricular fibrillation. He has received two biphasic shocks with 2 minutes of CPR after each; VF persists at the rhythm check. According to ERC 2025, the most appropriate next step is:
options: Deliver the third shock, resume CPR, then give adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg
Give lidocaine 100 mg before the third shock
Give adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg now, then deliver the third shock
Deliver three stacked shocks
Stop CPR and check for a pulse for 30 seconds
questions.expl:
**Why A:** In shockable rhythms ERC 2025 gives adrenaline 1 mg and amiodarone 300 mg only **after the 3rd shock**, during the CPR cycle that follows it. Each shock is followed straight away by 2 min of CPR with no pulse check, so pauses stay short. Giving drugs earlier has no proven benefit and may delay the shock.

**Why not the others:**
- B – lidocaine 100 mg is an alternative to amiodarone, and it is also given only after the 3rd shock.
- C – drugs come after the 3rd shock, not before it.
- D – stacked shocks are only for a witnessed, monitored arrest with a defibrillator at hand, and only as the first shocks.
- E – a 30-s pulse check stops perfusion; rhythm checks should take < 10 s.

**EDIC trap:** "after the 3rd shock" applies to **both** drugs.

**Ref:** Soar J, et al. ERC 2025 ALS, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding the PARAMEDIC2 trial:
options: Among survivors, severe neurological impairment was more frequent with adrenaline.
It was a double-blind placebo-controlled trial in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest.
30-day survival was significantly higher with adrenaline.
Survival with a favourable neurological outcome at discharge was significantly higher with adrenaline.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – severe neurological impairment (mRS 4–5) among survivors was 31.0% with adrenaline vs 17.8% with placebo.
- B (True) – double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT of 8014 adults with OHCA in 5 UK ambulance services.
- C (True) – 30-day survival (the primary outcome) was 3.2% vs 2.4% (adjusted OR 1.47; NNT ~112).
- D (False) – favourable neurological outcome (mRS ≤ 3) at discharge was 2.2% vs 1.9%, not significant. Adrenaline raises coronary perfusion pressure and ROSC, but may impair cerebral microcirculation.

**EDIC trap:** the primary outcome was positive. The neurological outcome was neutral.

**Ref:** Perkins GD, et al. PARAMEDIC2, N Engl J Med 2018.

questions.stem: In the ALPS trial of shock-refractory VF/pVT, compared with placebo:
options: Neither drug significantly improved overall survival to discharge, but both were associated with higher survival in bystander-witnessed arrests
Amiodarone increased mortality
Lidocaine was superior to amiodarone
Both drugs worsened neurological outcome
Amiodarone significantly improved survival to hospital discharge in the overall population
questions.expl:
**Why A:** ALPS (3026 patients, shock-refractory VF/pVT in OHCA) found survival to discharge of 24.4% with amiodarone, 23.7% with lidocaine and 21.0% with placebo. None of these differences was significant (amiodarone vs placebo p = 0.08). In bystander-witnessed arrests both drugs improved survival compared with placebo, which suggests that time to drug matters.

**Why not the others:**
- B – amiodarone did not raise mortality; survival was numerically higher.
- C – amiodarone and lidocaine had almost the same outcomes, so lidocaine is an equal alternative.
- D – good neurological outcome was similar in all arms (~17–19%).
- E – the 3.4-point gain over placebo was not statistically significant.

**Ref:** Kudenchuk PJ, et al. ALPS, N Engl J Med 2016.

questions.stem: Regarding waveform capnography during CPR (ERC 2025):
options: A persistent waveform helps exclude oesophageal intubation.
A sudden fall in ETCO₂ may indicate ROSC.
A low ETCO₂ value alone is sufficient to decide to terminate resuscitation.
A rise in ETCO₂ alone justifies stopping compressions to check for a pulse.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – a persistent waveform over several breaths confirms the tube is in the trachea and helps exclude oesophageal intubation, though it does not exclude endobronchial placement.
- B (False) – at ROSC, ETCO₂ **rises** suddenly because pulmonary blood flow returns. A sudden fall suggests tube displacement or loss of output.
- C (False) – a low ETCO₂ alone must not be used to stop CPR; values depend on CPR quality, ventilation and the cause of arrest.
- D (False) – a rise in ETCO₂ may signal ROSC, but compressions should not be stopped on this sign alone. Wait for the planned rhythm check.

**Ref:** Soar J, et al. ERC 2025 ALS, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: A patient in cardiac surgery ICU with an arterial line suffers PEA. According to ERC 2025, a reasonable initial approach to adrenaline is:
options: 5 mg IV bolus
Vasopressin 40 U instead of adrenaline
Wait until after the third shock
Small IV increments of 50–100 µg rather than an immediate 1 mg bolus
Adrenaline is contraindicated with an arterial line
questions.expl:
**Why D:** In a monitored arrest with an arterial line (e.g. after cardiac surgery), ERC 2025 allows small IV adrenaline doses of **50–100 µg**, titrated to arterial pressure. A full 1 mg bolus can cause severe rebound hypertension and arrhythmias after ROSC. If small doses fail, check for extravasation and move to 1 mg every 3–5 min.

**Why not the others:**
- A – high-dose adrenaline (5 mg) does not improve survival.
- B – vasopressin is not recommended instead of adrenaline in ALS.
- C – PEA is non-shockable, so there is no shock; adrenaline is given as soon as possible.
- E – an arterial line is a reason to titrate adrenaline, not a contraindication.

**Ref:** Soar J, et al. ERC 2025 ALS, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding defibrillation according to ERC 2025:
options: Higher energy should be used routinely in obese patients.
Pads may be placed directly over an implanted device.
The first biphasic (rectilinear or truncated exponential) shock should be at least 150 J.
In VF persisting after three shocks, changing to an antero-posterior pad position may be considered.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – obese patients get standard shock energies. Transthoracic impedance makes little difference with modern biphasic devices.
- B (False) – place pads **> 8 cm** from an ICD or pacemaker. The device can block current and be damaged.
- C (True) – the first biphasic shock (rectilinear or truncated exponential) is **≥ 150 J**; for pulsed biphasic it is 130–150 J. Escalate energy if the device allows.
- D (True) – in refractory VF, first confirm the antero-lateral pads are placed correctly, then consider switching to antero-posterior (vector change).

**EDIC trap:** if you do not know the device, use the highest energy available.

**Ref:** Soar J, et al. ERC 2025 ALS, Resuscitation 2025; Cheskes S, et al. DOSE VF, N Engl J Med 2022.

questions.stem: In the DOSE VF trial, survival to hospital discharge in refractory VF was highest with:
options: Standard defibrillation
Mechanical CPR
Double sequential external defibrillation
Adding lidocaine
Vector-change defibrillation
questions.expl:
**Why C:** DOSE VF randomised 405 OHCA patients in refractory VF (Ontario) to three strategies. Survival to discharge was **30.4% with double sequential external defibrillation (DSED)**, 21.7% with vector change and 13.3% with standard shocks. The trial stopped early (partly because of COVID-19) and the numbers are small. ERC 2025 therefore does not recommend DSED routinely.

**Why not the others:**
- A – standard defibrillation was the control arm and had the lowest survival.
- B – mechanical CPR was not an intervention in DOSE VF.
- D – lidocaine was not studied in DOSE VF; ALPS tested antiarrhythmics.
- E – vector change improved survival, but less than DSED.

**EDIC trap:** DSED was best in the trial, but the guideline recommends considering vector change, the simpler option.

**Ref:** Cheskes S, et al. DOSE VF, N Engl J Med 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding point-of-care ultrasound during cardiac arrest:
options: It cannot identify cardiac tamponade during CPR.
Absence of myocardial contractility alone is a reason to stop CPR.
Isolated right ventricular dilatation confirms pulmonary embolism.
Prolonged pauses in chest compressions are acceptable to obtain diagnostic images.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – finding **tamponade** (and tension pneumothorax) is one of the main uses of POCUS in arrest, and both are treatable.
- B (False) – absent myocardial contraction alone does not justify stopping CPR. Survival is poor, but the finding varies between operators and timing.
- C (False) – the RV dilates in every arrest, so isolated RV dilatation **does not** diagnose PE.
- D (False) – images must be taken by a skilled operator within the normal rhythm-check pause (< 10 s), ideally recorded and reviewed afterwards.

**EDIC trap:** ERC states explicitly that a dilated RV is not proof of PE.

**Ref:** Soar J, et al. ERC 2025 ALS, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: After tracheal intubation during CPR, ventilation should be delivered:
options: 30:2 with pauses for breaths
At 10 breaths/min with continuous chest compressions
At 20 breaths/min to correct acidosis
At 6 breaths/min to avoid hyperventilation, with pauses
Only when ETCO₂ falls below 1 kPa
questions.expl:
**Why B:** Once a tracheal tube or supraglottic airway is in place, ERC 2025 recommends **continuous compressions with 10 breaths/min** (each ~1 s, visible chest rise, highest FiO₂). Stopping for breaths lowers coronary perfusion pressure. Hyperventilation raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 30:2 is for an unsecured airway (bag-mask).
- C – 20/min is hyperventilation: less venous return and cerebral vasoconstriction; it does not correct acidosis during CPR.
- D – pauses are not needed after intubation, and 6/min risks hypoxaemia.
- E – ventilation is not titrated to ETCO₂ during CPR.

**Ref:** Soar J, et al. ERC 2025 ALS, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: Which are among the "4 Hs and 4 Ts" reversible causes of cardiac arrest?
options: Hypothermia
Toxins
Thrombosis (coronary or pulmonary)
Hypo/hyperkalaemia
questions.expl:
- A (True) – hypothermia (and hyperthermia) is one of the 4 Hs; in accidental hypothermia, adrenaline and shocks are modified.
- B (True) – toxins are one of the 4 Ts; give antidotes early and be ready for prolonged CPR or ECPR.
- C (True) – thrombosis, coronary or pulmonary, is one of the 4 Ts (PCI, or thrombolysis for PE).
- D (True) – hypo/hyperkalaemia and other metabolic disorders are one of the 4 Hs.

The full list: 4 Hs are hypoxia, hypovolaemia, hypo/hyperkalaemia/metabolic, hypo/hyperthermia; 4 Ts are thrombosis, tension pneumothorax, tamponade, toxins.

**EDIC trap:** "hypoglycaemia" and "hydrogen ions" come from older or American lists, not the ERC 4 Hs.

**Ref:** Soar J, et al. ERC 2025 ALS, Resuscitation 2025.

open.q: A 55-year-old man collapses in the ED; the monitor shows VF. Outline the ALS sequence for the first 10 minutes according to ERC 2025, including drug timing and what you would do if VF persists after three shocks.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- High-quality compressions with minimal interruptions; correct antero-lateral pad placement (lateral pad below the axilla, mid-axillary line).
- Single biphasic shock (first ≥ 150 J), immediately 2 min CPR without pulse check, then rhythm check; consider escalating energy if the device allows.
- Adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO after the 3rd shock, then every 3–5 min.
- Amiodarone 300 mg after the 3rd shock, 150 mg after the 5th (or lidocaine 100 mg + 50 mg).
- Refractory VF: confirm pad position, then consider vector change to antero-posterior; DSED not routinely recommended (DOSE VF small, stopped early).
- Highest FiO₂; intubation only by skilled operator with < 5 s pause, then 10 breaths/min with continuous compressions; waveform capnography.
- Actively search for 4Hs/4Ts (e.g. coronary thrombosis); consider ECPR as rescue in selected patients.

open.q: Explain why PARAMEDIC2 is described as "positive" yet adrenaline's benefit remains controversial, and why ERC 2025 still recommends it.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Primary outcome 30-day survival was higher with adrenaline (3.2% vs 2.4%, adj. OR 1.47; NNT ~112).
- Survival to admission much higher (23.8% vs 8.0%) – adrenaline increases ROSC.
- Favourable neurological outcome (mRS ≤ 3) not significantly different (2.2% vs 1.9%).
- Severe neurological impairment among survivors more frequent (31.0% vs 17.8%).
- Mechanism: α-effect ↑ coronary perfusion pressure, but impaired cerebral microcirculation; rescues patients with severe hypoxic injury.
- ERC 2025 retains adrenaline: as early as possible in non-shockable rhythms, after the 3rd shock in VF/pVT.

title: W09 · D2 – Post-ROSC care: oxygenation, MAP, coronary angiography

questions.stem: A 58-year-old is admitted after OHCA with ROSC after 15 minutes; he remains comatose. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with no ST elevation, he is haemodynamically stable on low-dose noradrenaline. According to ERC-ESICM 2025, the most appropriate approach is:
options: Delay catheterisation unless acute coronary occlusion is strongly suspected, and consider a whole-body CT
Coronary CT angiography only after 72 hours
Systemic thrombolysis
Coronary angiography is contraindicated after OHCA
Immediate coronary angiography in all patients after OHCA
questions.expl:
**Why A:** With no ST elevation, ERC-ESICM 2025 recommends **delaying coronary angiography** unless acute coronary occlusion is strongly suspected (haemodynamic or electrical instability, ongoing ischaemia). Many such patients have a non-coronary cause. A **biphasic whole-body CT** (head to pelvis, including CT pulmonary angiography) can find intracranial haemorrhage, PE, aortic dissection and injuries from CPR. COACT and TOMAHAWK showed no benefit from immediate angiography.

**Why not the others:**
- B – no guideline sets a fixed 72-h CT coronary angiography.
- C – systemic thrombolysis has no role without a diagnosis such as PE.
- D – angiography is not contraindicated; it is emergent in STEMI and delayed without it.
- E – routine immediate angiography for all patients was not beneficial (COACT, TOMAHAWK).

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation/Intensive Care Med 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding oxygenation and ventilation after ROSC (ERC-ESICM 2025):
options: Pulse oximetry may overestimate saturation in patients with darker skin.
Titrate SpO₂ to 94–98 % once reliably measured.
Target PaO₂ 20–25 kPa.
Target mild hypocapnia (PaCO₂ 3.5–4.0 kPa) to reduce intracranial pressure.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – new in 2025: pulse oximetry can overestimate SpO₂ in people with darker skin, and it is unreliable in low-flow states. Use arterial gases.
- B (True) – give FiO₂ 1.0 until SpO₂ can be measured reliably, then titrate to SpO₂ 94–98%.
- C (False) – the target is PaO₂ **10–13 kPa** (75–100 mmHg). Avoid both hypoxaemia (< 8 kPa) and hyperoxaemia.
- D (False) – aim for **normocapnia, PaCO₂ 4.7–6.0 kPa**. Hypocapnia causes cerebral vasoconstriction and worsens ischaemia.

**EDIC trap:** the post-ROSC SpO₂ target is 94–98%, not 88–92% and not 100%.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: In the BOX trial, comatose OHCA survivors were randomised to mean arterial pressure targets of:
options: 65 vs 85 mmHg
70 vs 90 mmHg
55 vs 65 mmHg
63 vs 77 mmHg
questions.expl:
**Why E:** BOX (789 comatose OHCA patients, two Danish centres, factorial design) compared **MAP 63 vs 77 mmHg**, blinded with a modified arterial pressure module. The primary outcome (death or severe disability or coma at 90 days) was **32% vs 34%** (HR 1.08), with no difference. ERC-ESICM 2025 therefore sets MAP > 60–65 mmHg.

**Why not the others:**
- A – 65 vs 85 mmHg were not the BOX arms; smaller trials (COMACARE, Neuroprotect) tested higher targets of roughly 80–100 mmHg.
- B – BOX did not use target ranges like 80–85 vs 65–70 mmHg; its arms were single values, 63 vs 77 mmHg.
- C – 70 vs 90 mmHg was not a BOX arm.
- D – 55 mmHg would be below any accepted post-ROSC target.

**Ref:** Kjaergaard J, et al. BOX, N Engl J Med 2022.

questions.stem: Regarding COACT and TOMAHAWK:
options: Both showed significantly improved survival with immediate angiography.
TOMAHAWK enrolled patients regardless of initial rhythm.
In TOMAHAWK, death or severe neurological deficit was numerically more frequent with immediate angiography.
COACT enrolled only patients with ST-segment elevation.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – neither trial showed better survival. In COACT, 90-day survival was 64.5% vs 67.2%; in TOMAHAWK, 30-day mortality was 54.0% vs 46.0%, which was worse with immediate angiography (p = 0.06).
- B (True) – TOMAHAWK enrolled OHCA of presumed coronary cause with **any initial rhythm** and no ST elevation.
- C (True) – death or severe neurological deficit was 64.3% vs 55.6%, numerically higher with immediate angiography.
- D (False) – COACT enrolled unconscious patients with a **shockable** rhythm and **no** ST elevation.

**EDIC trap:** COACT is shockable rhythms only; TOMAHAWK is all rhythms. STEMI still needs emergent angiography.

**Ref:** Lemkes JS, et al. COACT, N Engl J Med 2019; Desch S, et al. TOMAHAWK, N Engl J Med 2021.

questions.stem: Which post-ROSC intervention is recommended by ERC-ESICM 2025?
options: Routine prophylactic antibiotics
Routine hydrocortisone
MAP > 60–65 mmHg and avoidance of hypotension
Routine seizure prophylaxis with levetiracetam
Routine neuromuscular blockade for 24 h
questions.expl:
**Why C:** ERC-ESICM 2025 gives an explicit target of **MAP > 60–65 mmHg** and says to avoid hypotension, using fluids, noradrenaline and/or dobutamine as needed. BOX showed no benefit from a higher target (77 vs 63 mmHg). Hypotension after ROSC is linked to worse neurological outcome.

**Why not the others:**
- A – prophylactic antibiotics are not recommended. ANTHARTIC reduced early VAP but did not change mortality; keep a low threshold to treat pneumonia.
- B – routine corticosteroids are not recommended.
- D – seizure prophylaxis is not recommended; seizures are diagnosed by EEG and then treated.
- E – routine NMB is not recommended; it may be considered in severe ARDS or shivering.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: Components of the post-cardiac arrest syndrome include:
options: The persisting precipitating pathology
Post-arrest myocardial dysfunction
A systemic ischaemia–reperfusion response
Hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury
questions.expl:
- A (True) – the persisting precipitating cause (ACS, PE, haemorrhage, sepsis) needs targeted treatment.
- B (True) – post-arrest myocardial dysfunction (stunning) is usually reversible within 48–72 h; it may need dobutamine or mechanical support.
- C (True) – the systemic ischaemia–reperfusion response is "sepsis-like", with vasoplegia, capillary leak, coagulopathy and adrenal dysfunction.
- D (True) – hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury is the leading cause of death after OHCA, mostly through withdrawal of life-sustaining therapy.

**EDIC trap:** the syndrome has **four** components. Do not forget the precipitating cause.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: In the oxygen part of the BOX trial (PaO₂ 9–10 vs 13–14 kPa), the primary outcome:
options: Was significantly better with the liberal target
Was only reported for in-hospital arrests
Did not differ significantly between groups
Could not be assessed because the trial stopped early
Was significantly better with the restrictive target
questions.expl:
**Why C:** In the BOX oxygen comparison (789 patients), the primary outcome (death or severe disability or coma at 90 days) was **32.0% with the restrictive target vs 33.9% with the liberal target** (HR 0.95), which was not significant. This supports the moderate ERC-ESICM range of PaO₂ 10–13 kPa, avoiding both extremes.

**Why not the others:**
- A – the liberal target was not better.
- B – BOX enrolled OHCA only.
- D – BOX finished recruitment and reported its primary outcome.
- E – the restrictive target was not significantly better.

**Ref:** Schmidt H, et al. BOX oxygen, N Engl J Med 2022.

questions.stem: A comatose patient after ROSC is being cooled after spontaneous mild hypothermia. Regarding ventilation:
options: Hypothermia increases CO₂ production, so minute ventilation usually needs to be increased.
Hypoxaemia with PaO₂ < 8 kPa should be avoided.
Hyperoxaemia should be actively targeted to protect the brain.
Tidal volumes of 10–12 mL/kg ideal body weight are recommended to avoid hypercapnia.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – hypothermia **reduces** metabolic CO₂ production (VCO₂). If ventilation is unchanged, PaCO₂ falls, causing hypocapnia and cerebral vasoconstriction. Check PaCO₂ more often (new in 2025).
- B (True) – avoid hypoxaemia (PaO₂ < 8 kPa / 60 mmHg); the target is 10–13 kPa.
- C (False) – hyperoxaemia should be avoided; it may worsen reperfusion injury and has no proven benefit.
- D (False) – lung-protective ventilation with Vt **6–8 mL/kg IBW** is recommended. Correct CO₂ by changing rate, not by large tidal volumes.

**EDIC trap:** in hypothermia the danger is **hypocapnia**, not hypercapnia.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: A patient after OHCA has persistent ST elevation in leads V1–V4 after ROSC. The most appropriate step is:
options: Emergent cardiac catheterisation with PPCI if needed
Thrombolysis only if the patient wakes up
Conservative management because the patient is comatose
Delayed angiography after neuroprognostication at 72 h
Whole-body CT and angiography only if troponin rises
questions.expl:
**Why A:** Persistent ST elevation after ROSC (here anterior V1–V4) strongly suggests acute coronary occlusion. ERC-ESICM 2025 recommends **emergent cardiac catheterisation with PPCI if needed**, as in any STEMI. Coma is not a contraindication, because prognosis cannot be judged reliably at this stage.

**Why not the others:**
- B – PPCI is preferred over thrombolysis, and treatment must not wait for awakening.
- C – coma alone is not a reason to withhold reperfusion.
- D – waiting 72 h for prognostication would lose the myocardium.
- E – troponin always rises after CPR and defibrillation, so it does not help with timing; CT is mainly for patients without ST elevation.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: Regarding seizures and sedation after cardiac arrest (ERC-ESICM 2025):
options: Seizure prophylaxis is recommended for all comatose patients.
Levetiracetam or sodium valproate are suggested first-line antiseizure drugs.
EEG should be used to diagnose electrographic seizures.
Short-acting sedatives facilitate neurological assessment.
questions.expl:
- A (False) – seizure prophylaxis is **not** recommended. Treat clinical or electrographic seizures once diagnosed.
- B (True) – ERC-ESICM 2025 suggests **levetiracetam or sodium valproate** first line, together with sedatives.
- C (True) – use EEG to diagnose and monitor seizures, since many seizures in sedated patients are non-convulsive.
- D (True) – short-acting sedatives (e.g. propofol) and daily interruptions allow neurological examination and reduce confounding in prognostication.

**EDIC trap:** status myoclonus is a prognostic sign. It is not automatically a seizure, so record an EEG.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

open.q: A 64-year-old woman is admitted comatose after OHCA (initial rhythm PEA, ROSC after 18 min). ECG shows no ST elevation. Outline your first-day ICU management according to ERC-ESICM 2025.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- Intubate if not already; confirm with capnography; FiO₂ 1.0 until SpO₂ reliable, then SpO₂ 94–98%, PaO₂ 10–13 kPa, avoid hypoxaemia and hyperoxaemia.
- Normocapnia (PaCO₂ 4.7–6.0 kPa), Vt 6–8 mL/kg IBW; check PaCO₂ more often if hypothermic.
- MAP > 60–65 mmHg (SBP > 100 mmHg), fluids/noradrenaline/dobutamine as needed; avoid hypo- and hyperkalaemia.
- No ST elevation: delay coronary angiography unless acute occlusion strongly suspected (COACT, TOMAHAWK); biphasic whole-body CT including CTPA to look for non-cardiac causes and CPR injuries.
- Active fever prevention ≤ 37.5 °C; short-acting sedation.
- EEG for seizures; treat with levetiracetam/valproate, no prophylaxis.
- No routine corticosteroids, prophylactic antibiotics or NMB; standard glucose control.

open.q: Explain why COACT and TOMAHAWK did not support immediate coronary angiography after OHCA without ST elevation, and how their populations differed.
open.model:
Key points expected:
- COACT: only shockable initial rhythm, unconscious, no STEMI; 90-day survival 64.5% vs 67.2%, NS.
- TOMAHAWK: any initial rhythm with presumed coronary cause; 30-day mortality 54.0% vs 46.0% (p = 0.06), death or severe neurological deficit 64.3% vs 55.6% (worse with immediate).
- Many patients without STEMI have a non-coronary cause (respiratory, neurological, PE).
- Immediate catheterisation may delay correct diagnosis and intensive care.
- Prognosis is driven largely by hypoxic-ischaemic brain injury, not the coronary lesion.
- Hence ERC-ESICM 2025: delay unless occlusion strongly suspected; STEMI still emergent.

title: W09 · D3 – Temperature management and fever after cardiac arrest

questions.stem: In the TTM2 trial, compared with normothermia with early treatment of fever, targeted hypothermia at 33 °C:
options: Reduced the incidence of pneumonia
Reduced 6-month mortality
Did not reduce 6-month mortality and was associated with more arrhythmias causing haemodynamic compromise
Improved functional outcome
Was only tested in in-hospital cardiac arrest
questions.expl:
**Why C:** TTM2 randomised 1900 comatose OHCA patients to 33 °C (~28 h, then controlled rewarming) or to normothermia with early treatment of fever (device started at ≥ 37.8 °C). Six-month mortality was **50% vs 48%** (RR 1.04) and poor functional outcome was 55% in both groups. **Arrhythmias causing haemodynamic compromise were more frequent with hypothermia (24% vs 17%).**

**Why not the others:**
- A – pneumonia rates were similar; hypothermia tends to increase infection risk.
- B – mortality did not differ.
- D – functional outcome (mRS 4–6 at 6 months) was the same, 55% vs 55%.
- E – TTM2 enrolled OHCA only; IHCA was excluded.

**Ref:** Dankiewicz J, et al. TTM2, N Engl J Med 2021.

questions.stem: Regarding the HYPERION trial:
options: It included both in-hospital and out-of-hospital arrests.
The difference in good neurological outcome was statistically robust (high fragility index).
It enrolled only patients with a shockable initial rhythm.
It showed a significant reduction in mortality with 33 °C.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – HYPERION (584 patients, 25 French ICUs) enrolled both OHCA and IHCA.
- B (False) – the result is **fragile**: the fragility index is 1 (p = 0.04), so one changed outcome would remove significance. Certainty is low.
- C (False) – it enrolled only **non-shockable** rhythms (asystole/PEA), with GCS ≤ 8.
- D (False) – only good neurological outcome (CPC 1–2 at day 90) improved, 10.2% vs 5.7%. Mortality was similar (~81–83%).

**EDIC trap:** HYPERION is the only large positive hypothermia RCT, and it is in non-shockable rhythms. It did not change ERC-ESICM 2025 (fever prevention).

**Ref:** Lascarrou JB, et al. HYPERION, N Engl J Med 2019.

questions.stem: According to ERC-ESICM 2025, in a patient who remains comatose after ROSC, temperature management should be:
options: No temperature monitoring unless the patient is febrile
Rapid prehospital infusion of 2 L of 4 °C saline
Active cooling to 33 °C for 24 h in all patients
Active fever prevention targeting ≤ 37.5 °C
Active rewarming to 37 °C if the patient arrives at 35 °C
questions.expl:
**Why D:** ERC-ESICM 2025 uses the term "temperature control": **actively prevent fever, target ≤ 37.5 °C**, for 36–72 h in patients who remain comatose, with continuous core temperature monitoring. This follows TTM2, where 33 °C was no better than fever prevention and caused more arrhythmias.

**Why not the others:**
- A – core temperature must be monitored continuously in every comatose patient.
- B – prehospital rapid infusion of large volumes of cold fluid is recommended against; it caused more re-arrest and pulmonary oedema (Kim, JAMA 2014).
- C – routine 33 °C is not recommended after TTM2.
- E – mild hypothermia (32–36 °C) should not be actively rewarmed.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: In the TTM trial (2013):
options: Patients were randomised to 33 °C or 36 °C.
The intervention period lasted about 28 hours before rewarming.
Fever was avoided for 72 hours in both groups.
Mortality was significantly lower in the 33 °C group.
questions.expl:
- A (True) – TTM randomised 950 comatose OHCA patients of presumed cardiac cause to 33 °C or 36 °C.
- B (True) – the target was held for about 28 h (36 h including rewarming), then patients were rewarmed at 0.5 °C/h.
- C (True) – both groups were kept below 37.5 °C until 72 h, so the control arm was also fever-controlled.
- D (False) – mortality was **50% vs 48%** (HR 1.06), not significant, and neurological outcome did not differ.

**EDIC trap:** TTM compared two temperatures, both with fever control. It did not compare hypothermia with "no temperature management".

**Ref:** Nielsen N, et al. TTM, N Engl J Med 2013.

questions.stem: A comatose patient after OHCA arrives in the ICU with a core temperature of 35.2 °C. According to ERC-ESICM, you should:
options: Not actively rewarm, and prevent subsequent fever
Actively rewarm with a forced-air blanket to 37 °C
Start ECMO for rewarming
Give dantrolene
Infuse warm fluids to reach normothermia within 1 hour
questions.expl:
**Why A:** ERC-ESICM 2025 recommends that comatose patients with mild hypothermia (**32–36 °C**) after ROSC should **not be actively rewarmed** to normothermia. Let temperature rise slowly and passively, then prevent fever (≤ 37.5 °C) for 36–72 h, because rebound hyperthermia is common.

**Why not the others:**
- B – active rewarming to 37 °C is not recommended; it risks haemodynamic swings and rebound fever.
- C – ECMO rewarming is for accidental hypothermia with arrest or instability, usually < 30 °C, not 35 °C.
- D – dantrolene is for malignant hyperthermia, not hypothermia.
- E – rapid rewarming to normothermia within 1 h is not recommended.

**Ref:** Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025 Post-Resuscitation Care, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: Physiological consequences of induced hypothermia at 33 °C include:
options: Hyperkalaemia during cooling and hypokalaemia during rewarming
Increased clearance of sedatives and opioids
Risk of hypocapnia if ventilation is unchanged
Tachycardia
questions.expl:
- A (False) – it is the other way round. Cooling shifts K⁺ into cells and causes cold diuresis, giving **hypokalaemia**. During rewarming K⁺ comes back out, giving **hyperkalaemia**, so rewarm slowly.
- B (False) – cytochrome P450 activity falls, so drug clearance is **reduced**. Sedatives and opioids accumulate, which confounds neuroprognostication.
- C (True) – CO₂ production falls, so unchanged ventilation causes hypocapnia and cerebral vasoconstriction. Check PaCO₂ often.
- D (False) – hypothermia causes **bradycardia**, PR/QT prolongation and Osborn (J) waves.

Other effects: coagulopathy, infection, hyperglycaemia and shivering.

**Ref:** Polderman KH, Crit Care Med 2009; Nolan JP, et al. ERC-ESICM 2025, Resuscitation 2025.

questions.stem: In the TTM2 normothermia arm, the threshold temperature at which the cooling device was activated was:
questions.expl:
