questions.stem: Regarding severe community-acquired pneumonia:
options: ATS 2025 suggests corticosteroids also in severe influenza pneumonia.
CAPE COD included patients with septic shock and influenza.
MRSA and *Pseudomonas* should be covered routinely in all patients with severe CAP.
Empirical therapy is a β-lactam plus a macrolide.
questions.expl: CAPE COD **excluded** septic shock and influenza. Do not give corticosteroids in influenza (observational data show more harm). Cover MRSA/*Pseudomonas* only when individual risk factors are present. ([W12/D2](#W12-D2))

questions.stem: In the INTUBE study (29 countries), the most frequent major adverse peri-intubation event was:
options: Severe hypoxaemia
Aspiration
Cardiovascular instability
Oesophageal intubation
Cardiac arrest
questions.expl: Major events occurred in 45.2 %: cardiovascular instability 42.6 %, severe hypoxaemia 9.3 %, cardiac arrest 3.1 %. ([W12/D3](#W12-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding trials of airway management in critically ill adults:
options: In DEVICE, video laryngoscopy increased first-attempt success (85.1 vs 70.8 %).
In BOUGIE, a bougie significantly increased first-attempt success.
In the RSI trial, ketamine caused less cardiovascular collapse than etomidate.
In PREOXI, NIV preoxygenation halved hypoxaemia (9.1 vs 18.5 %).
questions.expl: BOUGIE was NS (80.4 vs 83.0 %). RSI: mortality similar; collapse was **more** common with ketamine (22.1 vs 17.0 %). ([W12/D3](#W12-D3))

questions.stem: A patient with a parapneumonic effusion has pleural fluid pH 7.10. A small-bore drain inserted 2 days ago is draining poorly, and loculations are seen. The patient is clinically stable. The next step supported by MIST2 is:
options: Intrapleural tPA plus DNase
Intrapleural streptokinase
Intrapleural DNase alone
Intrapleural tPA alone
Remove the drain and continue antibiotics only
questions.expl: In MIST2, only the combination of tPA + DNase worked. DNase alone was harmful (more surgical referrals), and tPA alone did not help. In MIST1, streptokinase was ineffective. ([W12/D5](#W12-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding tracheostomy and pneumothorax:
options: In TracMan, early tracheostomy (≤ 4 days) did not reduce mortality.
Lung point is a specific ultrasound sign of pneumothorax.
Percutaneous tracheostomy has fewer stoma infections than surgical tracheostomy.
In a laryngectomy patient, oxygen should be applied to the stoma.
questions.expl: After laryngectomy, the stoma is the only airway, so oxygenate (and intubate if needed) via the stoma, never via the mouth. ([W12/D4](#W12-D4), [W12/D5](#W12-D5))

questions.stem: A paralysed patient on volume control has constant flow 60 L/min, VT 500 mL, Ppeak 35, Pplat 25 and PEEP 5 cmH₂O (no PEEPi). Which set of values is correct?
options: R 20 cmH₂O/L/s; Cstat 20 mL/cmH₂O; τ 0.4 s
R 0.17 cmH₂O/L/s; Cstat 25 mL/cmH₂O; τ 0.004 s
R 10 cmH₂O/L/s; Cstat 16.7 mL/cmH₂O; τ 0.17 s
R 10 cmH₂O/L/s; Cstat 25 mL/cmH₂O; τ 0.25 s
R 10 cmH₂O/L/s; Cstat 50 mL/cmH₂O; τ 0.5 s
questions.expl: 60 L/min = 1 L/s → R = (35 − 25)/1 = 10. Cstat = 500/(25 − 5) = 25 mL/cmH₂O = 0.025 L/cmH₂O. τ = R × C = 10 × 0.025 = 0.25 s. (16.7 mL/cmH₂O is the **dynamic** compliance.) ([W13/D2](#W13-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding ventilation modes:
options: In VCV, a high inspiratory demand can cause flow starvation.
In PCV, VT ≈ (Pinsp + Pmus) × C, so strong efforts can produce large VTs at a "safe" displayed pressure.
NAVA and PAV+ improve patient–ventilator synchrony, but no mortality benefit has been shown.
In the study by Zhou 2017, APRV reduced mortality.
questions.expl: APRV (Zhou 2017, a small trial) gave more ventilator-free days, but mortality was NS. ([W13/D1](#W13-D1))

questions.stem: A patient on VCV has RR 20/min, VT 0.5 L, Ppeak 30, Pplat 25 and PEEP 10 cmH₂O. Using the simplified Gattinoni formula MP = 0.098 × RR × VT × (Ppeak − ½ ΔP), mechanical power is approximately:
options: 29 J/min
35 J/min
22 J/min
12 J/min
15 J/min
questions.expl: ΔP = 25 − 10 = 15; Ppeak − ½ΔP = 30 − 7.5 = 22.5; MP = 0.098 × 20 × 0.5 × 22.5 ≈ 22 J/min. In observational data (Serpa Neto 2018), MP > ~17 J/min was associated with higher mortality. MP is not a guideline target. ([W13/D4](#W13-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding effort assessment and VILI:
options: Raising PEEP raises mechanical power (linearly).
Pmus can be estimated as about ¾ of the airway occlusion pressure swing (ΔPocc).
P0.1 > 3.5 cmH₂O indicates high inspiratory effort.
Mechanical power is a guideline-recommended titration target.
questions.expl: Pmus ≈ −¾ ΔPocc. MP is an observational marker, and no RCT has titrated it. ([W13/D4](#W13-D4))

questions.stem: A patient with COPD on PSV 20 cmH₂O (external PEEP 0) has visible inspiratory efforts without ventilator triggering. The ventilator rate is 14/min, but the patient's neural rate is clearly higher. The most appropriate change is:
options: Increase trigger sensitivity to the maximum and increase PS
Switch to SIMV
Deepen sedation and add a neuromuscular blocker
Increase pressure support to 25 cmH₂O
Decrease pressure support and add external PEEP
questions.expl: These are ineffective efforts, caused by PEEPi and excessive support (large VT → longer expiration needed). Reduce PS/VT and add external PEEP below PEEPi. Do **not** increase PS. ([W13/D3](#W13-D3), [W13/D5](#W13-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding patient–ventilator asynchrony:
options: In Thille 2006, about a quarter of patients had an asynchrony index > 10 %, which was associated with longer ventilation.
Asynchrony index = asynchronous events / (ventilator cycles + ineffective efforts) × 100.
Premature cycling is corrected by increasing the cycle-off (% of peak flow) threshold.
An asynchrony index > 10 % is considered severe.
questions.expl: Premature cycling: **decrease** cycle-off %. Delayed cycling (COPD): increase cycle-off %. ([W13/D3](#W13-D3))

questions.stem: A ventilated patient has respiratory system resistance 20 cmH₂O/L/s and compliance 0.05 L/cmH₂O. With RR 20/min and I:E 1:2, roughly what fraction of VT is exhaled before the next breath?
questions.expl: τ = R × C = 1.0 s. Cycle 3 s → Te 2 s = 2τ → exhaled fraction = 1 − e⁻² ≈ 86 %. Full exhalation needs about 3τ (≈ 95 %). Lowering RR or shortening Ti lengthens Te. ([W13/D2](#W13-D2), [W13/D5](#W13-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding mechanical ventilation in status asthmaticus:
options: Plateau pressure should be < 30 cmH₂O, ideally < 25 cmH₂O.
An end-inspiratory lung volume (V_EI) ≥ 1.4 L was associated with complications (Williams).
External PEEP is absolutely contraindicated in asthma.
The goal is normocapnia, so RR should be increased as PaCO₂ rises.
questions.expl: Use permissive hypercapnia, because raising RR worsens dynamic hyperinflation. External PEEP is not contraindicated; base the decision on the Pplat response to a PEEP trial. ([W13/D5](#W13-D5))

title: W14 · D4 – Review: acid–base + electrolytes

questions.stem: A blood gas report shows HCO₃⁻ 20 mmol/L and pCO₂ 50 mmHg. Which reported pH is internally consistent?
questions.expl: [H⁺] = 24 × 50/20 = 60 nmol/L. pH 7.40 = 40 nmol/L, and each 0.01 of pH is about 1 nmol/L, so pH ≈ 7.20–7.22. Henderson-Hasselbalch: 20/(0.03 × 50) = 13.3; log 13.3 = 1.12 → pH ≈ 7.22. ([W05/D1](#W05-D1))

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock who is becoming exhausted has HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L and pCO₂ 32 mmHg.
options: The expected pCO₂ (Winter) is about 23 mmHg (21–25).
There is a concomitant respiratory acidosis.
Respiratory compensation can overshoot and bring pH above 7.40.
Full respiratory compensation for a metabolic acidosis takes 3–5 days.
questions.expl: 1.5 × 10 + 8 = 23 ± 2. A pCO₂ of 32 is higher than expected, so there is an additional respiratory acidosis (fatigue, impending respiratory failure). Compensation never overshoots. Respiratory compensation takes minutes to hours; **renal** compensation takes 3–5 days. ([W05/D1](#W05-D1))

questions.stem: An ICU patient has Na⁺ 136, Cl⁻ 104, HCO₃⁻ 20 mmol/L and albumin 16 g/L. Which interpretation is correct?
options: AG 12 – the low albumin causes acidosis
Corrected AG ≈ 6 – hyperchloraemic acidosis
Corrected AG ≈ 28 – toxic alcohol certain
Normal anion gap; no further work-up is needed
Corrected AG ≈ 18 – a hidden high-AG acidosis (check lactate, ketones, urea)
questions.expl: AG = 136 − (104 + 20) = 12; corrected AG = 12 + 0.25 × (40 − 16) = 12 + 6 = 18. Hypoalbuminaemia lowers the AG and masks unmeasured anions (Fencl). ([W05/D1](#W05-D1))

questions.stem: A patient with DKA who has also had several days of diarrhoea has: Na⁺ 138, Cl⁻ 110, HCO₃⁻ 10 mmol/L, albumin 40 g/L.
options: The anion gap is 18 mmol/L.
The "corrected HCO₃⁻" (HCO₃⁻ + ΔAG) of 16 mmol/L supports a coexisting normal-AG acidosis.
The delta ratio indicates a mixed high-AG and normal-AG metabolic acidosis.
The delta ratio is about 0.4.
questions.expl: AG = 138 − 120 = 18; ΔAG = 6; ΔHCO₃⁻ = 14; ratio 6/14 ≈ 0.43, which falls in the 0.4–0.8 band: HAGMA + NAGMA. A corrected HCO₃⁻ < ~22 also indicates NAGMA. ([W05/D1](#W05-D1))

questions.stem: A patient with liver cirrhosis has pCO₂ 25 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 18 mmol/L and pH 7.48. The best description is:
options: Mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic alkalosis
Acute respiratory alkalosis with an additional metabolic alkalosis
Acute respiratory alkalosis with appropriate compensation
Primary metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation
Chronic respiratory alkalosis with appropriate compensation
questions.expl: pCO₂ fell by 15 mmHg. Acute: HCO₃⁻ falls by 2 per 10 mmHg (expected ≈ 21). Chronic: falls by about 4 per 10 mmHg (expected ≈ 18). pH 7.48 means alkalaemia, so the primary disorder is respiratory alkalosis. ([W05/D1](#W05-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding the Stewart approach:
options: The independent variables are pCO₂, SID and ATOT.
Hypoalbuminaemia causes a metabolic acidosis.
Albumin is a strong ion.
The SID of 0.9 % NaCl is 0.
questions.expl: Albumin is a weak acid (part of ATOT). Hypoalbuminaemia **alkalinises** and can mask acidosis. ([W05/D2](#W05-D2))

questions.stem: A septic patient has Na⁺ 140, K⁺ 4, Ca²⁺ 2.2 mEq/L, Mg²⁺ 1.0 mEq/L, Cl⁻ 106, lactate 5 mmol/L, HCO₃⁻ 14 mmol/L, and an albumin + phosphate charge (A⁻) of 8 mmol/L. The strong ion gap (SIG) is about:
questions.expl: SIDa = (140 + 4 + 2.2 + 1.0) − (106 + 5) ≈ 36. SIDe = HCO₃⁻ + A⁻ = 14 + 8 = 22. SIG = 36 − 22 ≈ 14. This points to unmeasured anions **beyond** lactate (ketones, toxic alcohols, renal failure). ([W05/D2](#W05-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding the urine anion gap (UAG):
options: The UAG remains reliable with marked ketonuria.
UAG = U-Na⁺ + U-K⁺ − U-Cl⁻.
A negative UAG in normal-AG acidosis points to diarrhoea.
A positive UAG in normal-AG acidosis points to distal RTA.
questions.expl: The UAG is an indirect estimate of NH₄⁺ excretion. It is unreliable with polyuria, ketonuria, or U-Na⁺ < 20 mmol/L. ([W05/D2](#W05-D2))

questions.stem: Which cause produces **type B** lactic acidosis?
options: Carbon monoxide poisoning
Cardiogenic shock
Severe anaemia
Mesenteric ischaemia
Metformin
questions.expl: Type A = tissue hypoxia/hypoperfusion (including CO poisoning and severe anaemia). Type B = no obvious hypoxia: metformin, adrenaline/β₂-agonists, propofol, thiamine deficiency, liver failure. ([W05/D2](#W05-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding sodium bicarbonate in severe metabolic acidaemia:
options: Bicarbonate raises ionised calcium.
In BICAR-ICU, the primary composite outcome did not differ significantly (66 vs 71 %).
In BICARICU-2 (AKI KDIGO 2–3), 90-day mortality was significantly lower with bicarbonate.
In BICARICU-2, more patients received kidney replacement therapy with bicarbonate.
questions.expl: Bicarbonate **lowers** iCa²⁺. BICARICU-2: 90-day mortality 62.1 vs 61.7 % (NS), but **fewer** patients received KRT (35 vs 50 %). Other risks: hypernatraemia, hyperosmolality, and intracellular acidosis from CO₂. ([W05/D2](#W05-D2))

questions.stem: After a week of vomiting, a patient has pH 7.52, pCO₂ 47 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 34 mmol/L, K⁺ 2.8 mmol/L and urine Cl⁻ 10 mmol/L. The best management is:
options: 0.9 % NaCl with KCl
Acetazolamide
Hydrochloric acid infusion as first-line
Intubation for hypoventilation
Spironolactone
questions.expl: Expected pCO₂ = 40 + 0.7 × (34 − 24) = 47, so compensation is appropriate. U-Cl⁻ < 20 means chloride-responsive alkalosis → give NaCl + KCl. ([W05/D3](#W05-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding metabolic alkalosis:
options: In vomiting, urine Na⁺ is a better marker of volume status than urine Cl⁻.
Mineralocorticoid excess causes chloride-responsive alkalosis (U-Cl⁻ < 20) with hypotension.
In DIABOLO, acetazolamide significantly shortened mechanical ventilation in COPD.
"Paradoxical aciduria" results from Cl⁻/K⁺ depletion and aldosterone activation.
questions.expl: In vomiting, bicarbonaturia pulls Na⁺ into the urine, so use **U-Cl⁻**. Mineralocorticoid excess causes **chloride-resistant** alkalosis (U-Cl⁻ > 20) with **hypertension**. DIABOLO: 136.5 vs 163 h, NS. ([W05/D3](#W05-D3))

questions.stem: A patient after an overdose has pH 7.44, pCO₂ 24 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 16, Na⁺ 141 and Cl⁻ 103 mmol/L. The most likely diagnosis is:
options: Pure respiratory alkalosis
Salicylate poisoning – respiratory alkalosis + high-AG metabolic acidosis
Metabolic alkalosis + respiratory acidosis
Normal acid–base status
Compensated metabolic acidosis
questions.expl: AG = 141 − 119 = 22 → HAGMA. Winter predicts 1.5 × 16 + 8 = 32 ± 2; a pCO₂ of 24 is lower, so there is an additional respiratory alkalosis. Delta ratio = 10/8 = 1.25, which is a pure HAGMA. A normal pH does not mean the absence of a disorder. ([W05/D3](#W05-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding ketoacidoses (2024 DKA consensus):
options: In alcoholic ketoacidosis, the nitroprusside test overestimates ketosis.
Bicarbonate is indicated when pH is < 7.1.
DKA with pH 7.23 and HCO₃⁻ 8 mmol/L is "moderate", because pH is between 7.0 and 7.25.
A β-hydroxybutyrate ≥ 3.0 mmol/L is one of the diagnostic criteria.
questions.expl: Bicarbonate only when pH < 7.0. In AKA, β-OHB dominates and nitroprusside detects only acetoacetate/acetone, so it **underestimates** ketosis. HCO₃⁻ < 10 (or β-OHB > 6) alone is enough to classify DKA as **severe**. ([W05/D3](#W05-D3))

questions.stem: A patient in hyperglycaemic crisis has Na⁺ 126 mmol/L and glucose 39.2 mmol/L. Using the Katz correction (1.6 mmol/L per 5.6 mmol/L of glucose above 5.6), the corrected Na⁺ is about:
options: 142 mmol/L
136 mmol/L
131 mmol/L
146 mmol/L
128 mmol/L
questions.expl: (39.2 − 5.6)/5.6 = 6; 6 × 1.6 = 9.6; 126 + 9.6 ≈ 136. Hyperglycaemia causes a **hypertonic** (translocational) hyponatraemia. ([W05/D3](#W05-D3), [W06/D1](#W06-D1))

questions.stem: A confused patient has Na⁺ 135, glucose 10, urea 8 mmol/L, measured osmolality 320 mOsm/kg and undetectable ethanol.
options: The calculated osmolality is 288 mOsm/kg.
Ethylene glycol causes AKI with calcium oxalate crystals and hypocalcaemia; thiamine and pyridoxine are cofactors given in treatment.
A normal osmolal gap would exclude toxic alcohol poisoning.
An osmolal gap of 32 suggests a toxic alcohol.
questions.expl: 2 × 135 + 10 + 8 = 288; OG = 320 − 288 = 32 (normal < ~10). Late in the course, the OG falls as the AG rises, so a normal OG does not exclude toxic alcohol. ([W05/D3](#W05-D3))

questions.stem: A patient found with an empty bottle of rubbing alcohol has a raised osmolal gap, ketonaemia, a normal anion gap and normal pH. The likely toxin is:
options: Propylene glycol
Methanol
Isopropanol
Ethylene glycol
Salicylate
questions.expl: Isopropanol is metabolised to acetone, which gives ketosis without acidosis, a raised OG and a normal AG. Methanol and ethylene glycol cause a HAGMA. ([W05/D3](#W05-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding the diagnosis of hypotonic hyponatraemia (Spasovski 2014):
options: With urine osmolality > 100, a urine Na⁺ ≤ 30 mmol/L suggests SIAD.
A serum Na⁺ of 127 mmol/L is classified as "profound".
Urine osmolality ≤ 100 mOsm/kg suggests SIAD.
Hyponatraemia caused by hyperglycaemia is hypotonic.
questions.expl: U-Na⁺ ≤ 30 suggests **low effective circulating volume**; SIAD typically has U-Na⁺ > 30. U-osm ≤ 100 indicates excess water intake or low solute intake (ADH suppressed). Profound hyponatraemia is < 125 (125–129 = moderate). Hyperglycaemia causes a **hypertonic** hyponatraemia. ([W06/D1](#W06-D1))

questions.stem: A 45-year-old with Na⁺ 112 mmol/L has a generalised seizure. The first treatment is:
options: Fluid restriction to 800 mL/day
0.9 % NaCl 1 L over 1 h
150 mL 3 % NaCl IV over 20 min, recheck Na⁺, and repeat up to twice to achieve a rise of ~5 mmol/L
3 % NaCl infusion aiming for Na⁺ 130 within 6 h
Tolvaptan 15 mg orally
questions.expl: For severe symptoms, give a 150 mL bolus of 3 % NaCl over 20 min, up to 3 boluses in total, with a target rise of +5 mmol/L in the first hour. Limits: ≤ 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h, then ≤ 8 mmol/L per 24 h. ([W06/D1](#W06-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding the correction of chronic hyponatraemia:
options: In SALSA, rapid intermittent bolus therapy caused significantly more overcorrection than slow continuous infusion.
The limit is ≤ 10 mmol/L in the first 24 h and ≤ 8 mmol/L in each following 24 h.
Hypokalaemia, alcoholism, malnutrition and liver disease increase the risk of osmotic demyelination.
Overcorrection is treated with 10 mL/kg of free water over 1 h, ± desmopressin 2 µg IV.
questions.expl: SALSA: overcorrection 17.2 vs 24.2 % (NS), with less need to relower Na⁺ in the bolus group. ([W06/D1](#W06-D1))

questions.stem: A 60-kg woman (TBW = 0.5 × weight) has Na⁺ 118 mmol/L. Using the Adrogué-Madias formula, 1 L of 3 % NaCl (Na⁺ 513 mmol/L) is expected to raise serum Na⁺ by approximately:
options: 17.1 mmol/L
6.6 mmol/L
19.8 mmol/L
9.3 mmol/L
12.7 mmol/L
questions.expl: ΔNa⁺ = (513 − 118)/(30 + 1) = 395/31 ≈ 12.7 mmol/L per litre. The formula ignores ongoing diuresis, and aquaresis can cause a much larger rise, so check Na⁺ frequently. ([W06/D1](#W06-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding SIAD:
options: Fluid restriction is the first-line treatment.
Vaptans are recommended for profound hyponatraemia.
SIAD can be diagnosed in a patient who took a thiazide diuretic yesterday.
Urea (0.25–0.50 g/kg/day) is a second-line option.
questions.expl: The guideline recommends **against** vaptans in profound hyponatraemia. Diagnosing SIAD requires excluding recent diuretics and adrenal, thyroid, pituitary and renal insufficiency. ([W06/D1](#W06-D1))

questions.stem: An elderly woman weighing 50 kg (TBW = 0.45 × weight) has Na⁺ 164 mmol/L. Her free water deficit is approximately:
questions.expl: TBW = 22.5 L; deficit = 22.5 × (164/140 − 1) = 22.5 × 0.171 ≈ 3.9 L. Add ongoing losses. Chronic hypernatraemia is traditionally corrected at ≤ 10–12 mmol/L/day. ([W06/D1](#W06-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding hyperkalaemia:
options: Marked thrombocytosis can cause pseudohyperkalaemia.
Insulin 10 U is given with glucose 25 g; if pre-treatment glucose is < 7 mmol/L, follow with 10 % glucose at 50 mL/h for 5 h.
IV calcium lowers serum potassium within minutes.
Trimethoprim can cause hyperkalaemia by blocking ENaC.
questions.expl: Calcium stabilises the myocardial membrane but does **not** change K⁺. Insulin and salbutamol only shift K⁺ into cells, so it must then be removed (SZC, diuretic, dialysis). ([W06/D2](#W06-D2))

questions.stem: Only 20 % glucose is available to give with insulin 10 U for hyperkalaemia. The volume needed to provide 25 g of glucose is:
options: 100 mL
500 mL
50 mL
125 mL
250 mL

questions.stem: Regarding hypokalaemia:
options: IV KCl should preferably be diluted in a glucose-free solution.
Hypokalaemia that does not respond to KCl suggests hypomagnesaemia.
ECG signs include U waves, flat T waves, ST depression and a prolonged QT(U).
In hypokalaemic cardiac arrest, ERC 2025 recommends KCl 20 mmol IV over 2–3 min, then 10 mmol over 2 min.
questions.expl: Glucose stimulates insulin, which shifts more K⁺ into cells, so use a glucose-free solution. ([W06/D2](#W06-D2))

questions.stem: A septic patient has total calcium 1.85 mmol/L, albumin 18 g/L and measured ionised calcium 0.92 mmol/L. Which statement is correct?
options: Alkalosis would raise the ionised fraction
Routine calcium supplementation for asymptomatic mild hypocalcaemia in sepsis improves outcome
A low iCa²⁺ is always a laboratory artefact
The patient has true hypocalcaemia; in the ICU, rely on measured iCa²⁺ rather than "corrected" calcium
Corrected calcium is 2.29 mmol/L, so the patient is normocalcaemic
questions.expl: Corrected Ca = 1.85 + 0.02 × (40 − 18) = 2.29, which looks normal, but the measured iCa²⁺ (normal 1.1–1.3) is low. Alkalosis **lowers** iCa²⁺. There is no evidence that routine supplementation helps in asymptomatic sepsis. ([W06/D3](#W06-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding severe hypercalcaemia:
options: Calcitonin starts to act only after 2–4 days.
IV bisphosphonates start to work after 2–4 days.
Denosumab is an option in renal failure.
A loop diuretic is the routine first-line treatment.
questions.expl: Calcitonin acts within hours but shows tachyphylaxis within about 48 h; bisphosphonates take 2–4 days. First give IV isotonic fluid. A loop diuretic is used only for fluid overload. Glucocorticoids are for vitamin D-mediated hypercalcaemia (sarcoidosis, some lymphomas). ([W06/D3](#W06-D3))

questions.stem: A malnourished ICU patient starts enteral feeding. Phosphate falls from 0.95 to 0.60 mmol/L on day 2. Based on Doig (Lancet Respir Med 2015) and ESPEN 2019, the appropriate response is:
options: No action – the fall is < 0.5 mmol/L
Continue full feeding and give oral phosphate only
Restrict energy intake (≈ 20 kcal/h) for at least 48 h with IV phosphate, then increase gradually
Switch to parenteral nutrition at full target
Stop all nutrition for 5 days
questions.expl: Refeeding hypophosphataemia = Pi < 0.65 mmol/L with a fall > 0.16 mmol/L within 72 h of starting feeding. In Doig, caloric restriction did not reach significance for the primary outcome, but more patients were alive at day 60. ([W06/D3](#W06-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding phosphate and magnesium:
options: Severe hypophosphataemia can cause failure to wean from mechanical ventilation.
2 g of MgSO₄·7H₂O contains about 2 mmol of Mg²⁺.
Hypophosphataemia shifts the oxyhaemoglobin dissociation curve to the right by increasing 2,3-DPG.
A phosphate of 2.0 mg/dL corresponds to about 0.65 mmol/L.
questions.expl: Hypophosphataemia **lowers** 2,3-DPG, shifting the curve to the **left**. 1 g MgSO₄ ≈ 4 mmol, so 2 g ≈ 8 mmol. 2.0 × 0.323 ≈ 0.65 mmol/L. ([W06/D3](#W06-D3), [W06/D2](#W06-D2))

title: W14 · D5 – Mini-mock: 50 questions / 90 min

questions.stem: Which organ system is **not** part of the SOFA-2 score (JAMA 2025)?
options: Liver
Gastrointestinal tract
Kidney
Brain
Hemostasis
questions.expl: SOFA-2 covers six systems: brain, respiratory, cardiovascular, liver, kidney and hemostasis. GI and immune dysfunction are not included. ([W01/D1](#W01-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding the SSC 2026 guideline:
options: Fluids should be given until lactate is normal.
Anaerobic coverage is suggested routinely in all patients with sepsis.
A strong recommendation can rest on very low certainty of evidence.
Patients who need ICU care should be admitted within 6 h.
questions.expl: Measure lactate serially, but do not resuscitate to a normal lactate. Anaerobic coverage is suggested only when risk factors are present. Antibiotic timing in shock is a strong recommendation with very low certainty. ([W01/D2](#W01-D2))

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock needs noradrenaline 0.35 µg/kg/min, and the dose is still rising. The best next vasoactive step is:
options: Add vasopressin, up to about 0.03 U/min
Add dopamine
Replace noradrenaline with vasopressin monotherapy
Add vasopressin at 0.1 U/min
Add levosimendan
questions.expl: SSC 2026: when the NA dose is escalating, add vasopressin (in practice at ~0.25–0.5 µg/kg/min NA), with a maximum of ~0.03 U/min. In VASST, mortality was NS. Dopamine and levosimendan are not suggested. ([W01/D4](#W01-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding fungal infections in the ICU:
options: The IAPA definition requires a classical host factor.
Echinocandins penetrate well into the eye, CNS and urine.
Fluconazole is active against *Aspergillus*.
About 19 % of ICU patients with influenza developed influenza-associated pulmonary aspergillosis (IAPA).
questions.expl: In the IAPA definition, an ICU admission with influenza replaces host factors. Echinocandins penetrate **poorly** into the eye, CNS and urine. Fluconazole has no activity against *Aspergillus*. ([W02/D4](#W02-D4))

questions.stem: A patient has bacteraemia with KPC-producing *Klebsiella pneumoniae* susceptible to the new β-lactam combinations. The most appropriate targeted agent is:
options: Ertapenem
Cefepime
Meropenem-vaborbactam
Colistin plus meropenem
Aztreonam-avibactam, because it is the drug of choice for KPC
questions.expl: KPC: meropenem-vaborbactam, ceftazidime-avibactam or imipenem-relebactam, as monotherapy for susceptible strains. Aztreonam + avibactam (or cefiderocol) is for **MBL** producers. ([W02/D3](#W02-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding catheter-related bloodstream infection:
options: A tunnel infection can be treated with the catheter left in place and antibiotic lock therapy.
Uncomplicated Gram-negative CRBSI can be treated for 7 days.
The catheter should be removed if bacteraemia persists ≥ 72 h on appropriate therapy.
Uncomplicated CoNS CRBSI is treated for 4–6 weeks after catheter removal.
questions.expl: Tunnel infection, shock, *S. aureus*, Gram-negatives, enterococci and *Candida* are all indications for removal. Uncomplicated CoNS CRBSI: 5–7 days after removal. ([W03/D1](#W03-D1))

questions.stem: For suspected HSV encephalitis, the correct empirical acyclovir regimen is:
options: 10 mg/kg IV once daily for 10 days
5 mg/kg IV every 12 h for 7 days
30 mg/kg IV every 8 h for 3 days
800 mg orally five times a day for 7 days
10 mg/kg IV every 8 h for 14–21 days
questions.expl: If an early CSF PCR is negative, repeat it after 3–7 days and continue acyclovir in the meantime. ([W03/D2](#W03-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding selective decontamination:
options: In the Hammond 2022 meta-analysis, the mortality benefit was seen only in trials that included the IV component.
The positive results of de Smet 2009 come from a low-resistance setting (the Netherlands).
In SuDDICU, the difference in hospital mortality (27.0 vs 29.1 %) was not statistically significant.
In the Hammond 2022 meta-analysis, SDD reduced VAP (RR about 0.44).
questions.expl: The mortality benefit (RR 0.91) was seen only with the IV component. ([W03/D5](#W03-D5))

questions.stem: A patient with acute leukaemia and profound neutropenia has had fever for 6 days despite piperacillin-tazobactam. He is haemodynamically stable and cultures are negative. The best next step is:
options: Give G-CSF and wait
Switch to meropenem and add amikacin
CT of the chest and serum galactomannan to look for an invasive fungal infection
Add vancomycin empirically
Stop all antimicrobials
questions.expl: Fever persisting > 4–7 days in profound neutropenia should raise suspicion of an invasive mould infection. Do not simply escalate antibacterials, and do not add glycopeptides routinely. ([W03/D4](#W03-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding necrotising soft-tissue infections:
options: Bullae, crepitus and hypotension are early and sensitive signs.
Pain out of proportion to the clinical findings is a key early clue.
A typical empirical regimen is ceftriaxone monotherapy.
Confirmed group A streptococcal NSTI is treated with vancomycin alone.
questions.expl: Bullae, crepitus and hypotension are **late** and insensitive signs. Empirical therapy: vancomycin/linezolid + piperacillin-tazobactam/carbapenem + clindamycin; confirmed GAS: penicillin plus clindamycin (antitoxin effect). Surgery should be done as early as possible (< 6–24 h). ([W03/D3](#W03-D3))

questions.stem: Which fluid strategy is consistent with SSC 2026 for septic shock?
options: 0.9 % saline is preferred over balanced crystalloids
Gelatin is preferred in patients with AKI
HES is acceptable when albumin is unavailable
Balanced crystalloids are suggested over saline, except in traumatic brain injury
Albumin is the first-line resuscitation fluid
questions.expl: Balanced crystalloids are preferred over saline (conditional), except in TBI. Albumin is not used routinely, and HES is never used. ([W01/D3](#W01-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding vasopressors in septic shock:
options: In SOAP II, noradrenaline caused more arrhythmias than dopamine.
Vasopressors must never be started through a peripheral cannula.
SSC 2026 suggests a MAP target of 75–80 mmHg in patients aged ≥ 65 years.
Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor.
questions.expl: SOAP II: arrhythmias were more frequent with **dopamine** (24.1 vs 12.4 %). Peripheral vasopressors are acceptable to start with. In patients aged ≥ 65 years, the suggested MAP target is **60–65** mmHg (65 trial). ([W01/D4](#W01-D4))

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS is ventilated with VT 6 mL/kg PBW, is in sinus rhythm and is not breathing spontaneously. Pulse pressure variation is 5 %. The best interpretation is:
options: A PPV of 5 % indicates hypovolaemia
PPV is valid because the patient is in sinus rhythm
The patient is definitely not fluid responsive
The patient is fluid responsive
Low VT makes PPV unreliable (possible false negative); use PLR, EEO or a tidal volume challenge
questions.expl: PPV (threshold 13 %) needs VT ≥ 8 mL/kg, sinus rhythm, a closed chest and no IAH. ([W04/D2](#W04-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding capillary refill time-targeted resuscitation:
options: In ANDROMEDA-SHOCK, mortality was 34.9 vs 43.4 % (p = 0.06).
ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 showed lower mortality with CRT-targeted resuscitation.
SSC 2021 suggests against using CRT to guide resuscitation.
ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 was positive for a hierarchical composite (win ratio 1.16).
questions.expl: Mortality in ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 was 26.5 vs 26.6 %. SSC 2021 suggests CRT as an adjunct to other measures of perfusion. ([W04/D4](#W04-D4))

questions.stem: A patient in cardiogenic shock has MAP 60 mmHg and cardiac output 3.6 L/min. The cardiac power output is approximately:
questions.expl: CPO = MAP × CO / 451 = 60 × 3.6 / 451 = 216/451 ≈ 0.48 W. A low CPO is among the strongest haemodynamic predictors of mortality in CS. ([W07/D1](#W07-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding peripheral (femoral) VA-ECMO:
options: Increasing the FiO₂ of the oxygenator corrects upper-body hypoxaemia in Harlequin syndrome.
Oxygenation should be monitored from the right radial artery.
Upper-body hypoxaemia appears when the native heart recovers but lung gas exchange remains poor.
VA-ECMO increases LV afterload, which can cause LV distension and pulmonary oedema.
questions.expl: The oxygenator oxygenates only the ECMO blood. The fix is better lung gas exchange or a V-AV configuration. ([W07/D2](#W07-D2))

questions.stem: A patient with NSTEMI develops acute pulmonary oedema. The timing of invasive coronary angiography should be:
options: After 7 days of medical stabilisation
Only if troponin keeps rising
Within 72 h
Within 24 h (high risk)
Immediate (very high risk)
questions.expl: Very high-risk features (shock, acute HF, life-threatening arrhythmias, mechanical complications) require immediate angiography. ([W07/D3](#W07-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding decompensated heart failure (ESC 2026):
options: IV vasodilators are recommended (class I) whenever SBP is > 90 mmHg.
SGLT2 inhibitors should be stopped during hospitalisation.
Acetazolamide (ADVOR) or a thiazide added to a loop diuretic has a IIa recommendation.
HFmrEF was abolished; LVEF < 50 % is classified as HFrEF.
questions.expl: IV vasodilators can be considered when SBP is > 110 mmHg (IIb). SGLT2 inhibitors are started **during** hospitalisation (class I), with rapid titration of GDMT (STRONG-HF). ([W07/D4](#W07-D4))

questions.stem: A patient 3 years after heart transplantation has symptomatic bradycardia (HR 35/min, BP 80/50 mmHg). Which drug should **not** be used?
options: Adrenaline
Atropine
Transcutaneous pacing (non-drug)
Transvenous pacing (non-drug)
Isoprenaline
questions.expl: A denervated heart does not respond predictably to atropine, so avoid it after heart transplantation. Use isoprenaline/adrenaline and pacing instead. ([W08/D1](#W08-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding pulmonary embolism:
options: A pulmonary embolism response team (PERT) is suggested for more severe PE.
VA-ECMO can be considered as a bridge in refractory circulatory collapse or arrest (IIb C).
HI-PEITHO and PRAGUE-26 also reduced mortality.
In intermediate-high risk PE, catheter-directed thrombolysis (HI-PEITHO, PRAGUE-26) reduced early decompensation.
questions.expl: Mortality was not changed. Systemic thrombolysis is reserved for high-risk PE, or for rescue after deterioration. ([W08/D2](#W08-D2))

questions.stem: A woman at 34 weeks of pregnancy with severe pre-eclampsia has BP 178/112 mmHg and headache. The appropriate management is:
options: IV labetalol or nicardipine plus magnesium sulfate, target < 160/105 mmHg
Furosemide IV and oral nifedipine
No antihypertensive until BP is > 200/120 mmHg
Sodium nitroprusside to a BP of 120/80 mmHg
Enalapril IV
questions.expl: Pre-eclampsia: labetalol/nicardipine + MgSO₄, target < 160/105 mmHg. For pulmonary oedema use nitroglycerin. Do not use diuretics. ([W08/D4](#W08-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding infective endocarditis in the ICU:
options: In EASE, early surgery reduced embolic events.
Refractory pulmonary oedema or cardiogenic shock requires emergency surgery (within 24 h).
Ischaemic stroke is a reason to postpone indicated surgery by 4 weeks.
In POET, partial oral treatment was inferior to continued IV treatment in stable patients.
questions.expl: Ischaemic stroke is **not** a reason to postpone surgery. Postpone for ≥ 4 weeks only after significant intracranial haemorrhage. POET: partial oral treatment was **non-inferior**. ([W08/D5](#W08-D5))

questions.stem: During CPR for PEA, intraosseous access has just been obtained. Adrenaline should be given:
options: After the third cycle of CPR
Only after reversible causes have been excluded
As 3 mg via the tracheal tube
Not at all in PEA
Now, 1 mg IO
questions.expl: In non-shockable rhythms, give adrenaline 1 mg as soon as IV/IO access is available, then every 3–5 min. In VF/pVT, give it after the third shock. ([W09/D1](#W09-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding care after ROSC:
options: In BOX, a MAP target of 77 mmHg improved outcomes compared with 63 mmHg.
Routine prophylactic antibiotics are recommended.
Routine seizure prophylaxis is recommended.
In BOX-O₂, a restrictive PaO₂ target of 9–10 kPa improved outcomes compared with 13–14 kPa.
questions.expl: Neither BOX (MAP 63 vs 77 mmHg) nor BOX-O₂ (PaO₂ 9–10 vs 13–14 kPa) showed a difference. Routine corticosteroids, antibiotic prophylaxis, NMB and seizure prophylaxis are not recommended. ([W09/D2](#W09-D2))

questions.stem: A comatose post-arrest patient still has residual sedative effect at 72 h because of renal failure. Which predictor of poor neurological outcome is **least** affected by the sedatives?
options: Absent motor response to pain
Absent corneal reflex
Absent pupillary light reflex
Highly malignant EEG
Bilaterally absent N20 SSEP waves
questions.expl: SSEPs are resistant to sedation, whereas EEG and the clinical examination are affected by it. Use ≥ 2 predictors, at ≥ 72 h, with no confounders. ([W09/D4](#W09-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding ARDS epidemiology (LUNG SAFE and the lessons):
options: ARDS affected about 23 % of mechanically ventilated patients.
The Berlin definition includes patients on HFNO ≥ 30 L/min.
ARDS was under-recognised by clinicians.
Pneumonia is the most common cause of ARDS.
questions.expl: HFNO patients are included only in the 2024 **global** definition. ([W10/D1](#W10-D1))

questions.stem: Which trial compared 6 vs 12 mL/kg PBW with plateau limits of ≤ 30 vs ≤ 50 cmH₂O and found mortality of 31.0 vs 39.8 %?
options: LOVS
ALVEOLI
PROSEVA
ARMA
ACURASYS
questions.expl: ARMA (ARDS Network, 2000) was stopped early for benefit. ([W10/D2](#W10-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding PEEP trials:
options: ART showed less barotrauma with maximal recruitment.
The Briel meta-analysis suggested benefit of higher PEEP only when P/F ≤ 200.
LOVS increased refractory hypoxaemia.
EXPRESS increased ventilator-free days.
questions.expl: ART caused **more** barotrauma and higher mortality. LOVS **reduced** refractory hypoxaemia and rescue therapies. No single higher-PEEP RCT reduced mortality. ([W10/D3](#W10-D3))

questions.stem: The corticosteroid regimen tested in DEXA-ARDS was:
options: Methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days
Dexamethasone 10 mg every 6 h for 4 days
Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for 7 days
Dexamethasone 20 mg daily, then 10 mg daily, for a total of 10 days
Dexamethasone 6 mg daily for 10 days
questions.expl: DEXA-ARDS: 60-day mortality 21 vs 36 %, and 4.8 more ventilator-free days. 6 mg = RECOVERY (COVID-19); 10 mg q6h × 4 days = meningitis. ([W10/D4](#W10-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding non-invasive support in the ESICM 2023 ARDS/AHRF guideline:
options: HFNO is recommended over conventional oxygen to reduce intubation.
In COVID-19, CPAP/NIV is suggested to reduce intubation.
In COVID-19, awake prone positioning is suggested (conditional).
HFNO reduces mortality compared with conventional oxygen.
questions.expl: The strong recommendation for HFNO is based on the outcome "intubation", not mortality. ([W10/D5](#W10-D5))

questions.stem: A patient is extubated successfully 3 days after the first attempt at separation from the ventilator. In the WIND classification, this is:
options: Prolonged weaning
Short weaning
Simple weaning
Weaning failure
Difficult weaning
questions.expl: WIND: short < 1 day, difficult 1–7 days, prolonged ≥ 7 days (mortality 6/17/29 %). "Simple" is a Boles category. ([W11/D4](#W11-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding oxygen trials:
options: Together, these trials show that a conservative oxygen target lowers mortality.
HOT-ICU found no difference in 90-day mortality.
LOCO2 targeted PaO₂ 90–105 mmHg in the conservative arm.
ICU-ROX targeted SpO₂ 88–92 % in the conservative arm.
questions.expl: LOCO2 targeted PaO₂ **55–70** mmHg (in ARDS), and was stopped early because of harm. ICU-ROX conservative arm: upper SpO₂ limit of 97 %. None of these trials showed a mortality benefit. ([W11/D2](#W11-D2))

questions.stem: A 50-year-old in the ICU has severe influenza A pneumonia without shock. Regarding adjunctive hydrocortisone:
options: Recommended only with fludrocortisone
Recommended, based on CAPE COD
Mandatory if HFNO is needed
Not recommended: CAPE COD excluded influenza, and ATS 2025 advises against steroids in influenza
Recommended if CRP > 150 mg/L
questions.expl: Observational data link steroids in influenza to higher mortality and superinfections. Oseltamivir is indicated. ([W12/D2](#W12-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding the DAS 2018 guideline for tracheal intubation in critically ill adults:
options: Plan D uses scalpel–bougie–tube cricothyroidotomy as the default technique.
Plan B uses a second-generation supraglottic airway device.
Waveform capnography is used to confirm tracheal intubation.
Plan A allows a maximum of 3 attempts, plus 1 attempt by a more experienced operator.
questions.expl: Plan D (CICO) = scalpel–bougie–tube front-of-neck access. "No trace = wrong place." ([W12/D3](#W12-D3))

questions.stem: A patient with a 5-day-old percutaneous tracheostomy desaturates suddenly. Oxygen is applied to the face and stoma, and the inner cannula is removed, but a suction catheter will not pass. The next step is:
options: Ventilate vigorously with a bag through the tracheostomy tube
Give nebulised salbutamol
Insert a larger suction catheter through the tube
Deflate the cuff and, if there is no improvement, remove the tracheostomy tube
Perform an urgent chest X-ray
questions.expl: If the catheter does not pass, bagging through the tube can cause surgical emphysema. Deflate the cuff, then remove the tube, and oxygenate through the mouth/stoma (unless the patient has had a laryngectomy). ([W12/D4](#W12-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding pleural infection:
options: A pleural fluid pH of 7.3 on its own mandates a chest drain.
Small-bore drains (≤ 14 F) are suitable.
In MIST1, intrapleural streptokinase did not improve outcomes.
In MIST2, DNase alone was harmful.
questions.expl: The drain threshold is pH ≤ 7.2. At pH 7.2–7.4, use LDH > 900 IU/L (glucose < 3.3 mmol/L if pH is unavailable). ([W12/D5](#W12-D5))

questions.stem: A non-anaesthetist ICU physician is about to intubate a patient with Mallampati class III and GCS 6. There is no OSA, no reduced neck mobility, mouth opening > 3 cm and SpO₂ 92 %. The MACOCHA score is:
questions.expl: Mallampati III–IV 5 + coma 1 + non-anaesthetist 1 = 7. A score ≥ 3 means high risk of difficult intubation. ([W12/D3](#W12-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding intrinsic PEEP (PEEPi):
options: PEEPi is measured with an end-expiratory hold in a passive patient.
In Caramez et al., all patients had a paradoxical response (falling Pplat) to external PEEP.
Active expiration falsely lowers the measured PEEPi.
In assisted ventilation of COPD, external PEEP set below PEEPi reduces the work of triggering.
questions.expl: Caramez: a paradoxical response occurred in 5 of 8 patients. Active expiratory muscle contraction falsely **raises** measured PEEPi. Titrate external PEEP by the Pplat response. ([W13/D5](#W13-D5))

questions.stem: An anxious patient has pH 7.48, pCO₂ 30 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 22 mmol/L. The best description is:
options: Acute respiratory alkalosis with appropriate compensation
Chronic respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis with an additional metabolic acidosis
Laboratory error – the values are inconsistent
Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
questions.expl: pCO₂ fell by 10, so acute compensation predicts HCO₃⁻ 24 − 2 = 22. Consistency check: [H⁺] = 24 × 30/22 ≈ 33 nmol/L → pH ≈ 7.47–7.48. ([W05/D1](#W05-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding infusion fluids and acid–base:
options: Large volumes of 0.9 % NaCl raise the plasma SID.
The in vivo SID of Plasma-Lyte 148 is about 50 mmol/L.
In SMART, balanced crystalloids lowered the composite MAKE30 (14.3 vs 15.4 %).
The in vivo SID of Ringer's lactate is about 28 mmol/L.
questions.expl: Saline has an SID of 0, so it **dilutes** plasma SID → hyperchloraemic acidosis. ([W05/D2](#W05-D2))

questions.stem: A patient with blurred vision, a high-AG acidosis, a raised osmolal gap and bilateral putaminal lesions is treated with fomepizole and haemodialysis. Which cofactor should also be given?
options: Vitamin K
Pyridoxine
Thiamine alone
Folate (folinic acid)
Calcium gluconate
questions.expl: This is methanol poisoning (toxic metabolite formic acid): give folate. Thiamine + pyridoxine are the cofactors for ethylene glycol. ([W05/D3](#W05-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding hyperkalaemia (ERC 2025):
options: Nebulised salbutamol alone is enough treatment for severe hyperkalaemia.
Insulin with glucose is the fastest way to lower serum K⁺.
Moderate hyperkalaemia is 5.5–5.9 mmol/L and severe is ≥ 6.0 mmol/L.
In hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest, CaCl₂ and sodium bicarbonate can be given through the same line without flushing.
questions.expl: ERC: moderate 6.0–6.4, severe ≥ 6.5 mmol/L. CaCl₂ and bicarbonate precipitate (CaCO₃), so use separate lines or flush. Salbutamol (10–20 mg) is additive to insulin, but not enough on its own. ([W06/D2](#W06-D2))

questions.stem: A patient after severe TBI develops polyuria of 400 mL/h, urine osmolality 150 mOsm/kg and Na⁺ 152 mmol/L. The most likely diagnosis and treatment are:
options: Osmotic diuresis – stop mannitol
Nephrogenic DI – thiazide
SIAD – fluid restriction
Cerebral salt wasting – 3 % NaCl
Central DI – desmopressin
questions.expl: Polyuria with urine osmolality < 300 means DI. In the ICU, central DI occurs after brain death, TBI and neurosurgery, and responds to desmopressin. ([W06/D1](#W06-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding refeeding syndrome (NICE CG32):
options: BMI < 18.5 kg/m² alone puts the patient at high risk.
In high-risk patients, feeding should start at no more than 10 kcal/kg/day.
Thiamine should be given only after feeding has been established.
Two of the following also put the patient at high risk: BMI < 18.5, weight loss > 10 % in 3–6 months, little intake for > 5 days, alcohol or drug misuse.
questions.expl: One criterion alone = BMI < 16, weight loss > 15 % in 3–6 months, little intake > 10 days, or low K⁺/PO₄³⁻/Mg²⁺; BMI < 18.5 counts only as one of two minor criteria. Give thiamine and B vitamins **before** feeding starts and during the first 10 days. ([W06/D3](#W06-D3))

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on metformin has septic shock from cholangitis with anuric AKI, lactate 12 mmol/L, pH 7.08, PaCO₂ 30 mmHg and HCO₃⁻ 9 mmol/L. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The lactate is purely type A, so metformin is irrelevant
Sodium bicarbonate is recommended to improve haemodynamics
Hypoperfusion and metformin may both contribute; bicarbonate may be considered at pH ≤ 7.2 with AKI, as it reduced the need for RRT without changing mortality
Fluids should be given until lactate is normal
Bicarbonate reduced 90-day mortality in BICARICU-2
questions.expl: The type A/B division is imperfect. In sepsis, hypoperfusion, adrenergic stimulation and reduced clearance combine, and metformin is a type B cause. SSC 2021: consider bicarbonate at pH ≤ 7.2 with AKIN 2–3 (weak). BICARICU-2: less KRT (35 vs 50 %), mortality unchanged. Winter: 1.5 × 9 + 8 = 21.5 ± 2, so PaCO₂ 30 indicates an additional respiratory acidosis. ([W05/D2](#W05-D2), [W05/D1](#W05-D1), [W01/D2](#W01-D2))

questions.stem: A patient with ARDS from pneumonia has P/F 120, driving pressure 19 cmH₂O, PaCO₂ 52 mmHg, and a dilated RV with a D-shaped LV on echo.
options: Raising the respiratory rate to correct the hypercapnia also increases mechanical power.
P/F < 150 and PaCO₂ ≥ 48 mmHg are risk factors for acute cor pulmonale.
Pneumonia as the cause of ARDS is a risk factor for acute cor pulmonale.
Prone positioning is one of the measures used to unload the RV.
questions.expl: RV-protective ventilation: lower the driving pressure (≥ 18 is a risk factor), correct hypercapnia and use prone positioning; increasing PEEP may worsen RV afterload. RR enters mechanical power with exponent 1.4. ([W07/D5](#W07-D5), [W04/D5](#W04-D5), [W13/D4](#W13-D4))

questions.stem: A patient after OHCA was treated at 33 °C and has renal and hepatic dysfunction. On day 3 he remains unresponsive. Why should neuroprognostication be interpreted with particular caution here?
options: SSEPs are invalid after targeted temperature management
NSE cannot be measured after hypothermia
Hypothermia increases sedative clearance, so the sedatives wear off too quickly
Hypothermia improves the reliability of the clinical examination
Hypothermia (and organ dysfunction) reduces the clearance of sedatives, which can confound clinical and EEG findings
questions.expl: Hypothermia reduces the clearance of sedatives, so residual sedation can mimic poor neurology and lead to a self-fulfilling prophecy. Wait, exclude confounders, and use multimodal predictors (SSEP is resistant to sedation). ([W09/D3](#W09-D3), [W09/D4](#W09-D4))

questions.stem: A patient with severe COPD (baseline PaCO₂ 8 kPa, HCO₃⁻ 34 mmol/L) is intubated for an exacerbation.
options: If severe hypotension develops soon after intubation, briefly disconnecting the ventilator is diagnostic and therapeutic.
Rapid normalisation of PaCO₂ can cause a post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis.
The ventilation target is the patient's usual PaCO₂.
Increasing the respiratory rate to normalise PaCO₂ reduces auto-PEEP.
questions.expl: A higher RR shortens expiratory time and **worsens** dynamic hyperinflation. If the patient is hypotensive, disconnect and exclude pneumothorax. ([W05/D3](#W05-D3), [W12/D1](#W12-D1), [W13/D5](#W13-D5))

questions.stem: A malnourished alcoholic patient was treated for DKA with insulin and started on enteral feeding. On day 5 he repeatedly fails SBTs with rapid shallow breathing. Phosphate is 0.25 mmol/L. The most likely contributor is:
options: Critical illness polyneuropathy only
Hypermagnesaemia
Severe hypophosphataemia causing respiratory muscle weakness
Metabolic alkalosis from acetazolamide
Hypercalcaemia
questions.expl: Insulin and refeeding shift phosphate into cells. Below about 0.32 mmol/L, hypophosphataemia causes respiratory muscle weakness and weaning failure, as well as low 2,3-DPG and haemolysis. Replace phosphate (IV) and check K⁺, Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺. ([W06/D3](#W06-D3), [W11/D4](#W11-D4))

questions.stem: A patient with septic shock on noradrenaline 0.3 µg/kg/min for 6 h develops new atrial fibrillation at 150/min.
options: In STRESS-L, landiolol improved outcomes in tachycardic septic shock.
He does not yet meet the criteria for hydrocortisone.
The first step is to treat triggers (sepsis, fluid status, K⁺/Mg²⁺, catecholamine dose).
If the patient is unstable, synchronised cardioversion with an initial shock at maximum energy is indicated (ERC 2025).
questions.expl: STRESS-L showed no benefit and a signal of harm. If cardioversion fails, give amiodarone 300 mg. Hydrocortisone is indicated for NA ≥ 0.25 µg/kg/min for ≥ 4 h, which he meets. ([W08/D1](#W08-D1), [W01/D5](#W01-D5))

title: Monthly review – February (Sat 27 Feb 2027)

questions.stem: A 45-year-old on VV-ECMO for severe ARDS has PaO₂ 9.5 kPa (71 mmHg), PaCO₂ 8.0 kPa (60 mmHg) and pH 7.27. ECMO blood flow is 4.0 L/min and sweep gas flow 2 L/min. The ventilator is set to plateau pressure 24 cmH₂O, PEEP 12 cmH₂O, RR 12/min. Which change most directly lowers PaCO₂ while keeping ultra-protective ventilation?
options: Increase plateau pressure to 32 cmH₂O
Increase extracorporeal blood flow
Increase the ventilator respiratory rate to 30/min
Increase sweep gas flow
Convert to VA-ECMO
questions.expl: On VV-ECMO, CO₂ removal depends mainly on sweep gas flow through the oxygenator. Oxygenation depends mainly on blood flow relative to the patient's cardiac output. Raising RR or plateau pressure defeats the purpose of "lung rest". VA-ECMO is for cardiac failure. ([W11/D1](#W11-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding the CESAR trial (Lancet 2009):
options: Patients were randomised to transfer to an ECMO centre for consideration of ECMO, or to conventional management in the referring hospital.
Nearly all (> 95 %) patients in the ECMO arm actually received ECMO.
The control arm followed a mandatory lung-protective ventilation protocol.
CESAR proved that ECMO itself reduces mortality in ARDS.
questions.expl: The control arm had no protocol, and lung-protective ventilation was used in 93 % vs 70 %. Only 68 of 90 patients (~75 %) received ECMO. CESAR showed the benefit of a **referral strategy** to an ECMO centre: death or severe disability at 6 months was 37 vs 53 %. It did not show the benefit of ECMO itself. ([W11/D1](#W11-D1))

questions.stem: All of the following patients have severe ARDS despite optimised ventilation. Which one meets the EOLIA entry criteria and none of its exclusions?
options: pH 7.28 with PaCO₂ 65 mmHg for 8 hours, ventilated for 2 days
P/F 70 mmHg for 4 hours, ventilated for 2 days
P/F 45 mmHg for 4 hours, ventilated for 3 days
P/F 90 mmHg for 12 hours, ventilated for 1 day
P/F 45 mmHg for 5 hours, ventilated for 9 days
questions.expl: The EOLIA criteria are P/F < 50 mmHg for > 3 h, P/F < 80 mmHg for > 6 h, or pH < 7.25 with PaCO₂ ≥ 60 mmHg for > 6 h. Ventilation for > 7 days was an exclusion criterion (E). In B, P/F < 80 has not lasted 6 h. In A, pH is not < 7.25. ([W11/D1](#W11-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding the EOLIA trial (NEJM 2018):
options: Ischaemic stroke was less frequent in the ECMO group.
The ECMO-arm ventilation protocol limited plateau pressure to ≤ 24 cmH₂O with PEEP ≥ 10 cmH₂O.
Bleeding requiring transfusion was more frequent in the ECMO group (46 % vs 28 %).
Control patients who crossed over to rescue ECMO had a 60-day mortality of 57 %.
questions.expl: Ischaemic stroke was 0 % with ECMO vs 5 % in controls. Severe thrombocytopenia (27 vs 16 %) was also more common with ECMO. Crossover occurred in 28 % of controls. ([W11/D1](#W11-D1))

questions.stem: In the post hoc Bayesian reanalysis of EOLIA (Goligher, JAMA 2018), what was the posterior probability of **any** mortality benefit (RR < 1) when a **strongly sceptical** prior was used?
questions.expl: Across priors, the probability of any benefit was 88–99 %: 88 % with the strongly sceptical prior and 96 % with the minimally informative prior. The probability of a **large** benefit (RR < 0.67) ranged from 0 to 48 %, and the probability of ARR ≥ 20 % was only 0–4 %. ([W11/D1](#W11-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding the harms of oxygen:
options: Hyperoxia causes coronary and cerebral vasodilatation.
Absorption atelectasis at FiO₂ close to 1.0 results from accumulation of nitrogen in low-V/Q alveoli.
In the IOTA meta-analysis, liberal oxygen reduced in-hospital mortality.
Pulse oximetry tends to underestimate SaO₂, so low SpO₂ targets carry little risk of occult hypoxaemia.
questions.expl: Hyperoxia causes systemic **vasoconstriction** and lowers cardiac output. Absorption atelectasis results from **washout** of nitrogen – oxygen is absorbed and the alveolus collapses. IOTA: liberal oxygen **increased** in-hospital mortality (RR 1.21). Pulse oximetry can **overestimate** SaO₂, especially with darker skin pigmentation and poor perfusion. This raises the risk of occult hypoxaemia at low targets. ([W11/D2](#W11-D2))

questions.stem: In the LOCO2 trial (ARDS; conservative target PaO₂ 55–70 mmHg vs liberal 90–105 mmHg), which finding was reported in the conservative arm?
options: Lower 28-day mortality
Mesenteric ischaemia in 5 % vs 0 %
More ventilator-free days, with completion of planned enrolment
Lower 90-day mortality
No safety signal
questions.expl: LOCO2 was stopped early for safety concerns and futility. 90-day mortality was **higher** with the conservative target (44.4 vs 30.4 %). Mesenteric ischaemia occurred in 5 vs 0 %. ([W11/D2](#W11-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding large ICU oxygen-target RCTs:
options: Post hoc analyses of ICU-ROX suggested a benefit of conservative oxygen in sepsis.
HOT-ICU also enrolled non-ventilated patients.
In UK-ROX, the achieved SpO₂ differed between groups by only about 2 %.
In HOT-ICU, the achieved median PaO₂ in the lower-target group was about 55 mmHg (~7.3 kPa), below the 8-kPa target.
questions.expl: ICU-ROX showed a hypothesis-generating benefit signal for hypoxic-ischaemic encephalopathy and a signal of **worse** outcome in sepsis. UK-ROX did not confirm either signal. In HOT-ICU, the achieved median PaO₂ in the lower-target group was about 71 mmHg (~9.4 kPa), above the target. Small separation between arms is one reason the large trials were neutral. ([W11/D2](#W11-D2))

questions.stem: A ventilated patient with moderate ARDS is on FiO₂ 0.6. Based on the lessons from LOCO2, which statement best describes the lower limit of oxygenation?
options: SpO₂ 80 % is acceptable if lactate is normal
PaO₂ 45 mmHg is acceptable as part of permissive hypoxaemia
SpO₂ must be kept ≥ 98 % at all times
PaO₂ must be kept > 100 mmHg to protect the gut
Do not go below PaO₂ ~55–60 mmHg / SpO₂ ~88 %
questions.expl: A reasonable corridor for most critically ill patients is SpO₂ ~92–96 % or PaO₂ ~60–90 mmHg, avoiding both extremes. In ARDS, do not go below PaO₂ ~55–60 mmHg / SpO₂ ~88 %. Sustained SpO₂ 98–100 % at FiO₂ > 0.4 means unnecessary oxygen. ([W11/D2](#W11-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding HFNO and the FLORALI trial:
options: In FLORALI, the primary outcome (intubation by day 28) did not differ significantly between groups.
HFNO washes out nasopharyngeal dead space.
FLORALI excluded patients with cardiogenic pulmonary oedema and patients with PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg.
HFNO produces a low, uncontrolled positive airway pressure that depends on flow and mouth closure.
questions.expl: Intubation was 38 vs 47 vs 50 % (p = 0.18, NS). Fewer intubations were seen only in the post hoc P/F ≤ 200 subgroup. 90-day mortality (12 vs 23 vs 28 %) favoured HFNO. ([W11/D3](#W11-D3))

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia has been on HFNO for 6 hours with FiO₂ 0.5, SpO₂ 95 % and RR 28/min. What is the ROX index and its interpretation?
options: ROX ≈ 3.4: high risk of HFNO failure
ROX ≈ 6.8: above 4.88, lower risk of intubation
ROX ≈ 0.15: uninterpretable
ROX ≈ 53: very low risk
ROX ≈ 2.7: high risk, intubate now
questions.expl: ROX = (SpO₂/FiO₂)/RR = (95/0.5)/28 = 190/28 ≈ **6.8**. ROX ≥ 4.88 at 2, 6 or 12 h is associated with a lower risk of intubation. At 6 h, ROX < 3.47 indicates high risk. ([W11/D3](#W11-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding prediction of failure of non-invasive support in hypoxaemic respiratory failure:
options: In HACOR, heart rate carries the greatest weight.
P-SILI is a clinical syndrome proven in randomised trials.
In Carteaux et al. (Crit Care Med 2016), an expired tidal volume > 9.5 mL/kg PBW on NIV predicted NIV failure.
HACOR was developed for HFNO, and a score > 5 after 1 hour indicates high risk of failure.
questions.expl: **Consciousness** (GCS) carries the greatest weight in HACOR. HACOR was developed for **NIV** (ROX is for HFNO). P-SILI is a **concept/hypothesis** (Brochard, AJRCCM 2017) and is used as an argument against delaying intubation when drive is uncontrolled. ([W11/D3](#W11-D3))

questions.stem: In the single-centre trial by Patel et al. (JAMA 2016) of helmet vs face-mask NIV in ARDS, the intubation rates were:
questions.expl: 90-day mortality was 34.1 vs 56.4 %. The trial was small, single-centre and stopped early for efficacy, so it is hypothesis-generating. B = HENIVOT (helmet vs HFNO), A = FLORALI, D = Hernández I, E = HIGH-WEAN. ([W11/D3](#W11-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding guidelines for non-invasive respiratory support:
options: ESICM 2023 recommends HFNO to reduce mortality.
ERS 2022 suggests trying NIV before HFNC in hypercapnic COPD exacerbation.
ESICM 2023 recommends HFNO over conventional oxygen in AHRF to reduce intubation (strong recommendation, moderate certainty).
ERS/ATS 2017 strongly recommends NIV or CPAP in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
questions.expl: ESICM makes no mortality recommendation and has high certainty that HFNO does not change mortality. ESICM gives no recommendation on HFNO vs CPAP/NIV in AHRF in general. ([W11/D3](#W11-D3))

questions.stem: According to the ERS/ATS/ESICM weaning consensus (Boles 2007), weaning success is defined as:
options: Passing a spontaneous breathing trial
Extubation and absence of ventilatory support for 7 days
Extubation and absence of ventilatory support for 24 h
Extubation and absence of ventilatory support for 48 h
Extubation directly onto prophylactic NIV
questions.expl: Weaning failure is a failed SBT, reintubation or resumption of ventilatory support, or death within 48 h after extubation. A patient extubated onto NIV counts as "weaning in progress". ([W11/D4](#W11-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding the spontaneous breathing trial (SBT):
options: ATS/ACCP 2017 suggests that the initial SBT uses inspiratory pressure augmentation of 5–8 cmH₂O rather than a T-piece or CPAP.
In Subirà et al. (JAMA 2019), reintubation was significantly higher after a 30-min PSV SBT than after a 2-h T-piece trial.
In Subirà et al., hospital mortality was lower in the PSV group (10.4 % vs 14.9 %).
Most patients who fail an SBT do so only after the first 90 minutes.
questions.expl: Reintubation was 11.1 vs 11.9 % (NS). Successful extubation was 82.3 vs 74.0 %. The ATS/ACCP recommendation is conditional, moderate certainty. Most SBT failures occur within the first ~20 minutes. ([W11/D4](#W11-D4))

questions.stem: A patient's first separation attempt (an SBT) fails on day 6 of ventilation. She is successfully extubated 4 days after that first attempt and needs no further support. How is she classified by WIND (Béduneau 2017)?
options: Simple weaning
"No weaning" group
Group 1 – short weaning; ICU mortality ~6 %
Group 3 – prolonged weaning; ICU mortality ~29 %
Group 2 – difficult weaning; ICU mortality ~17 %
questions.expl: WIND counts from the **first separation attempt**: < 1 day = short, 1–7 days = difficult, ≥ 7 days = prolonged. ICU mortality was 6 / 17 / 29 %. "Simple" is a Boles category. ([W11/D4](#W11-D4))

questions.stem: Comparing the Boles (2007) and WIND (2017) weaning classifications:
options: In Boles, "difficult weaning" means failing the first SBT and succeeding within 3 SBTs or 7 days.
The Boles classification starts counting from the first SBT.
WIND defines the start of weaning as the day of intubation.
WIND could classify only about half of ventilated patients.
questions.expl: It was **Boles** that could not classify about half of patients. WIND classified 99 %. WIND starts at the first separation attempt (an SBT or extubation without an SBT). ([W11/D4](#W11-D4))

questions.stem: During spontaneous breathing, a patient has RR 30/min and tidal volume 400 mL. What is the RSBI and its interpretation?
options: 75 breaths/min/L: below the 105 threshold, but this does not guarantee successful weaning
12 breaths/min/L: very low, guaranteed success
133 breaths/min/L: predicts weaning failure
75 breaths/min/L: guarantees successful extubation
0.013: uninterpretable
questions.expl: RSBI = f/V_T (in litres) = 30/0.4 = **75**. RSBI ≤ 105 is associated with success. It has high sensitivity and NPV but low specificity (0.64), so a low RSBI does not guarantee success. RSBI is an aid and does not replace the SBT. ([W11/D4](#W11-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding causes of weaning failure:
options: After a failed SBT, the SBT should be repeated after 1 hour.
In weaning-induced pulmonary oedema, the switch to spontaneous breathing increases venous return and LV afterload.
Metabolic alkalosis can contribute through hypoventilation.
Hypophosphataemia can contribute to weaning failure.
questions.expl: After a failed SBT, look for the cause, rest the patient on comfortable ventilation and repeat the SBT **after 24 h**. ([W11/D4](#W11-D4))

questions.stem: In high-risk patients, Hernández et al. (JAMA 2016) compared HFNO with NIV for 24 h after extubation. Which result is correct?
options: HFNO was inferior to NIV
HFNO was superior, with reintubation 4.9 % vs 12.2 %
HFNO was non-inferior (reintubation 22.8 % vs 19.1 %), with less postextubation respiratory failure (26.9 % vs 39.8 %)
NIV was well tolerated and never interrupted
NIV reduced ICU mortality
questions.expl: The non-inferiority margin was 10 %. NIV was often interrupted because of adverse effects (43 vs 0 %). Option B is Hernández I (low-risk patients, HFNO vs conventional O₂). ([W11/D5](#W11-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding postextubation stridor and the cuff leak test (ATS/ACCP 2017):
options: A cuff leak test is suggested for all ventilated patients before extubation.
In the guideline meta-analysis, corticosteroids did not reduce reintubation.
A universally validated cuff-leak volume threshold exists.
Risk factors include traumatic intubation, intubation > 6 days, a large tube and female sex.
questions.expl: Corticosteroids reduced reintubation (5.8 % vs 17.0 %). Thresholds varied between studies (e.g. 88–283 mL, or 10–24 % of V_T). The test is suggested **only in high-risk patients**, because blanket testing produces false positives and delays extubation. Reintubation after a failed cuff leak test is also a risk factor. ([W11/D5](#W11-D5))

questions.stem: A patient with a COPD exacerbation has dyspnoea VAS 7, RR 28/min, HR 110/min, SpO₂ 89 %, CRP 45 mg/L, PaCO₂ 52 mmHg and pH 7.31. Symptoms worsened over 5 days. According to the Rome proposal (adopted by GOLD), the exacerbation is:
options: Not an exacerbation
Mild
Severe
Moderate
Unclassifiable without knowing the place of treatment
questions.expl: Severity is graded by objective parameters, not by the place of treatment. "Severe" requires **hypercapnia and acidosis** (PaCO₂ > 45 mmHg and pH < 7.35) in addition. The definition requires worsening over ≤ 14 days. ([W12/D1](#W12-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding drug treatment of a COPD exacerbation:
options: Methylxanthines are recommended as an add-on bronchodilator.
In REDUCE, 5 days of prednisone 40 mg was non-inferior to 14 days.
IV corticosteroids are superior to oral corticosteroids even if the patient can swallow.
Antibiotics are indicated whenever NIV or invasive ventilation is required.
questions.expl: In REDUCE, re-exacerbation within 6 months was 35.9 vs 36.8 % at half the cumulative dose. Oral corticosteroids are equivalent to IV if the patient can swallow. Methylxanthines are not recommended (adverse effects). Antibiotics are typically given for 5 days. ([W12/D1](#W12-D1))

questions.stem: In which situation does ERS/ATS 2017 suggest **not** using NIV?
options: Facilitating weaning in a hypercapnic patient
COPD exacerbation with pH 7.30 and RR 26/min despite standard therapy
COPD exacerbation with pH 7.22 that would otherwise need intubation and is not deteriorating rapidly
COPD exacerbation with pH 7.33 and PaCO₂ 60 mmHg
COPD with PaCO₂ 55 mmHg and pH 7.38
questions.expl: For hypercapnia **without acidosis**, ERS/ATS suggests not using NIV (conditional, low certainty). B and D: strong recommendation, high certainty. C: a trial of NIV (strong, moderate). A: conditional, moderate. ([W12/D1](#W12-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding NIV in hypercapnic COPD exacerbation:
options: NIV is absolutely contraindicated when pH is < 7.25.
An arterial blood gas after 1–2 h without improvement in pH/PaCO₂ predicts NIV failure.
EPAP should be set at 0 cmH₂O because it worsens hyperinflation.
In meta-analyses, NIV reduced intubation but not mortality.
questions.expl: There is no lower pH limit below which NIV is absolutely contraindicated – the lower the pH, the higher the risk of failure, so monitor in the ICU with intubation immediately available. EPAP of ~4–6 cmH₂O offsets intrinsic PEEP and improves triggering. NIV reduced both mortality (RR 0.63) and intubation (RR 0.41). ([W12/D1](#W12-D1))

questions.stem: Which finding in a patient with acute severe asthma most strongly signals impending respiratory failure?
options: PEF 60 % of predicted
Loud widespread wheeze
PaCO₂ 4.0 kPa in a tachypnoeic patient
PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa (normal) in a tachypnoeic, exhausted patient
SpO₂ 96 % on room air
questions.expl: A normal or rising PaCO₂ in a tachypnoeic asthmatic is a warning sign of failure. Other life-threatening features include drowsiness, confusion, a "silent chest", PEF < 25–30 % and inability to speak. ([W12/D1](#W12-D1))

questions.stem: Regarding acute severe asthma (GINA 2025, ERS/ATS 2017):
options: Antibiotics should be given routinely.
In adults, oxygen is titrated to SpO₂ 98–100 %.
IV magnesium sulfate is not recommended in severe exacerbations.
ERS/ATS 2017 strongly recommends NIV in acute asthma.
questions.expl: Antibiotics are given only for clear infection. Adult SpO₂ target is 93–95 %. IV magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 min is used for severe exacerbations not responding to initial treatment. For asthma, ERS/ATS makes **no recommendation** on NIV (insufficient evidence). ([W12/D1](#W12-D1))

questions.stem: A ventilated COPD patient on volume control with constant flow has a peak pressure that rises from 30 to 45 cmH₂O, while plateau pressure stays at 22 cmH₂O. The most likely cause is:
options: Tension pneumothorax
Progression to ARDS
Bronchospasm, secretions or a kinked tube
Worsening dynamic hyperinflation
Right main bronchus intubation
questions.expl: A higher Ppeak with an unchanged Pplat means increased **resistance**. If both rise, compliance has fallen or hyperinflation has worsened (pneumothorax, endobronchial intubation, atelectasis, dynamic hyperinflation). ([W12/D1](#W12-D1), [W13/D2](#W13-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding the ATS/IDSA 2019 criteria for severe community-acquired pneumonia:
options: Respiratory rate ≥ 30/min is a minor criterion.
Septic shock requiring vasopressors is a major criterion.
PaO₂/FiO₂ ≤ 250 is a minor criterion.
Thrombocytopenia < 100 × 10⁹/L is a minor criterion.
questions.expl: Severe CAP = 1 major (vasopressor-requiring shock, invasive ventilation) or ≥ 3 minor criteria. ([W12/D2](#W12-D2))

questions.stem: A 55-year-old returns from a hotel stay with high fever, relative bradycardia, diarrhoea, hyponatraemia and raised CK. He is admitted to the ICU with severe CAP. The urinary Legionella antigen is negative. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Legionella is excluded if the sputum Gram stain is negative
Switch to β-lactam monotherapy, which covers Legionella
Repeat the urinary antigen; if negative, Legionella is excluded
The test detects only *L. pneumophila* serogroup 1, so send PCR/culture from the lower respiratory tract and keep atypical cover
A negative test excludes Legionella; stop the macrolide
questions.expl: Legionella, Mycoplasma and Chlamydophila are not covered by β-lactams. They need a macrolide or a fluoroquinolone (doxycycline is an alternative for Legionella). ([W12/D2](#W12-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding the CAPE COD trial (NEJM 2023):
options: Hydrocortisone reduced insulin requirements.
Hydrocortisone was given at 400 mg/day for 7 days.
Patients with septic shock on vasopressors at enrolment were included.
Patients with influenza were included and benefited most.
questions.expl: Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day for 4 days, then tapered (total 8 or 14 days). Septic shock on vasopressors and PCR-positive influenza were exclusion criteria. Hydrocortisone **increased** insulin requirements. 28-day mortality was 6.2 vs 11.9 %. ([W12/D2](#W12-D2))

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes the REMAP-CAP corticosteroid domain (ICM 2025)?
options: It used dexamethasone 6 mg/day for 10 days
It showed a significant reduction in 28-day mortality
It used methylprednisolone 40 mg/day for 7 days, with 60-day mortality 16 % vs 18 %
It used hydrocortisone 50 mg 6-hourly for 7 days and was stopped for futility
It excluded patients with influenza and shock
questions.expl: 90-day mortality was 15 vs 9.8 %. A large benefit is unlikely, but a small benefit or harm was not excluded. Allocation was unequal (536 vs 122), giving wide intervals. Option C describes ESCAPe. REMAP-CAP, unlike CAPE COD, included influenza and shock. ([W12/D2](#W12-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding empirical treatment of severe CAP:
options: Routine anaerobic cover is recommended for suspected aspiration pneumonia.
Oseltamivir may be given empirically during influenza season when PCR is unavailable.
ERS/ESICM 2023 suggests adding a macrolide rather than a fluoroquinolone to a β-lactam.
Procalcitonin should be used to decide whether to start antibiotics.
questions.expl: Aspiration is treated as standard CAP, without routine anaerobic cover (except abscess/empyema). Procalcitonin is used to **shorten** antibiotic duration, not to decide on starting antibiotics. ([W12/D2](#W12-D2))

questions.stem: A patient with pneumonia has a moderate parapneumonic effusion that is safely accessible on ultrasound. Pleural pH (blood gas analyser) is 7.30, pleural LDH is 1200 IU/L and he remains febrile. According to BTS 2023, the next step is:
options: Intrapleural streptokinase
Immediate VATS decortication
Consider a chest drain (small-bore, ≤ 14 F, ultrasound-guided)
Intrapleural tPA alone
No drainage; antibiotics alone because pH > 7.2
questions.expl: pH > 7.2 and < 7.4 is intermediate risk: measure LDH, and consider drainage when LDH > 900 IU/L with clinical features. Streptokinase (MIST1), tPA alone and DNase alone are not effective. tPA + DNase is used for a residual collection when the drain has stopped draining. ([W12/D5](#W12-D5))

questions.stem: Regarding peri-intubation risk in the ICU:
options: In INTUBE, cardiovascular instability (42.6 %) was the most frequent major peri-intubation event.
In INTUBE, first-pass success was only about 80 %.
A MACOCHA score ≥ 3 indicates low risk of difficult intubation.
In the MACOCHA score, Mallampati III–IV scores 1 point.
questions.expl: MACOCHA ≥ 3 = **high** risk (range 0–12); Mallampati III–IV scores 5 points. In INTUBE, a major event occurred in 45.2 %, severe hypoxaemia in 9.3 % and cardiac arrest in 3.1 %. ([W12/D3](#W12-D3))

questions.stem: An ICU resident (not an anaesthetist) is about to intubate a patient with obstructive sleep apnoea, Mallampati II, mouth opening 4 cm, normal neck mobility, GCS 6 and SpO₂ 75 %. What is the MACOCHA score?
options: 5 – high risk of difficult intubation
questions.expl: OSA 2 + coma (GCS < 8) 1 + severe hypoxaemia (SpO₂ < 80 %) 1 + non-anaesthetist 1 = **5**. Mallampati II, normal mouth opening and normal neck mobility score 0. ([W12/D3](#W12-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding RCTs of emergency airway management in critically ill adults:
options: In DEVICE, videolaryngoscopy reduced severe complications.
In BOUGIE, a bougie significantly increased first-pass success.
In DEVICE, videolaryngoscopy increased first-pass success (85.1 % vs 70.8 %).
In PreVent, bag-mask ventilation between induction and laryngoscopy significantly increased aspiration.
questions.expl: Severe complications in DEVICE were 21.4 vs 20.9 %. BOUGIE was negative (80.4 vs 83.0 %). PreVent halved severe hypoxaemia (10.9 vs 22.8 %) without a difference in aspiration (2.5 vs 4.0 %). ([W12/D3](#W12-D3))

questions.stem: The RSI trial (NEJM 2025) compared ketamine and etomidate for emergency intubation. Which finding is correct?
options: Ketamine reduced 28-day mortality
Mortality did not differ, and cardiovascular collapse was more frequent with ketamine (22.1 % vs 17.0 %)
Ketamine caused more severe hypoxaemia
Etomidate increased mortality through adrenal suppression
Cardiovascular collapse was similar in both groups
questions.expl: In-hospital 28-day mortality was 28.1 vs 29.1 % (NS). Concern about etomidate inhibiting 11β-hydroxylase did not translate into higher mortality. In patients at high risk of collapse, use a reduced dose of any induction agent. ([W12/D3](#W12-D3))

questions.stem: Regarding the "physiologically difficult airway" and drugs for intubation:
options: Succinylcholine is contraindicated in hyperkalaemia and in burns older than 24–72 h.
In a patient with DKA and severe metabolic acidosis, the high pre-intubation minute ventilation must be maintained after intubation.
Sugammadex reverses rocuronium but does not by itself solve a CICO situation caused by oedema or obstruction.
Propofol causes less hypotension than ketamine or etomidate.
questions.expl: Propofol lowers blood pressure **more** markedly. A sudden fall in minute ventilation in severe metabolic acidosis can cause a precipitous fall in pH and cardiac arrest. ([W12/D3](#W12-D3))

questions.stem: The SETPOINT2 trial (JAMA 2022) randomised ventilated patients with severe stroke to tracheostomy within 5 days or after day 10. What did it show?
options: Fewer days of sedation, with lower 30-day mortality
Better functional outcome with early tracheostomy
Higher procedural complication rates with late tracheostomy
No improvement in functional outcome (mRS 0–4 at 6 months: 43.5 % vs 47.1 %)
Lower 6-month mortality with early tracheostomy
questions.expl: 6-month mortality was 35.0 vs 29.6 % (NS). Like TracMan (no mortality difference), early tracheostomy did not improve hard outcomes. The decision should be individual, typically at ~10 days if extubation is not realistic. ([W12/D4](#W12-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding tracheostomy technique and complications:
options: An unstable cervical spine favours surgical tracheostomy.
Compared with surgical tracheostomy, percutaneous dilatational tracheostomy was associated with fewer stoma infections (Putensen 2014).
Cuff pressure should be kept at 20–30 cmH₂O.
A tracheo-innominate fistula typically presents within the first 24 hours.
questions.expl: A tracheo-innominate fistula typically presents in **weeks 1–4**, often after a "sentinel bleed". Displacement of an immature stoma is the most dangerous early complication. ([W12/D4](#W12-D4))

questions.stem: Two weeks after tracheostomy, a patient has a small bleed from the stoma, followed an hour later by brisk arterial bleeding around the tube. The immediate first manoeuvre is to:
options: Perform bronchoscopy to locate the source
Overinflate the tracheostomy cuff; if this fails, apply digital compression of the artery against the sternum through the stoma, and call a vascular/thoracic surgeon
Arrange CT angiography before any intervention
Remove the tracheostomy tube
Give nebulised tranexamic acid and observe
questions.expl: A sentinel bleed followed by massive haemorrhage suggests a tracheo-innominate fistula. Overinflate the cuff first. If that fails, use digital compression and orotracheal intubation with the cuff placed distally, and get immediate surgery. ([W12/D4](#W12-D4))

questions.stem: Regarding pneumothorax and bronchopleural fistula:
options: Absent lung sliding is specific for pneumothorax.
In a ventilated patient with bronchopleural fistula, chest-drain suction should be increased to reduce the air leak.
In Brown et al. (NEJM 2020), conservative management of moderate-to-large primary spontaneous pneumothorax was inferior for re-expansion at 8 weeks.
A lung point on ultrasound is highly specific for pneumothorax.
questions.expl: Absent lung sliding also occurs with endobronchial intubation, pleurodesis, apnoea and ARDS. In BPF, **minimise** suction (it increases flow through the fistula) and use the lowest V_T, Pplat and PEEP with a short inspiratory time. Brown: conservative management was non-inferior, and ~15 % needed intervention. ([W12/D5](#W12-D5))

questions.stem: A paralysed patient on VCV has V_T 450 mL, constant inspiratory flow 45 L/min, Ppeak 33 cmH₂O, Pplat 24 cmH₂O, set PEEP 6 cmH₂O and total PEEP 6 cmH₂O. What are the static compliance and airway resistance?
options: C_stat 16.7 mL/cmH₂O; R 9 cmH₂O/L/s
C_stat 25 mL/cmH₂O; R 12 cmH₂O/L/s
C_stat 25 mL/cmH₂O; R 9 cmH₂O/L/s
C_stat 18.75 mL/cmH₂O; R 12 cmH₂O/L/s
C_stat 16.7 mL/cmH₂O; R 12 cmH₂O/L/s
questions.expl: C_stat = V_T/(Pplat − PEEP_tot) = 450/(24 − 6) = **25 mL/cmH₂O**. Flow 45 L/min = 0.75 L/s, so R = (33 − 24)/0.75 = **12 cmH₂O/L/s**. 16.7 mL/cmH₂O is C_dyn = 450/(33 − 6). R = 9 is the error of not converting flow to L/s. ([W13/D2](#W13-D2))

questions.stem: Match the waveform description to its interpretation:
options: "Sawtooth" oscillations on the flow–time curve → secretions or water in the circuit.
A concave (downward-bowed) inspiratory pressure–time curve in VCV → alveolar overdistension.
A "scooped" expiratory limb of the flow–volume loop → small-airway obstruction.
In PCV, inspiratory flow that has not reached zero at the end of Ti → Ti shorter than ~3τ, so V_T is not fully delivered.
questions.expl: A concave pressure curve in VCV is **flow starvation** (patient demand exceeds set flow). Overdistension is shown by "beaking" (upper-end flattening) of the P–V loop. ([W13/D2](#W13-D2))

questions.stem: A passive patient has airway resistance 20 cmH₂O/L/s and compliance 50 mL/cmH₂O. Expiratory time is 2 s. What is the time constant, and roughly what fraction of V_T is exhaled?
options: τ 1000 s; negligible exhalation
questions.expl: τ = R × C = 20 × 0.05 L/cmH₂O = **1.0 s**. Te 2 s = 2τ, so ~86 % is exhaled (1τ ≈ 63 %, 3τ ≈ 95 %, 5τ ≈ 99 %). Option E is the error of not converting mL to L. ([W13/D2](#W13-D2))

questions.stem: Regarding oesophageal pressure (P_es) monitoring:
options: Chiumello (AJRCCM 2008) found that the ratio E_L/E_rs varied from 0.33 to 0.95.
